headline: Can People Predict the Future?
title: Feeling the Future: Experimental Evidence for Anomalous Retroactive Influences on Cognition and Affect
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Participants took a word-recall test. Only afterward did the computer randomly select words for them to practice. The author reported that participants had recalled more of the words they would later practice. Three independent attempts to reproduce the retroactive word-recall effect failed. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0033423

headline: Can your heartbeat anticipate whether a roulette bet wins?
title: Electrophysiology of Intuition: Pre-stimulus Responses in Group and Individual Participants Using a Roulette Paradigm
venue: Global Advances in Health and Medicine
note: The authors compared pre-outcome physiological signals across wins and losses in a computer roulette task. Grouping by the later result supplied the comparison used to argue for anticipation.

headline: Can your skin react to a disturbing picture before it appears?
title: Anomalous anticipatory response on randomized future conditions
note: The authors grouped skin-conductance recordings by which type of randomly selected image appeared after the recorded interval. They interpreted a pre-image difference as an anomalous anticipatory response.

headline: Can your heart respond to the next emotional image before you see it?
title: Electrophysiological Evidence of Intuition: Part 1. The Surprising Role of the Heart
venue: The Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine
note: The authors compared physiological recordings from before calm and emotional images. They interpreted differences in heart-rate dynamics as the heart receiving information about the future stimulus.

headline: Can a picture shown later make you avoid it before it appears?
title: Feeling the Future Again: Retroactive Avoidance of Negative Stimuli
note: Across seven experiments, the investigators recorded choices before stimuli were displayed and compared responses by the stimuli that followed. They interpreted selected differences as avoidance running backward in time.

headline: Can pooled physiological recordings reveal a reaction to an unpredictable event?
title: Predictive Physiological Anticipation Preceding Seemingly Unpredictable Stimuli: A Meta-Analysis
note: The authors pooled 26 studies and estimated an average difference in pre-stimulus recordings. The result depends on how recordings, stimulus categories and study estimates were combined.

headline: Can someone mentally send you a picture while your senses are deliberately muffled?
title: Does Psi Exist? Replicable Evidence for an Anomalous Process of Information Transfer
note: The authors summarized earlier results and analyzed a series of automated Ganzfeld trials using choices among potential targets. A subsequent meta-analysis of later studies did not recover an above-chance result (doi:10.1037/0033-2909.125.4.387).

headline: Does pooling Ganzfeld studies make picture guessing look better than chance?
title: Meta-analysis of free-response studies, 1992–2008: assessing the noise reduction model in parapsychology
note: The authors combined standardized results from sensory-reduction experiments and other target-guessing paradigms. They interpreted the pooled Ganzfeld result as support for anomalous information transfer.

headline: Can a person’s physiology reveal when someone remotely stares at them?
title: Distant intentionality and the feeling of being stared at: two meta-analyses
note: The authors pooled separate sets of studies on distant intention and remote staring, using physiological outcomes. They discussed how evidence changed with study quality and the number of independent studies.

headline: Do major world events make random-number generators stop looking random?
title: Correlations of Continuous Random Data with Major World Events
note: The authors combined measurements from a worldwide network of random-number generators around selected events and reported statistical departures from chance. The paper also examined alternative event windows and statistics around September 11.

headline: Can striking a power pose raise your testosterone?
title: Power Posing: Brief Nonverbal Displays Affect Neuroendocrine Levels and Risk Tolerance
note: Participants held expansive or contracted poses, gave saliva samples and decided whether to gamble. The authors linked expansive poses to higher testosterone, lower cortisol and a greater willingness to take risks. A larger replication did not recover the reported hormone changes or risk-taking effect. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797614553946

headline: Does holding hot coffee make a stranger seem warmer?
title: Experiencing Physical Warmth Promotes Interpersonal Warmth
note: On the way to the lab, participants briefly held someone else's hot or iced coffee. Those who held the hot cup later rated a person described in writing as having a warmer personality. Two high-powered replication attempts did not recover an interpersonal warmth effect. https://doi.org/10.1027/1864-9335/a000361

headline: Can the word “Florida” slow your walk down the hall?
title: Automaticity of Social Behavior: Direct Effects of Trait Construct and Stereotype Activation on Action
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Participants unscrambled sentences containing words associated with American stereotypes of older people, including “Florida.” The authors reported that people exposed to those words walked more slowly as they left the lab. A follow-up using automated timing did not reproduce the original walking-speed effect in its first experiment. In a second experiment the result depended on experimenter expectations. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0029081

headline: Can reading a few pages of literary fiction help you read someone's eyes?
title: Reading Literary Fiction Improves Theory of Mind
note: After reading short texts, participants took social cognition tests. One showed only a person's eyes and asked which word best described their mental state. The authors interpreted the literary fiction group's performance as an improvement in theory of mind. A replication attempt did not recover the single-passage effect on the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test. Later studies reported mixed evidence. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27642659/ https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-018-0408-2

headline: Are hurricanes deadlier when they have women's names?
title: Female Hurricanes Are Deadlier Than Male Hurricanes
note: The authors analyzed historical US hurricane records and asked participants to judge hypothetical storms with different names. They argued that more feminine names make people underestimate danger and take fewer precautions. Published critiques found that the hurricane mortality result depended on analysis choices. The original authors disputed those analyses. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25092347/ https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25228757/

headline: If you resist the cookies and eat radishes, will you give up sooner on a puzzle?
title: Ego Depletion: Is the Active Self a Limited Resource?
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Participants faced radishes and tempting treats. The authors reported that people allowed to eat only radishes gave up sooner on a subsequent unsolvable puzzle, and argued that exercising self-control had depleted a limited resource. A preregistered multilab test of the broader ego-depletion hypothesis using different tasks found an estimated effect near zero. https://doi.org/10.1177/1745691616652873

headline: Does a guilty conscience make a wet wipe more appealing?
title: Washing Away Your Sins: Threatened Morality and Physical Cleansing
note: The authors asked people to recall an unethical act and examined their interest in cleaning products. In another experiment, they compared how often people volunteered to help after either wiping their hands or leaving them alone. Three replication experiments failed to reproduce the effect of recalling an unethical act on preference for cleansing products. https://doi.org/10.1080/01973533.2013.856792

headline: Can literally sitting outside a box make you better at thinking outside the box?
title: Embodied metaphors and creative “acts”
note: The researchers compared scores on creativity tasks after participants enacted familiar metaphors for creative thinking, including completing a task physically outside a box.

headline: Does tensing your muscles firm up your willpower?
title: From Firm Muscles to Firm Willpower: Understanding the Role of Embodied Cognition in Self-Regulation
note: The authors manipulated muscle tension in several self-control tasks. They interpreted different choices and behaviors under certain goals and timing conditions as firmer willpower.

headline: Can a heavier clipboard make you think you will remember more?
title: Embodiment meets metamemory: weight as a cue for metacognitive judgments
venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
note: The authors varied physical weight and recorded predicted memory performance. They used changes in judgments of learning to argue that bodily cues can influence metacognition.

headline: Do people sway forward when imagining the future and backward when remembering the past?
title: Moving Through Time
note: The researchers compared small postural movements while participants thought about past and future events. They interpreted average sway differences as an embodiment of mental time travel.

headline: Can a longer line on an org chart make the same boss seem more powerful?
title: High in the hierarchy: How vertical location and judgments of leaders’ power are interrelated
venue: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
note: The authors varied the vertical separation on organizational charts and compared perceived leader power. They also tested whether described power influenced the way participants drew a chart.

headline: Can a bulky glove change which side feels like the “good” side?
title: When Left Is “Right”: Motor Fluency Shapes Abstract Concepts
note: The authors compared people with impaired hand movement after a stroke and tested a temporary movement manipulation using gloves. They interpreted side choices as changes in the spatial mapping of good and bad.

headline: Does a cosmetic injection change how fast people read angry or sad sentences?
title: Cosmetic use of botulinum toxin-A affects processing of emotional language
note: The study compared reading times before and after cosmetic treatment that reduced frowning. The authors interpreted selective changes in sentence-reading times as evidence for facial feedback during comprehension.

headline: Can bending your arm make a Chinese character seem more likable?
title: Rudimentary determinants of attitudes: II. Arm flexion and extension have differential effects on attitudes
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Participants evaluated unfamiliar characters while doing arm movements. Later rankings favored characters previously seen during arm flexion under some initial task instructions.

headline: Do people with slightly warmer mouths report feeling closer to others?
title: A Pilot Study Examining Physical and Social Warmth: Higher (Non-Febrile) Oral Temperature Is Associated with Greater Feelings of Social Connection
note: The authors compared oral temperature with reported social connection. They interpreted the association in this pilot sample as a possible link between physical and social warmth.

headline: Do a heat pack and a message from a loved one activate a shared brain response?
title: Shared neural mechanisms underlying social warmth and physical warmth
note: The authors compared fMRI responses during physical warmth and while reading messages from close others. They interpreted overlapping neural activity across the contrasts as a common mechanism.

headline: Does telling someone a book is important make them think it weighs more?
title: Weighty Matters: Importance Literally Feels Heavy
note: Participants received different information about a book’s importance before judging its weight. The reported result concerns estimates of the book’s physical weight after the description.

headline: Does a book’s weight affect how important it seems only if you know what it is about?
title: To judge a book by its weight you need to know its content: Knowledge moderates the use of embodied cues
note: The authors varied book weight and examined readers’ knowledge of titles or plots. The studies attributed differences in importance judgments to weight specifically when participants knew the content.

headline: Does a heavy book have to stay in your hands to feel more important?
title: Situated Embodiment: When Physical Weight Does and Does Not Inform Judgments of Importance
note: The authors varied whether people still held a book while rating it and whether the purpose was framed as assessing importance or graphics. The role of the physical cue was estimated across these contexts.

headline: Does noticing a clipboard’s weight change whether it influences judgments of importance?
title: The Role of Conscious Attention in How Weight Serves as an Embodiment of Importance
note: The experiments varied weight and whether participants paid attention to their bodily experience. The authors used the pattern across conditions to argue for a role of conscious attention.

headline: Does actively touching someone else make their skin feel softer than your own?
title: Active Interpersonal Touch Gives Rise to the Social Softness Illusion
note: The authors contrasted ratings of self and other touch under different stroking conditions. They interpreted the softness ratings as a social perception effect specific to certain forms of touch.

headline: Does washing your hands change your moral ratings and pupil responses?
title: Hand Washing Induces a Clean Slate Effect in Moral Judgments: A Pupillometry and Eye-Tracking Study
note: The study compared moral judgments and eye measures after washing hands or a control activity. The authors interpreted condition differences as evidence for a clean-slate effect.

headline: Can watching someone wash their hands change how guilty you feel?
title: Washing the guilt away: effects of personal versus vicarious cleansing on guilty feelings and prosocial behavior
note: The authors tested personal and observed cleansing after eliciting guilt. They used differences in guilt ratings and later helping as evidence about whether another person’s washing could have similar effects.

headline: Can thinking about being physically clean make a stressful event seem less stressful?
title: Cognitions about bodily purity attenuate stress perception
note: The authors manipulated or evoked ideas of bodily cleanliness and compared appraisals of stress. They interpreted the reported reactions through the metaphor of a clean slate.

headline: Do left-handers put “good” on the left and right-handers put it on the right?
title: Embodiment of abstract concepts: good and bad in right- and left-handers
note: The authors compared spatial assignments of positively and negatively described items by handedness. They interpreted the association as evidence that hand fluency shapes abstract concepts of good and bad.

headline: Can imagining movement switch which side people treat as better?
title: Motor Imagery Shapes Abstract Concepts
note: The study compared judgments after participants imagined actions involving different patterns of hand fluency. The outcome was a left-versus-right choice in an evaluation task.

headline: Can watching someone struggle with one hand change which side looks good to you?
title: Observed actions affect body-specific associations between space and valence
note: The authors varied which hand a person in a demonstration used more fluently. They interpreted observers’ later left-right choices as evidence that watching another person’s actions can alter spatial evaluations.

headline: Can cultural customs override which side left-handers call good?
title: Can culture influence body-specific associations between space and valence?
note: The authors compared left-right evaluations and handedness in populations with different conventions about hand use. They assessed how choices varied with both physical and cultural experience.

headline: Can success or failure with one hand change which side feels good?
title: When “good” is not always right: effect of the consequences of motor action on valence-space associations
note: The authors manipulated the consequences of hand actions and measured later choices connecting left or right space to positive or negative properties.

headline: Does placing a positive word higher on a screen make its meaning easier to classify?
title: Why the Sunny Side Is Up: Associations Between Affect and Vertical Position
note: The authors compared speed of classifying positive and negative words shown at different heights. They interpreted the response-time interactions as evidence for spatial organization of affect.

headline: Can sitting on a train change which day “next Wednesday’s meeting was moved forward” means?
title: The roles of body and mind in abstract thought
note: The researchers measured responses to ambiguous scheduling language under different movement and imagery contexts, including travel. They interpreted response patterns as effects of spatial experience on thinking about time.

headline: Does watching an object travel farther make its duration seem longer?
title: Time in the mind: using space to think about time
note: The authors varied distance and duration in computerized displays. They compared judgments in both directions and used the asymmetric interference to argue that spatial experience structures judgments of time.

headline: Do approach-like and avoidance-like movements change what people remember about emotional words?
title: Approach and avoidance: the influence of proprioceptive and exteroceptive cues on encoding of affective information
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors varied movement- and context-based cues and compared subsequent memory for emotionally valenced material. The measured outcomes were recall or recognition in the experiments.

headline: Does nodding your head make you more persuaded by a good argument and less by a bad one?
title: Overt head movements and persuasion: a self-validation analysis
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors compared nodding and head-shaking while participants received stronger or weaker arguments. They attributed the interaction to confidence in thoughts about the message.

headline: Does sitting up straight make you believe your own self-evaluation more?
title: Body posture effects on self-evaluation: A self-validation approach
note: Participants listed favorable or unfavorable traits with upright or slouched backs. The authors used the interaction on subsequent self-ratings to infer that posture changes confidence in one’s own thoughts.

headline: Can sitting upright change how people speak and feel during a stressful task?
title: Do slumped and upright postures affect stress responses? A randomized trial
note: The authors assigned postures before a stress task and compared mood, words used in speech and physiological measures. The measures were collected under the imposed postures and the laboratory stressor.

headline: Does moving your arms in smooth curves make your ideas more creative?
title: Fluid movement and creativity
note: The authors assigned participants to make fluid versus less fluid movements, then compared performance on creativity tasks. They used statistical differences in those scores to infer an effect of movement fluidity.

headline: Does walking produce more creative ideas than sitting?
title: Give your ideas some legs: the positive effect of walking on creative thinking
venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
note: The experiments compared walking and sitting across divergent and convergent thinking tests. The advantage was mainly on divergent tasks that scored the generation of alternative ideas.

headline: Can changing how you walk change which negative words you remember?
title: How we walk affects what we remember: gait modifications through biofeedback change negative affective memory bias
venue: Journal of Behavior Therapy and Experimental Psychiatry
note: The authors used feedback to change gait and compared memory for positive and negative words. They interpreted the difference in recall as a shift in emotional memory bias.

headline: Does reading about moving an object toward you make it easier to respond in that direction?
title: Grounding language in action
note: The authors compared response times for sentence judgments with movements more or less compatible with the described action. A later preregistered replication of one version found no reliable effect across 18 labs (doi:10.3758/s13423-021-01927-8).

headline: Can changing when a person moves reverse the action effect of a sentence?
title: Temporal Dynamics of the Action–Sentence Compatibility Effect
note: The researchers varied motor-response timing relative to reading a sentence and compared compatibility effects. They interpreted the timing dependence as evidence about the relationship between language and motor action.

headline: Does understanding an abstract sentence change motor-system activity?
title: Processing Abstract Language Modulates Motor System Activity
note: The paper compared behavioral and motor-system measurements during sentences about concrete and abstract transfers. The authors interpreted changes across conditions as motor involvement in comprehension.

headline: Does reading about turning something affect how fast you turn a knob?
title: Seeing, acting, understanding: motor resonance in language comprehension
note: The authors compared manual rotation performance while people read about actions. They attributed directional compatibility at parts of a sentence to motor resonance during comprehension.

headline: Does reducing facial movement change how strongly people say they feel an emotion?
title: The effects of BOTOX injections on emotional experience
note: The study compared emotional responses to video clips before and after different cosmetic treatments. Its results concern reported intensity under the particular clips and comparison groups.

headline: Can changing facial feedback alter how accurately people recognize emotions in photos?
title: Embodied Emotion Perception
note: The studies compared emotion-recognition scores under different facial-feedback conditions. The authors used task accuracy to infer a role for facial feedback in reading someone else’s emotions.

headline: Does making a smile with a pencil change how pleasant an image feels?
title: Duchenne smile, emotional experience, and autonomic reactivity: a test of the facial feedback hypothesis
note: The researchers arranged facial configurations and compared reported feelings and physiological responses. They treated changes in ratings under particular configurations as evidence for facial feedback.

headline: Does a target look closer when you plan to reach it with a tool?
title: Tool use affects perceived distance, but only when you intend to use it
venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
note: The authors varied whether people could or intended to reach a target with a tool, then compared distance judgments. They interpreted an intention-dependent difference as a change in perceived distance.

headline: Do you remember an object’s height differently depending on how high your eyes were?
title: Memory for target height is scaled to observer height
note: The authors varied the observer’s position and compared later target-height estimates. They interpreted the reconstruction pattern as a memory representation scaled to the body.

headline: Can making walking feel harder change how far away a target looks?
title: The role of effort in perceiving distance
note: The studies compared distance judgments after manipulating anticipated walking effort. The authors used differences across conditions to argue that effort contributes to perceived distance.

headline: Can physical pain make someone feel rejected while others are including them?
title: When do socially accepted people feel ostracized? Physical pain triggers social pain
note: The researchers compared reports of exclusion across physical conditions during an otherwise inclusive social interaction. They interpreted higher subjective rejection ratings as an effect of physical pain on social pain.

headline: Does tolerance for physical pain track how much rejection hurts?
title: An experimental study of shared sensitivity to physical pain and social rejection
note: The authors compared measures of physical pain sensitivity with self-reported social distress and tested how social rejection affected physical pain measures.

headline: Can being left out make physical pain feel either sharper or duller?
title: Social exclusion and pain sensitivity: why exclusion sometimes hurts and sometimes numbs
note: The authors compared physical pain responses under different experiences of exclusion and interpretations of the event. They used the differences to explain opposite patterns of pain sensitivity.

headline: Are immoral words faster to classify when they are printed in black?
title: The color of sin: white and black are perceptual symbols of moral purity and pollution
note: The authors compared word-classification responses and judgments involving black and white stimuli. They interpreted color-sensitive moral judgments and other task differences as a link between morality and perceptual symbols.

headline: Does brighter light make moral ideas more salient?
title: In broad daylight, we trust in God! Brightness, the salience of morality, and ethical behavior
note: The researchers compared ethical judgments and behavior under different brightness conditions. They interpreted the observed differences through the metaphor linking light and goodness.

headline: Can pulling rather than pushing make people eat more?
title: The influence of approach and avoidance motor actions on food intake
note: The experiments varied arm actions associated with approach or avoidance and compared how much food participants ate, interpreting the differences as motivational feedback.

headline: Is God easier to recognize when the word appears higher on a screen?
title: What's “up” with God? Vertical space as a representation of the divine
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The experiments used word location and related tasks to test whether people represent God and the Devil in upper and lower space.

headline: Can taking a step backward improve cognitive control?
title: Body locomotion as regulatory process: Stepping backward enhances cognitive control
note: The authors compared performance on a Stroop task after steps in different directions and interpreted the backward-step advantage as heightened cognitive control.

headline: Does moving backward bring more memories back?
title: It takes me back: The mnemonic time-travel effect
note: The experiments compared actual, imagined and visually simulated movement directions before testing recall. A preregistered close replication of Experiment 4 did not reproduce the reported memory benefit (https://doi.org/10.1027/1618-3169/a000461).

headline: Can a virtual Einstein body improve planning scores?
title: Virtually Being Einstein Results in an Improvement in Cognitive Task Performance and a Decrease in Age Bias
note: Participants used a virtual Einstein or ordinary adult body. The planning result depended on participants’ self-esteem, and age bias was assessed with an implicit task.

headline: Can you give yourself better advice from Freud’s body?
title: Conversations between self and self as Sigmund Freud—A virtual body ownership paradigm for self counselling
note: Participants alternated between virtual bodies to discuss their own problems. The paper compared mood after self-dialogue with a Freud avatar and with a duplicate of the participant’s avatar.

headline: Does spending time in a virtual child body make adults judge objects as larger?
title: Illusory ownership of a virtual child body causes overestimation of object sizes and implicit attitude changes
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Adults estimated object size while embodied as a child or an equally short adult. The paper also reported changes in a child-versus-adult implicit association task.

headline: Does rough texture make an ambiguous conversation sound more hostile?
title: Rough primes and rough conversations: evidence for a modality-specific basis to mental metaphors
note: After rough or smooth touch, participants evaluated a social interaction. The authors connected the ratings and fMRI contrasts to a sensory basis for the metaphor of rough interactions.

headline: Can holding a heavier box change how you tackle a logic problem?
title: Embodied Information in Cognitive Tasks: Haptic Weight Sensations Affect Task Performance and Processing Style
note: The study varied experienced weight during cognitive tasks and interpreted the differences across task types as evidence of a shift in processing style.

headline: Can squeezing a soft ball change how feminine a stranger seems?
title: The effects of haptic experience on interpersonal perception and self-perception
venue: The Japanese Journal of Experimental Social Psychology
note: Twenty-one women squeezed a soft or hard ball. The authors reported differences in ratings of an unfamiliar woman and in some self-ratings.

headline: Does warmer body temperature track how connected you feel that day?
title: Physical and social warmth: Warmer daily body temperature is associated with greater feelings of social connection
note: The researchers compared repeated temperature readings with social connection ratings and interpreted the association as a daily-life link between physical and social warmth.

headline: Can holding warmth change how the brain responds to loved ones?
title: A body-to-mind perspective on social connection: Physical warmth potentiates brain activity to close others and subsequent feelings of social connection
note: The experiments compared responses to close others under physical warmth and control conditions. The paper related the fMRI contrasts to subsequent reports of social connection.

headline: Can tasting something sweet make people offer a stranger more money?
title: Experiencing sweet taste is associated with an increase in prosocial behavior
note: The authors compared allocations in a dictator game after sweet, salty and neutral tastes. The reported generosity difference was for sweet versus salty.

headline: Can a sweet taste make strangers seem more attractive?
title: Sweet taste experience improves prosocial intentions and attractiveness ratings
note: The experiments compared attractiveness ratings and intentions to help after different taste experiences.

headline: Can the smell of a man’s sweat change a woman’s answer to a moral dilemma?
title: Women smelling men's masked body odors show enhanced harm aversion in moral dilemmas
note: The researchers compared moral dilemma responses across masked body-odor and control conditions and interpreted a subgroup difference as heightened harm aversion.

headline: Can ambient scents shift how much you pay or how you gamble?
title: The effect of olfactory sensory cues on willingness to pay and choice under risk
venue: Journal of Behavioral and Experimental Economics
note: The experiment varied ambient scent and measured willingness to pay and choices under risk. The claims come from comparisons of those elicited decisions.

headline: Do stronger or less pleasant smells change moral choices?
title: Relative Contribution of Odour Intensity and Valence to Moral Decisions
note: The authors varied odor intensity and pleasantness and examined responses to moral dilemmas.

headline: Can slouching make people with depression remember more negative words?
title: Sitting posture makes a difference—embodiment effects on depressive memory bias
note: Participants with depression sat upright or slumped before a recall task. The reported memory bias came from comparative recall of positive and negative words.

headline: Can holding your arm bent favor creative insight?
title: The effects of approach and avoidance motor actions on the elements of creative insight
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Participants held their arms in flexion or extension while performing reasoning tasks. The authors interpreted differences across task types as changes in how people process information.

headline: Can performing an approach action put people in a more creative mode?
title: The Influence of Approach and Avoidance Motor Actions on Creative Cognition
note: The authors manipulated motor actions associated with approach or avoidance and compared participants’ scores on creative generation tasks.

headline: Can flexing your arm bring more pleasant memories to mind?
title: Motor actions in retrieval of valenced information: a motor congruence effect
note: The researchers compared retrieval of positive and negative information during different arm actions and interpreted the pattern as motor congruence.

headline: Do the memory effects of pulling and pushing depend on how you move?
title: Motor actions in retrieval of valenced information: II. Boundary conditions for motor congruence effects
note: The authors varied movement conditions and tested whether the match between action and emotional content changed retrieval.

headline: Could nodding while listening make a persuasive message more convincing?
title: The role of overt head movement and attention in persuasion
note: The study manipulated head movements during a persuasive message and examined how attention changed the resulting attitude ratings.

headline: Does nodding your head work like approaching, while shaking it works like retreating?
title: Nodding and shaking of the head as simulated approach and avoidance responses
note: The authors compared responses to affective cues during nodding and shaking and interpreted the pattern in terms of approach and avoidance.

headline: Can an environment that makes you spread out change how many risks you take?
title: Manipulating posture implicitly through environmental constraints influences mood and risk-taking behaviour
note: The experiment used environmental constraints to induce expansive or contractive posture. The reported risk-taking effect was measured with a computerized balloon task.

headline: Can standing tall help you put a more positive spin on something unpleasant?
title: Stand tall, think bright: How embodied experience unlocks the power of posture in emotion regulation
note: The study manipulated posture and assessed emotional responding during regulation. The authors interpreted the task results as an effect of posture on emotion regulation.

headline: Can biting a pen make it harder to recognize some facial expressions?
title: Face to face: blocking facial mimicry can selectively impair recognition of emotional expressions
note: The authors inhibited facial movements and compared recognition of different expressions. Effects differed by expression and interference condition.

headline: Can Botox change when you notice someone’s expression becoming emotional?
title: The effects of Botulinum toxin on the detection of gradual changes in facial emotion
note: Participants judged gradual expression changes in a comparison involving botulinum toxin. The authors examined whether facial feedback contributes to detecting those changes.

headline: Does keeping time together make pairs cooperate better afterward?
title: The rhythm of joint action: Synchrony promotes cooperative ability
note: The study manipulated coordinated movement before a joint task. The authors used performance on the later task to infer a cooperative benefit.

headline: Can moving in sync make people more willing to follow an aggressive instruction?
title: Synchronous activity boosts compliance with requests to aggress
note: The authors compared compliance with an experimenter’s aggressive request after synchronous or control activity.

headline: Does moving in step increase obedience to a harmful request?
title: Synchrony and destructive obedience
note: The experiment linked coordinated movement to compliance with an experimenter's destructive instruction.

headline: Does rowing in sync raise pain tolerance?
title: Rowers’ high: behavioural synchrony is correlated with elevated pain thresholds
note: The researchers compared pain thresholds after group and solo rowing. They interpreted the difference as indirect evidence about endorphin activity.

headline: Does music make synchronized movement better at getting people to help?
title: Music strengthens prosocial effects of interpersonal synchronization – If you move in time with the beat
note: The study compared movement timing conditions and examined whether music changed subsequent helping behavior.

headline: Can borrowing a different virtual body change scores on a racial bias test?
title: Experiencing ownership over a dark-skinned body reduces implicit racial bias
note: Participants experienced differently presented virtual bodies. The outcome was a change on an implicit association test after the virtual experience.

headline: Can an illusory hand change implicit attitudes toward an outgroup?
title: Change my body, change my mind: the effects of illusory ownership of an outgroup hand on implicit attitudes toward that outgroup
note: The researchers induced rubber-hand ownership under different conditions and examined the relationship between reported ownership and change on an implicit attitude test.

headline: Can time in a virtual body still shift implicit racial bias a week later?
title: Virtual Embodiment of White People in a Black Virtual Body Leads to a Sustained Reduction in Their Implicit Racial Bias
note: The study used differently presented avatars and followed up with an implicit association test. Its claim concerns changes on that test.

headline: Can watching your virtual body talk make you think you said the words?
title: Body ownership causes illusory self-attribution of speaking and influences subsequent real speaking
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Participants experienced ownership of a speaking avatar. The authors measured self-attribution of speech and changes in subsequent vocal pitch.

headline: Can swapping bodies with a friend change how you rate your own personality?
title: Perception of Our Own Body Influences Self-Concept and Self-Incoherence Impairs Episodic Memory
note: In a body-swap illusion with a friend, participants’ self-ratings shifted toward how they rated the friend. The paper linked the extent of self-incoherence with memory performance.

headline: Does counting your heartbeat reveal who will make better gut decisions?
title: Listening to Your Heart: How Interoception Shapes Emotion Experience and Intuitive Decision Making
note: The authors compared heartbeat-perception accuracy with emotional experience and a gambling task. They interpreted the pattern as evidence that access to bodily signals contributes to intuitive decisions.

headline: Can swishing glucose and spitting it out improve self-control?
title: The gargle effect: rinsing the mouth with glucose enhances self-control
note: The experiment compared glucose and control mouth rinses on a later self-control task. The authors attributed the result to signaling rather than absorbed glucose.

headline: Does tasting glucose affect patience differently from swallowing it?
title: Resource forecasting: Differential effects of glucose taste and ingestion on delay discounting and self-control
note: The study separated tasting from ingesting glucose and compared choices between earlier and later rewards.

headline: Does a sugary drink cool a hot temper in the lab?
title: Sweetened blood cools hot tempers: physiological self-control and aggression
note: One experiment compared sweetened drinks and operationalized aggression through a laboratory task. The authors interpreted the result in terms of glucose and self-control.

headline: Can glucose shift how much people favor money now over money later?
title: Glucose-specific signaling effects on delay discounting in intertemporal choice
note: The researchers compared carbohydrate conditions and estimated delay discounting from choices between sooner and later rewards.

headline: Does enduring pain together make strangers cooperate?
title: Pain as social glue: shared pain increases cooperation
note: Participants completed painful or nonpainful activities in groups before reporting social ties or playing a cooperation game.

headline: Do better putters see a bigger hole?
title: Putting to a bigger hole: Golf performance relates to perceived size
note: Golfers selected a circle matching their impression of hole size. The authors interpreted the link between putting performance and selected circle size as an effect on perception.

headline: Can expecting pain make the source look closer?
title: The close proximity of threat: altered distance perception in the anticipation of pain
note: Participants judged the distance of stimuli associated with pain. The authors interpreted distance estimates as evidence that anticipated pain changes spatial perception.

headline: Do threatening stimuli seem closer than equally distant harmless ones?
title: Affective Signals of Threat Increase Perceived Proximity
note: The researchers compared distance estimates for threatening and less threatening stimuli and inferred that threat affects perceived proximity.

headline: Does revealing a secret make a hill look less steep?
title: Relieving the Burdens of Secrecy: Revealing Secrets Influences Judgments of Hill Slant and Distance
note: The studies compared hill and distance estimates after reflecting on secrets with different disclosure conditions. The authors interpreted the estimates as relief of a physical burden.

headline: Does being hungry change how harshly people judge ethical violations?
title: The effect of hunger and satiety in the judgment of ethical violations
note: The researchers compared judgments of ethical violations in hungry and satiated conditions, treating ratings as a measure of ethical judgment.

headline: Does turning your head left make you say smaller random numbers?
title: Head turns bias the brain's internal random generator
note: Participants generated numbers while turning their heads. The authors connected differences between successive numbers to a spatial representation of number magnitude.

headline: Can a spatial prompt change whether you move a meeting to Monday or Friday?
title: Metaphoric structuring: understanding time through spatial metaphors
note: The study used spatial priming and ambiguous temporal questions. The authors interpreted shifts in the answers as evidence that people use spatial structures to reason about time.

headline: Can moving marbles upward bring happier memories to mind?
title: Motor action and emotional memory
note: Participants moved marbles up or down while recalling personal experiences. The authors related the timing and valence of recollections to the direction of the movement.

headline: Can making a number sign with your fingers change how fast you understand a numeral?
title: Finger posing primes number comprehension
note: Participants adopted finger configurations before processing numbers. The authors interpreted congruency effects as evidence that finger postures contribute to number comprehension.

headline: Do finger poses for numbers change how the two sides of the brain process numerals?
title: The influence of self-experienced iconic finger-postures on numerical processing: Hemispheric asymmetries in semantic integration
note: The authors compared processing of numerals after congruent or incongruent finger poses and interpreted differences across presentation sides in terms of hemispheric asymmetry.

headline: Do better football kickers see a bigger goal?
title: Kicking to bigger uprights: field goal kicking performance influences perceived size
note: The researchers related field-goal performance to estimates of the goal’s size. They interpreted the estimates as a difference in perception.

headline: Can being told you missed a target make a small target seem larger?
title: Action feedback affects the perception of action-related objects beyond actual action success
note: The authors manipulated performance feedback independently of actual stylus accuracy. Failure feedback shifted estimates of small and large targets in opposite directions.

headline: Does a hand on your shoulder make you take bigger financial risks?
title: Physical Contact and Financial Risk Taking
note: The authors compared choices after brief touch and control conditions. They proposed that feelings of security accounted for some of the differences in financial risk-taking.

headline: Can a slow stroke with a brush ease the feeling of being excluded?
title: The soothing function of touch: affective touch reduces feelings of social exclusion
note: Participants experienced exclusion in a virtual ball-toss game and received slow or fast brush strokes. The outcome was self-reported social exclusion.

headline: Can a remotely delivered touch make someone more willing to help?
title: The Virtual Midas Touch: Helping Behavior After a Mediated Social Touch
note: The study delivered mediated touch through a device and compared behavior on a subsequent request for help.

headline: Does flying like Superman in virtual reality make people help in the lab afterward?
title: Virtual Superheroes: Using Superpowers in Virtual Reality to Encourage Prosocial Behavior
note: Participants moved through a virtual city by flying or riding in a helicopter. Helping was assessed afterward when an experimenter dropped objects.

headline: Does inhabiting a powerful avatar make people feel invulnerable?
title: Embodying the avatar of an omnipotent agent modulates the perception of one's own abilities and enhances feelings of invulnerability
note: The researchers compared virtual-avatar conditions and measured judgments about participants’ own abilities and invulnerability.

headline: Does marching in step make an opponent look smaller?
title: Marching into battle: synchronized walking diminishes the conceptualized formidability of an antagonist in men
note: Men walked in or out of step with another person and estimated an apparent antagonist’s physical size and muscularity.

headline: Can tapping in sync make you like the experimenter more?
title: It's All in the Timing: Interpersonal Synchrony Increases Affiliation
note: Participants tapped in a task with different timing conditions. The authors compared later affiliation ratings.

headline: Does making music together make four-year-olds more helpful afterward?
title: Joint music making promotes prosocial behavior in 4-year-old children
note: Children participated in joint music or a comparison activity. The authors measured helping and cooperation afterward.

headline: If someone copies your movements, are you more likely to help a different person?
title: The spillover effect of mimicry: Being mimicked by one person increases prosocial behavior toward another person
note: The authors manipulated whether one person mimicked a participant and measured prosocial behavior toward another person.

headline: Can posing a smile change which faces you remember?
title: Effects of posed smiling on memory for happy and sad facial expressions
note: The researchers varied participants’ facial configurations while they viewed emotional faces and assessed later recognition.

headline: Do other people’s faces and movements look happier when you smile?
title: Your Face and Moves Seem Happier When I Smile: Facial Action Influences the Perception of Emotional Faces and Biological Motion Stimuli
note: The experiments manipulated facial action and compared emotion judgments for faces and displays of biological motion.

headline: Can changing your own expression make another person's emotion look more intense?
title: Facial Feedback Affects Perceived Intensity but Not Quality of Emotional Expressions
note: Participants judged emotional expressions under different facial feedback conditions. The reported differences concerned intensity ratings.

headline: Does seeing a face at a particular point in your heartbeat make you more open to someone else’s opinion?
title: Social interoception: Perceiving events during cardiac afferent activity makes people more suggestible to other people's influence
note: Participants saw faces during systole or diastole and rated trustworthiness. The study examined how cardiac timing affected the weight they gave to other people’s judgments.

headline: Does an empty stomach make harming someone seem more or less acceptable?
title: Hunger Bias or Gut Instinct? Responses to Judgments of Harm Depending on Visceral State Versus Intuitive Decision-Making
note: The researchers examined harm judgments in relation to hunger, thirst and reliance on intuitive decision-making. The paper tested individual differences and experimental conditions.

headline: Can an ice-water task make a guilty memory feel less troubling?
title: Cleansing the Soul by Hurting the Flesh: The Guilt-Reducing Effect of Pain
note: Participants recalled an event and immersed a hand in ice water or a comparison condition. The inference about expiating guilt used self-reported guilt after the task.

headline: Can practicing a powerful pose make you less anxious or better at noticing your heartbeat?
title: Using bodily postures to reduce anxiety and improve interoception: A comparison between powerful and neutral poses
note: The authors compared powerful with neutral poses using anxiety measures and a heartbeat-perception task. The comparison tests a narrower claim than changes in everyday bodily awareness.

headline: Does sitting upright change mood and working-memory scores?
title: Embodiment: I sat, I felt, I performed – Posture effects on mood and cognitive performance
note: The researchers manipulated sitting posture and used mood ratings and cognitive tasks to test for downstream differences.

headline: Can swinging your arms help you solve a puzzle without realizing why?
title: Swinging into thought: Directed movement guides insight in problem solving
note: Participants performed directed movements during a two-string insight puzzle. The authors compared solution rates under movements with different relationships to the solution.

headline: Can smelling tears change how aggressively men play a game?
title: A chemical signal in human female tears lowers aggression in males
note: The experiments compared exposure to women's emotional tears with control exposure. The aggression claim refers to choices in a laboratory game.

headline: Are people named Dennis more likely to become dentists?
title: Why Susie sells seashells by the seashore: implicit egotism and major life decisions
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Before trivia night, should you spend a few minutes thinking about a professor?
title: The Relation Between Perception and Behavior, or How to Win a Game of Trivial Pursuit
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The original study reported better general-knowledge scores after participants thought about professors than after they thought about soccer hooligans. A registered multilab replication did not recover the predicted priming effect. https://doi.org/10.1177/1745691618755704

headline: Can a glimpse of Rodin's Thinker shake your faith?
title: Analytic Thinking Promotes Religious Disbelief
note: In one experiment, participants saw photographs of The Thinker or a discus thrower before rating their religious beliefs. The authors interpreted a difference in ratings as evidence that prompting analytical thinking weakens belief. A direct replication of the Thinker experiment found no decrease in reported religious belief. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0172636

headline: Does praying for your partner make you less likely to cheat on them?
title: Faith and unfaithfulness: can praying for your partner reduce infidelity?
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The paper used several measures of behavior outside a relationship, including reports collected over six weeks. The authors interpreted differences associated with partner-focused prayer as reduced infidelity.

headline: Can religious words refill an exhausted supply of self-control?
title: Religion replenishes self-control
note: The authors used religious primes before tasks such as persistence and delaying gratification. They interpreted differences in task performance as replenishing self-control.

headline: Does praying for someone make you more willing to forgive them?
title: Motivating Change in Relationships: Can Prayer Increase Forgiveness?
note: The authors assigned participants to pray for a partner or friend or to a comparison activity. They reported greater self-rated forgiveness and modeled selfless concern as part of the explanation.

headline: Does praying for someone who made you angry change how aggressively you respond?
title: “Pray for Those Who Mistreat You”: Effects of Prayer on Anger and Aggression
note: After provoking participants, the authors compared prayer with thinking about a target. They reported differences in anger, a laboratory aggression measure, and reactions to another provocation across three experiments.

headline: Can an assigned prayer routine change how much alcohol people say they drink?
title: Invocations and intoxication: does prayer decrease alcohol consumption?
note: The paper combined survey associations with prayer assignments and reported less self-reported alcohol consumption in the prayer conditions. The measured outcome was reported drinking.

headline: Does praying for a partner change how cooperative people say they would be?
title: Shifting toward cooperative tendencies and forgiveness: How partner-focused prayer transforms motivation
note: The researchers compared partner-focused prayer with other activities and measured cooperation-related tendencies and forgiveness. They interpreted changes on those measures as changes in relationship motivation.

headline: Do religious words make people take more charity pamphlets?
title: Nonconscious influences of religion on prosociality: a priming study
note: The authors compared accessibility of prosocial concepts and willingness to take charity pamphlets after exposure to religious or comparison words. They used the pamphlet behavior as a measure of prosociality.

headline: Do religious words make people cheat less in a lab task?
title: Honesty: One Effect of Primed Religious Representations
venue: The International Journal for the Psychology of Religion
note: The authors primed religious representations and compared cheating on an experimental task. They interpreted the task result as an automatic effect on honesty.

headline: Does unscrambling Christian words change how people split money or cooperate?
title: Implicit influences of Christian religious representations on dictator and prisoner's dilemma game decisions
note: The study compared allocations and cooperation decisions after a scrambled-sentence exercise. The authors interpreted the game choices as an effect of implicitly activated religious concepts.

headline: Does seeing the word “God” make people help outsiders while “religion” makes them help insiders?
title: Different Effects of Religion and God on Prosociality With the Ingroup and Outgroup
note: The authors varied the prime and whether the recipient belonged to an in-group. They interpreted the resulting choices as different effects of God and institutional religion. A later follow-up obtained no reliable distinction in its intergroup-attitude outcomes (doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0147178).

headline: Does briefly flashing Christian words change racial-attitude scores?
title: Priming Christian Religious Concepts Increases Racial Prejudice
note: Participants saw masked Christian or neutral words. The authors interpreted differences in ratings and prejudice measures as effects of the prime on racial attitudes.

headline: Do people give different answers about outsiders near a cathedral than near a civic building?
title: Differences in Attitudes Toward Outgroups in Religious and Nonreligious Contexts in a Multinational Sample: A Situational Context Priming Study
venue: The International Journal for the Psychology of Religion
note: The authors surveyed people near religious or nonreligious landmarks and compared outgroup attitudes after statistical adjustment. Location served as the religious-context measure.

headline: Can a crucifix in a picture change what a moral judgment feels like?
title: Pictures Are Worth a Thousand Words and a Moral Decision or Two: Religious Symbols Prime Moral Judgments
venue: The International Journal for the Psychology of Religion
note: The authors compared responses to moral scenarios under different pictorial primes. The measured results concern judgments under the particular image and scenario conditions.

headline: Does telling adults that a ghost is in the lab make them cheat less?
title: Reasoning about dead agents reveals possible adaptive trends
note: The authors compared cheating on a competitive task after telling some participants about a supposed ghost. A separate experiment examined how learning that someone had died changed trait ratings.

headline: Do children take an unexpected light going out as a message from an invisible princess?
title: Children's attributions of intentions to an invisible agent
note: The experiment compared children who had or had not been told about an invisible helper. The authors linked age and condition differences in how children responded to unexpected events to their interpretation of the events as deliberate messages.

headline: Do children treat impossible stories as more plausible after exposure to religion?
title: Judgments About Fact and Fiction by Children From Religious and Nonreligious Backgrounds
note: The authors compared children’s classifications of characters in realistic, religious and fantastical stories. They related classifications to religious schooling and church exposure.

headline: Does remembering a time you trusted your gut make belief in God stronger?
title: Divine intuition: cognitive style influences belief in God
note: The paper related cognitive-reflection answers to belief in God and compared self-reported belief after participants recalled episodes of intuition or reflection.

headline: Can answers to a few reasoning problems tell who believes in God or paranormal events?
title: Analytic cognitive style predicts religious and paranormal belief
note: The authors compared performance on tasks containing tempting intuitive answers with survey measures of religious and paranormal belief. They interpreted the score relationships in terms of cognitive style.

headline: Do atheists in secular countries still favor belief in God in a thought experiment?
title: Belief in belief: Even atheists in secular countries show intuitive preferences favoring religious belief
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: The authors used vignette judgments across countries to infer an intuitive preference for believers, including among atheist respondents. The measured outcome was a judgment in the task.

headline: Do people give more after a ritual with synchronized movement?
title: How do rituals affect cooperation? An experimental field study comparing nine ritual types
note: The authors compared nine ritual settings and studied how synchrony and participants’ judgments of sacredness related to choices in a cooperation game.

headline: Does walking over fire put participants and spectators in different moods?
title: The fire-walker's high: affect and physiological responses in an extreme collective ritual
note: The authors compared heart-rate and affect measures among different roles in a ritual. The comparisons were made among participants and observers at the event.

headline: Can taking part in a painful ritual improve how healthy people say they feel?
title: Effects of Extreme Ritual Practices on Psychophysiological Well-Being
note: The authors used questionnaire and physiological measurements surrounding a religious ritual to examine perceived and measured well-being. They interpreted differences over time and across levels of ritual participation.

headline: Does doing a familiar temple ritual calm people after they prepare a speech?
title: The role of ritual behaviour in anxiety reduction: an investigation of Marathi religious practices in Mauritius
venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B
note: The authors induced anxiety and compared participants performing habitual ritual with participants in a control condition. They used self-reports and heart-rate variability as anxiety measures.

headline: Did belief in supernatural punishment help Austronesian societies become more politically complex?
title: Broad supernatural punishment but not moralizing high gods precede the evolution of political complexity in Austronesia
venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B
note: The authors used coded traits and a phylogenetic model to estimate the ordering of changes in supernatural punishment and political complexity. The ordering was reconstructed from the model.

headline: Can the geographic burden of infectious disease explain why places have different numbers of religions?
title: Assortative sociality, limited dispersal, infectious disease and the genesis of the global pattern of religion diversity
venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B
note: The authors related regional pathogen measures to measures of religious diversity. They interpreted those relationships as support for reduced dispersal and stronger in-group ties.

headline: Can parasite prevalence explain why people in some regions report stronger religious ties?
title: Parasite-stress promotes in-group assortative sociality: the cases of strong family ties and heightened religiosity
note: The authors analyzed geographic measures of parasite burden, family ties and religiosity. They interpreted correlations among those measures as evidence for an adaptive social response.

headline: How far above a coin toss can people guess KMT versus DPP from a candidate’s photo?
title: Taiwanese Political Parties can be Categorized by Face, by Those Who Reported Making Face-To-Trait Inferences
note: Participants classified selected photos of Taiwanese candidates. Average accuracy was 52.4% for undergraduates and 55.7% for other adults shown full faces. The paper attributed the pattern particularly to respondents who said they inferred traits from faces.

headline: Do people assign movie villains to the party they oppose?
title: Heroes and villains: motivated projection of political identities
note: U.S. and British respondents assigned fictional heroes and villains to political sides. Much of the pattern came from assigning opponents’ identities to villains. The result measures viewers’ political projections onto fictional targets.

headline: Do the sounds parents choose for baby names track their politics?
title: Liberellas Versus Konservatives: Social Status, Ideology, and Birth Names in the United States
note: The authors linked California birth names to geographic voting and census data. They classified names using speech sounds and related those classifications to local voting patterns, interpreting the pattern among White families as an ideological difference in naming preferences.

headline: Can a car or hobby in a campaign photo make a candidate look like a Republican or Democrat?
title: Cued by Culture: Political Imagery and Partisan Evaluations
note: Respondents assigned party leanings to ordinary items and activities. Including cultural cues in candidate photos changed perceived partisanship, but rarely shifted judgments when clear policy information was supplied.

headline: Why did a study titled “Why Do Liberals Drink Lattes?” leave the latte question unmeasured?
title: Why Do Liberals Drink Lattes?
note: The authors measured lifestyle and ideology patterns across General Social Survey items and modeled how social contact could amplify small differences. The latte in the title served as an illustration. A later survey directly asked about latte drinking (doi:10.1017/S1049096518000574).

headline: Does drinking lattes go with being liberal, and is globalization part of the explanation?
title: The Real Reason Liberals Drink Lattes
note: A national survey measured latte preference and political ideology. The authors found a relationship and concluded that attitudes toward globalization accounted for more of it than the other explanations they examined. The comparison used survey responses.

headline: Can books bought together online tell which sciences appeal to the political left or right?
title: Millions of online book co-purchases reveal partisan differences in the consumption of science
note: The authors compared science titles co-purchased with books they coded as liberal or conservative. They interpreted patterns in book-to-book links as partisan differences in appetite for basic versus applied science. Buyers’ political views were not directly measured.

headline: Do people who read more Harry Potter books rate Donald Trump less favorably?
title: Harry Potter and the Deathly Donald
note: Survey data connected reported reading of the series to evaluations of Trump and to related policy attitudes. The paper interpreted differences after adjustment as evidence of a possible influence of the books.

headline: How accurate are people who guess someone’s party from their lifestyle?
title: Stereotypes and Stereotyping: Measuring the Accuracy of Lifestyle-Based Judgments on Political Affiliation
venue: International Journal of Public Opinion Research
note: The authors tested which lifestyle cues shaped perceived party affiliation and assessed how closely observers’ guesses tracked affiliation. The study compared ratings and cue validity in its Canadian survey and profile tasks.

headline: Can strangers guess a person’s vote from a short demographic profile?
title: Can citizens guess how other citizens voted based on demographic characteristics?
note: Participants made guesses about people described by profiles drawn from the 2017 British Election Study. The investigators benchmarked the guesses against respondents’ reported votes and examined which observable characteristics people used.

headline: Do people guess someone’s party from policy opinions while their own affiliations track social groups?
title: Groups, Behaviors, and Issues as Cues of Partisan Attachments in the Public
note: In a profile task, participants usually relied more on policy positions than on behaviors or group labels. In analyses of participants’ own affiliations, group identity was more predictive than the profile experiment implied.

headline: Can guessing an applicant’s politics from their face change how you rate them for a job?
title: Partisan Discrimination Without Explicit Partisan Cues
venue: Journal of Social and Political Psychology
note: Two studies linked partisan impressions formed from photographs to evaluations of job applicants and stated willingness to interact. The operative variable was perceived affiliation.

headline: Can a politician’s headshot give away their views on immigration?
title: Can People Detect Ideological Stance from Facial Photographs?
note: The authors used European Parliament headshots to test whether people could classify politicians’ immigration stance. The results did not support using the photographs to identify that specific policy position.

headline: Does a politician’s face get read as more Republican when it looks more sex-typical?
title: Appearance-based politics: Sex-typed facial cues communicate political party affiliation
note: The researchers compared faces of members of Congress and related ratings of sex-typicality to party judgments in a separate study. The inference relied on politicians’ portraits and the way observers rated their faces.

headline: Does preferring country music give away your political leanings?
title: Party rocking: Exploring the relationship between music preference, partisanship, and political attitudes
note: The authors linked survey responses about music genres to self-reported partisanship and ideology. Country music showed a pronounced partisan divide in the study’s data.

headline: Can learning a favorite musician’s ideology shift the listener’s own political answers?
title: You must like me for me. New experimental evidence on the interplay between musical preferences and ideological attitudes
venue: Journal of Elections, Public Opinion and Parties
note: A U.S. survey experiment tested how information about musicians’ political leanings affected stated musical and political preferences. The findings concern responses in that experiment.

headline: Can the stories in TV shows explain what Democrats and Republicans still watch together?
title: Shared Screens: Scripted Television’s Communal Space in a Polarized Nation
note: The author used national consumer survey data to identify scripted shows with audiences spread across ideologies, then coded their story features. A show’s audience composition was a measured property, while its narrative features were compared across titles.

headline: Can what you watch, read and listen to map the political divide?
title: The Polarization of Popular Culture: Tracing the Size, Shape, and Depth of the “Oil Spill”
note: The authors used reports of engagement with and attitudes toward popular culture to estimate how tastes align with ideology, race and geography. They distinguished the cultural products that people consume from the ones they say they like or dislike.

headline: Can the accounts people follow on social media reveal Sweden’s political blocs?
title: Partisan tastes or ideological divides? Everyday interests and political identities in a multi-party system
note: The authors grouped the accounts followed by politically engaged Swedish users into interest categories. They reported that the resulting clusters lined up more closely with wider ideological blocs than with individual parties.

headline: Can a list of American pastimes and products sort people into political cultures?
title: Politicultural Sorting: Mapping Ideological Differences in American Leisure and Consumption
note: The author compared lifestyle items across self-described ideological groups and modeled patterns of leisure and consumption. The resulting clusters depend on which activities and products were included.

headline: Can Pepsi or a TV show acquire a political score from the accounts its followers also follow?
title: Cultural Fault Lines and Political Polarization
venue: Proceedings of the ACM Web Science Conference
note: The study used overlapping Twitter followerships to place cultural and commercial accounts on a political scale. The position represents the model’s estimate from audience overlap.

headline: Can the popularity of a sport tell you whether an area leans left or right?
title: Red sport, blue sport: political ideology and the popularity of sports in the United States
venue: International Journal of Sport Policy and Politics
note: The author examined geographic correlations between political ideology and the popularity of 53 sports. The unit of analysis was an area, so the results compare places rather than measuring fans’ individual politics.

headline: Do parents name more daughters Reagan to signal their party in places with many Democrats?
title: Nominal Partisanship: Names as Political Identity Signals
note: The author compared state-level party composition and the frequency of the name Reagan for newborn girls. The claim about parents signaling political identity was inferred from state-by-year patterns.

headline: Can political insiders spot a signal in a tweet that outsiders miss?
title: Strategic identity signaling in heterogeneous networks
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: The authors analyzed political identity signals in tweets and ran a behavioral experiment about which signals people chose for different audiences. A signal’s covertness depended on how well in-group and out-group readers recognized it.

headline: Do liberals and conservatives exaggerate one another’s moral priorities?
title: The Moral Stereotypes of Liberals and Conservatives: Exaggeration of Differences across the Political Spectrum
note: Participants answered a moral questionnaire as themselves or how they imagined a typical liberal or conservative would answer. Perceived differences were generally larger than the differences between groups’ own answers.

headline: Do people think the typical Republican is much richer than Republicans actually are?
title: The Parties in Our Heads: Misperceptions about Party Composition and Their Consequences
note: The authors compared survey estimates of each party’s composition with benchmarks. Respondents overestimated the prevalence of some stereotypical groups. A later paper tested how adding a population-wide benchmark changes the interpretation (doi:10.1093/poq/nfab062).

headline: Can someone’s car or favorite TV show change whether you want to spend time with them?
title: How the Politicization of Everyday Activities Affects the Public Sphere: The Effects of Partisan Stereotypes on Cross-Cutting Interactions
note: Two surveys varied everyday profile cues and measured inferred political leanings and hypothetical willingness to interact. The outcomes were expressed judgments about potential interactions.

headline: Do people overestimate how much a political label changes what others would buy?
title: Party over product: People exaggerate the influence of political cues on others’ consumption preferences
venue: International Journal of Research in Marketing
note: The authors compared predictions about how other people would respond to politically marked products with those people’s stated preferences. Respondents expected a bigger role for politics than the preference ratings showed.

headline: How often do people say they ended a friendship or other relationship over politics?
title: Political breakups: Interpersonal consequences of polarization
note: Across four U.S. datasets, the authors studied self-reported losses of relationships attributed to politics. One survey found that 37% reported a political breakup, most often involving friends.

headline: Can an assigned college roommate move your political views toward theirs?
title: College roommates have a modest but significant influence on each other’s political ideology
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: The authors used roommate assignment and two surveys of first-year students at two U.S. universities. They estimated a modest shift toward roommates’ reported ideological positions over the academic year.

headline: Does a party label outweigh shared race or religion when judging a potential friend?
title: Why can't we be friends? Untangling conjoined polarization in America
note: A U.S. survey experiment varied several social identities in hypothetical profiles. Political identity was the strongest cue in the authors’ comparisons of attitudes and stated willingness to interact.

headline: Would people accept less pay to work for someone from their own party?
title: The Economic Consequences of Partisanship in a Polarized Era
note: The authors tested whether a counterparty’s partisan cues changed economic decisions, including choices in an online labor task. They found differences in willingness to take lower compensation in that setting.

headline: Does a different party label make a dating profile seem less compatible?
title: Why do young US Americans avoid cross-partisan dating? A closer look at mediators and variation by gender and party
note: Young U.S. adults evaluated profiles that varied partisan information. The authors used immediate ratings of similarity and character and anticipated social approval to model why the party cue changed reported date interest.

headline: Does holding a fish in a dating photo make you look conservative?
title: Ideological cues: Fishing photos and US flags reduce romantic interest among liberal daters on dating apps
note: Participants judged dating profiles with fish or U.S. flags. The authors reported that these cues made profiles look more conservative to some observers and changed romantic interest among liberal respondents. The profiles were rated for perceived ideology.

headline: Can seeing the forest before the trees give away your politics?
title: The tree to the left, the forest to the right: political attitude and perceptual bias
note: Participants completed tasks with hierarchical figures or a visual size illusion. The authors linked greater attention to overall forms with more right-wing self-placement and interpreted that pattern as reflecting cognitive rigidity.

headline: Are early birds more conservative and night owls more liberal?
title: Conservative Larks, Liberal Owls: The Relationship between Chronotype and Political Ideology
note: The author linked morningness and eveningness measures to self-reported ideology. The analysis compared sleep timing preferences and political responses and discussed several possible directions for the relationship.

headline: Can preferring dogs over cats give away where you land politically?
title: Pets and Politics: Do Liberals and Conservatives Differ in Their Preferences for Cats Versus Dogs?
note: The authors linked greater conservatism to lower liking for cats and a stronger relative preference for dogs in an online sample. They compared self-reported pet ratings and reaction-time scores for associations with dogs and cats.

headline: Can the willingness to buy misshapen produce give away political ideology?
title: Preference for imperfect produce: The influence of political ideology and openness to experience
note: The authors compared preference for visually imperfect fruit and vegetables by ideology and modeled openness to experience as a mechanism. The claimed link concerns the produce and choice settings used in their studies.

headline: Do Thanksgiving visits run shorter when guests come from an opposing party’s precinct?
title: The effect of partisanship and political advertising on close family ties
note: The authors estimated dinner durations from smartphone locations and political disagreement from precinct voting, using inferred home precincts for travelers and the precincts where they visited. Visits estimated to cross partisan lines were shorter in the model.

headline: Can a typeface make the same words look more Republican or Democratic?
title: What’s in a Font?: Ideological Perceptions of Typography
