note: Participants rated the ideological impressions of typefaces and styles. Ratings varied across stimuli and by the observers’ party identification. The outcome was a perceived political cue.

headline: Does a green label put conservatives off the same energy-efficient light bulb?
title: Political ideology affects energy-efficiency attitudes and choices
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: The researchers varied whether a compact fluorescent bulb carried an environmental message. At equal prices, the message reduced selection of that bulb among more conservative participants in the experiment.

headline: Do your politics show up in whether you treat your dog as an equal or buy it designer accessories?
title: Red dog, blue dog: the influence of political identity on owner–pet relationships and owners’ purchases of pet-related products and services
note: The authors compared pet owners’ self-reported relationships and spending intentions and drew on two secondary data sources. They linked political identity to treating pets as equals versus emphasizing control and to different kinds of pet purchases.

headline: Can the way students move around campus and spend their time give away their politics?
title: Lifestyle polarization on a college campus: Do liberals and conservatives behave differently in everyday life?
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors compared undergraduates’ political orientation with everyday behavior using multiple types of data, including passive smartphone sensing. The proposed lifestyle differences describe a campus cohort and are tied to the behaviors captured by those measures.

headline: Can the themes in your favorite music give away your political worldview?
title: Entertainment Use and Political Ideology: Linking Worldviews to Media Content
note: The authors scored the moral language of song lyrics by genre and linked those genre scores to survey respondents’ reported listening, musical preferences and ideology. The study joins aggregate genre profiles to individual responses.

headline: Do left- and right-leaning people go for different sports?
title: It’s the ideology, stupid! Do sport participation and sport consumer choices differ between the left and the right?
venue: International Journal of Sport Policy and Politics
note: The authors compared political ideology to survey measures of how people participate in and consume sport. The categories describe the study’s survey respondents and the set of sports and activities measured.

headline: Do left-leaning people say they joke differently?
title: The politics of being funny: Humor styles, trait humorousness, and political orientations
note: Left-oriented respondents reported more affiliative and aggressive humor styles. The authors found no evidence of greater overall humorousness in the political left, and their measures of humor style relied on questionnaire responses.

headline: Can choosing generic groceries over national brands tell you how conservative an area is?
title: Ideology and Brand Consumption
note: The authors linked supermarket market shares for established versus generic brands and new products to geographic measures of Republican voting and religiosity. The shopping and polling figures were combined at an aggregate level.

headline: Does refusing to try unfamiliar food go with more conservative attitudes?
title: Dining with liberals and conservatives: The social underpinnings of food neophobia
note: In Italian samples the authors related reluctance to try unfamiliar foods to conservative attitudes and other social measures. The paper links food neophobia scale responses to sociopolitical responses, without observing what respondents ordered for dinner.

headline: Can you see someone's politics in how they rank tradition and environmental impact when buying food?
title: Political ideology shapes heterogeneous preferences for food values
note: The authors related conservatism to greater weights on food naturalness and tradition and lower weights on environmental impact. The estimated priorities come from comparisons among specified food values.

headline: Does worrying about food waste make liberals eat more of a large portion?
title: Bringing Our Values to the Table: Political Ideology, Food Waste, and Overconsumption
venue: Journal of the Association for Consumer Research
note: Two experiments drew attention to food waste when serving large portions. The authors reported opposite changes in consumption by ideology and interpreted the liberal response as an attempt to avoid environmental waste.

headline: Can conservatism explain who quits a vegetarian diet and goes back to meat?
title: Conservatism predicts lapses from vegetarian/vegan diets to meat consumption (through lower social justice concerns and social support)
note: The authors compared current and former vegetarians and vegans. Their model linked conservatism to reported return to eating meat and attributed part of the link to social support and social justice concerns.

headline: Do conservatives more often choose products described as worse on the listed features?
title: How Political Ideology Shapes Preferences for Observably Inferior Products
note: The studies compared choices among products described on observable dimensions, some dominated by an alternative on those dimensions. The authors reported stronger preferences for these options among conservatives and interpreted the pattern through beliefs about how markets work.

headline: Do conservative shoppers prefer products that signal they are better while liberals want to look different?
title: Better or Different? How Political Ideology Shapes Preferences for Differentiation in the Social Hierarchy
note: The authors compared product options designed to signal higher rank or individuality. They linked ideology to preferences for those signals and interpreted the pattern as reflecting acceptance of hierarchy.

headline: Does choosing the practical option over the fun one give away your politics?
title: The Politics of Choice: Political Ideology and Intolerance of Ambiguity
note: The studies compared practical and pleasure-oriented consumer choices and related preferences to political ideology. The authors interpreted the preference for practical options among more conservative participants in terms of lower tolerance for ambiguity.

headline: Are conservatives more willing to buy from a brand cast as a servant than as a partner?
title: Political Ideology and Anthropomorphized Servant Versus Partner Brand Roles
note: The authors framed brands as human-like partners or servants and compared purchase intentions by ideology. They linked conservative respondents’ stronger willingness to buy from servant brands to social dominance orientation and reported relaxation.

headline: Does being emotionally attached to a favorite brand go with being more conservative?
title: Political ideology and brand attachment
venue: International Journal of Research in Marketing
note: Five studies linked conservatism to stronger brand attachment. The authors interpreted questionnaire and experimental patterns as evidence that attachment to a brand can ease uncertainty.

headline: Can political identity show up in how satisfied people are with a purchase?
title: How Political Identity Shapes Customer Satisfaction
note: The authors compared customer satisfaction across products and services, including restaurant ratings, and linked higher conservative satisfaction with self-chosen purchases to reported belief in free will and trust in decisions.

headline: Does choosing a local rather than a global cultural experience track political ideology?
title: Political Ideology and Cultural Consumption: The Role of Flexibility in Shaping Liberal and Conservative Preferences for Global-Local Experiences
venue: Journal of the Association for Consumer Research
note: The studies compared interest in cultural experiences framed as global or local. The authors used differences by ideology to argue that cognitive flexibility helps account for the preferences.

headline: Do conservative writers talk about the past while liberal writers talk about the future?
title: The politics of time: Conservatives differentially reference the past and liberals differentially reference the future
note: The authors counted time references in 600 texts from political websites and analyzed a second language sample. They interpreted differences in references to the past and future as differences in temporal focus.

headline: Can swearing and word choice on Twitter distinguish followers of Democratic and Republican accounts?
title: Twitter Language Use Reflects Psychological Differences between Democrats and Republicans
note: The authors compared words and categories in posts by users selected via the political accounts they followed. They interpreted differences, including in profanity, through psychological word categories. The political labels were derived from following behavior.

headline: Can someone’s pattern of Reddit replies give away their political leanings outside political forums?
title: Political Homophily in a Large-Scale Online Communication Network
note: The authors estimated latent ideology from Reddit behavior and used that estimate to compare whom users interacted with across forums. Nonpolitical forums displayed less same-ideology clustering than political ones.

headline: Do liberals and conservatives retweet their members of Congress differently?
title: Liberals and conservatives share information differently on social media
note: The authors studied retweets of U.S. members of Congress and compared users whose ideological positions were estimated from prior retweet behavior. The comparison relates one set of sharing decisions to labels inferred from another.

headline: Does what people miss about the past give away their politics?
title: Different Pasts for Different Political Folk: Political Orientation Predicts Collective Nostalgia Content
note: The authors compared what respondents said they missed about their country. They organized responses into different themes and related those themes to self-reported ideology.

headline: Does describing a progressive idea as a return to the past make conservatives more willing to endorse it?
title: Past-focused temporal communication overcomes conservatives' resistance to liberal political ideas
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors reframed liberal ideas using past- or future-focused wording and compared participant responses by ideology. The reported change concerns judgments of the framed messages.

headline: Do people hide their politics on dating profiles even though partners tend to agree?
title: Do bedroom eyes wear political glasses? The role of politics in human mate attraction
note: The authors examined what singles disclosed in internet dating profiles and compared this with patterns of ideological similarity among couples. Political preferences were less often disclosed than other personal attributes.

headline: Do your politics show up in whom you trust with money in a lab game?
title: Political Ideology, Trust, and Cooperation: In-group Favoritism among Republicans and Democrats during a US National Election
note: Participants made decisions in incentivized economic games with partly described partners during an election. The authors compared cooperation and expectations when people knew the partner’s party identity.

headline: Can where you draw your circle of concern around family, strangers and animals give away your politics?
title: Ideological differences in the expanse of the moral circle
note: The authors compared moral concern allocated to categories such as friends, family, the nation, the world and nonhuman entities. They interpreted different allocation patterns as differences in the scope of liberals’ and conservatives’ moral concern.

headline: Do liberals say they want to empathize more with strangers than conservatives do?
title: Are Liberals and Conservatives Equally Motivated to Feel Empathy Toward Others?
note: The authors compared desired empathy and responses to different targets by ideology. Desired empathy was rated by participants and varied with who they were asked to empathize with.

headline: Can an IQ test at age ten tell who will hold more liberal social attitudes twenty years later?
title: Bright Children Become Enlightened Adults
note: In a British birth cohort, an aggregate score on childhood cognitive tests was related to survey responses on social issues at age thirty. The authors treated the resulting attitude dimension as a measure of liberal and antitraditional views.

headline: Can childhood cognitive scores explain adult prejudice through political ideology?
title: Bright minds and dark attitudes: lower cognitive ability predicts greater prejudice through right-wing ideology and low intergroup contact
note: The authors used cohort and survey data in which cognitive test scores, ideological attitudes, intergroup contact and prejudice measures were observed at different points or in different samples. They interpreted statistical pathways as explanations for the reported links.

headline: Can the experiences someone reports from their school years explain where they land politically at age thirty?
title: Personality, Childhood Experience, and Political Ideology
note: The author related adolescent measures and later personality and politics responses in the U.S. Add Health cohort. The proposed links rely on statistical comparisons of pupils’ reported experiences and later ideology.

headline: Do openness and conscientiousness point in the same political direction around the world?
title: Personality Traits and Political Ideology: A First Global Assessment
note: The authors related questionnaire measures of the Big Five to left–right self-placement in 21 countries. They compared the strength and direction of these correlations across national contexts.

headline: Can four dark personality scores tell you how politically extreme someone is?
title: The impact of dark tetrad traits on political orientation and extremism: an analysis in the course of a presidential election
note: During an Austrian presidential election the authors related narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy and everyday sadism scores to orientation and extremity. The measured traits and political positions were survey responses.

headline: Can creative-personality scores and willingness to take social risks distinguish party affiliation?
title: The ‘Right’ Side of Creativity: Creative Personality and Social Risk-Taking Predict Political Party Affiliation
note: The authors compared questionnaire scores and measures of creativity with party affiliation. They identified social risk-taking and creative-personality scores as predictors in their models.

headline: Can how you solve a three-word puzzle give away your political leanings?
title: The politics of insight
note: Participants solved word-association puzzles and indicated whether each solution arrived via insight or step-by-step analysis. The authors compared those reported routes to an answer with political orientation.

headline: Can a battery of perception and decision tasks reveal nationalism, conservatism or dogmatism?
title: The cognitive and perceptual correlates of ideological attitudes: a data-driven approach
venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B
note: The researchers related a large set of objective tasks and personality questionnaires to ideology surveys. They interpreted modeled patterns across tasks as cognitive and perceptual correlates of ideological attitudes.

headline: Does judging your own performance on a visual task tell you how radical your beliefs are?
title: Metacognitive Failure as a Feature of Those Holding Radical Beliefs
note: Participants completed visual judgments and rated their confidence. The authors related reduced metacognitive sensitivity and updating of confidence after new evidence to political radicalism measured with questionnaires.

headline: Can card sorting and word puzzles give away attitudes toward Brexit?
title: Cognitive underpinnings of nationalistic ideology in the context of Brexit
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: The authors linked performance on card-sorting and word-association tasks to the flexibility with which respondents defined national identity and to Brexit attitudes. The proposed pathway came from statistical modeling of behavior and survey answers.

headline: Can your scores on memory and task-switching tests give away your politics?
title: Political Ideology and Executive Functioning: The Effect of Conservatism and Liberalism on Cognitive Flexibility and Working Memory Performance
note: The authors compared performance on executive-function tasks with reported ideology. They inferred differences in working memory and cognitive flexibility from specific task scores.

headline: Do conservatives sound more certain about their answers to everyday judgments?
title: The confident conservative: Ideological differences in judgment and decision-making confidence
note: The researchers compared reported confidence across judgment and decision tasks. Their interpretation of ideological differences relied on ratings of confidence in the study answers.

headline: Can a few trick questions separate reflective liberals from intuitive conservatives?
title: Reflective liberals and intuitive conservatives: A look at the Cognitive Reflection Test and ideology
note: The authors compared replies on Cognitive Reflection Test items with measures of ideology. Reported differences were concentrated in social attitudes, and later work found that the relationship depended on which measures were used (doi:10.1017/S1930297500005684).

headline: Can seeing gains as someone else’s losses reveal your politics?
title: The politics of zero-sum thinking: The relationship between political ideology and the belief that life is a zero-sum game
note: The authors asked participants to evaluate scenarios and compared answers as a function of ideology. The observed direction varied with the target of comparisons, making the result sensitive to which groups and outcomes the questions described.

headline: Do the risks you say you would take give away your political leanings?
title: Risk Propensity Among Liberals and Conservatives: The Effect of Risk Perception, Expected Benefits, and Risk Domain
note: The paper compared self-reported risk perceptions, expected benefits and willingness to take risks across five domains. The ideological pattern depended on the type of behavior asked about.

headline: Did support for Obama depend on the time of the month?
title: The Fluctuating Female Vote: Politics, Religion, and the Ovulatory Cycle
note: During the 2012 US presidential election, researchers compared women's political preferences with their reported menstrual cycles and relationship status. They reported that single women were more likely to support Barack Obama when estimated fertility was higher. A follow-up found no evidence that estimated cycle phase predicted political attitudes, religiosity, or candidate preferences. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797613520236

headline: Same golf ball. Call it lucky and more putts go in?
title: Keep Your Fingers Crossed!: How Superstition Improves Performance
note: Researchers told some participants that the golf ball they were about to use was lucky. The original paper reported that these participants sank more putts. Two follow-up putting experiments found no putting advantage from calling the ball lucky. https://doi.org/10.1027/1864-9335/a000190

headline: Does a reminder of money make you less helpful?
title: The psychological consequences of money
note: Across nine experiments, the authors reported that cues associated with money reduced help-seeking and helping, and increased preferences for solitary activities.

headline: Does a heavier clipboard make fairness more important?
title: Weight as an Embodiment of Importance
note: The authors reported that clipboard weight changed ratings of monetary value and the importance of fair procedures. A direct replication and related tests found no effect on judgments of issue importance in the moral domain. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0134808

headline: Can you wash away your buyer's remorse?
title: Washing away postdecisional dissonance
note: Handwashing after choosing between alternatives was reported to reduce the tendency to subsequently justify one's choice.

headline: Do baseball players whose names start with K strike out more often?
title: Moniker Maladies: When Names Sabotage Success
note: The authors reported that baseball players with K-initial names struck out more often, and that people with initials matching a negative outcome showed related patterns in other datasets.

headline: Can a roll of the dice nudge a legal expert's sentencing recommendation?
title: Playing Dice With Criminal Sentences: The Influence of Irrelevant Anchors on Experts’ Judicial Decision Making
note: Legal professionals evaluating a hypothetical case recommended longer sentences after higher dice-generated anchors, even though they knew the numbers were random.

headline: Can a college football upset add time to a juvenile’s sentence?
title: Emotional Judges and Unlucky Juveniles
note: The authors linked unexpected Louisiana State football losses to longer dispositions in juvenile court records, particularly for judges who had attended LSU. The analysis uses historical case and game records to infer a response to the losses.

headline: Is a defendant less likely to get prison time on their birthday?
title: Clash of norms judicial leniency on defendant birthdays
note: In French court records, prison sentences were less frequent and shorter on defendants’ birthdays. The authors inferred birthday leniency from the timing pattern and also reported a separate pattern in the rounding of U.S. federal sentences.

headline: Do judges hand down more lenient rulings during Ramadan?
title: Ramadan fasting increases leniency in judges from Pakistan and India
note: The authors linked Ramadan and variation in fasting hours to more acquittals by Muslim judges using court records in Pakistan and India. The exposure was inferred from calendar and daylight information in the archival analysis.

headline: Does a hot day make an immigration judge less likely to rule in your favor?
title: Temperature and Decisions: Evidence from 207,000 Court Cases
note: The authors linked warmer outdoor temperatures to fewer favorable immigration rulings in their preferred model. Temperature was measured outside the courthouse. A published comment reported sensitivity to coding corrections and sample expansion (doi:10.1257/app.20200118). The authors’ correction reported similar main linear estimates and acknowledged the external-validity result (doi:10.1257/app.20200068).

headline: Do asylum judges behave as if they are due for a rejection after granting asylum?
title: Decision Making Under the Gambler’s Fallacy: Evidence from Asylum Judges, Loan Officers, and Baseball Umpires
note: The authors found negative dependence between nearby asylum decisions by the same judge and interpreted it as evidence of the gambler’s fallacy. The records describe the verdict sequence, while the inference about judges’ beliefs comes from the model.

headline: Does having a daughter change how an appeals judge rules on gender issues?
title: Identifying Judicial Empathy: Does Having Daughters Cause Judges to Rule for Women's Issues?
note: The authors compared appellate votes by judges with daughters and judges with sons only, conditioning on family size. They interpreted the pattern in gender-related cases as evidence for a causal effect of having a daughter.

headline: Do judges recommend shorter prison terms when they count in months instead of years?
title: Can Judges Make Reliable Numeric Judgments? Distorted Damages and Skewed Sentences
note: In hypothetical cases, participating trial judges assigned shorter sentences when asked to state the term in months. Other experiments in the same paper tested damages figures taken from a television court show and the ordering of cases.

headline: Can mentioning a jurisdictional cutoff sway a judge’s estimate of damages?
title: Inside the Judicial Mind
note: Judges read a hypothetical case. Mentioning a motion based on the federal jurisdictional threshold shifted estimates of damages even though the threshold did not establish what the plaintiff had lost.

headline: Can looking untrustworthy in a mugshot line up with a death sentence?
title: Facial Trustworthiness Predicts Extreme Criminal-Sentencing Outcomes
note: Raters judged photographs of defendants. Their trustworthiness ratings were compared with life and death sentences, including a comparison involving exonerated people. A later comment examined the role of uncontrolled differences between photographs (doi:10.1177/0033294119889582).

headline: Do baby-faced defendants win more small-claims cases involving intent?
title: The Impact of Litigants' Baby-Facedness and Attractiveness on Adjudications in Small Claims Courts
note: The researchers rated faces in 506 actual small-claims cases and linked defendants’ baby-facedness to more favorable outcomes in cases involving intentional actions. The study related observer ratings to existing court outcomes.

headline: Can strangers spot a criminal from a headshot?
title: The Accuracy of Inferences About Criminality Based on Facial Appearance
venue: Journal of Social, Evolutionary, and Cultural Psychology
note: In two experiments, observers classified selected photos of convicted and nonconvicted people at above-chance rates. The claim about facial inferences rests on the photo sets and the categories of people represented in them.

headline: Can a facial tattoo make a mock defendant look guiltier without changing the recommended punishment?
title: Criminal Stereotypes in the Courtroom: Facial Tattoos Affect Guilt and Punishment Differently
note: Across three experiments, adding a facial tattoo shifted guilt judgments. The authors did not find a corresponding increase in punishment ratings and inferred a role for perceived criminal appearance from their statistical model.

headline: Does a prison-style tattoo make a mock defendant seem more dangerous and guilty?
title: The Defendant with the Prison Tattoo: The Effect of Tattoos on Mock Jurors’ Perceptions
note: Participants rated photographs and evaluated a simulated case. The authors modeled perceived dangerousness as a mediator between the presence of a tattoo and perceived guilt.

headline: Does swapping a suit for prison clothes change the verdict in a mock trial?
title: The Cloak of Innocence: Perception of Attire in the Courtroom
venue: Journal of Police and Criminal Psychology
note: Participants evaluated an assault scenario with the defendant shown in a suit or prison clothes. The prison-clothes condition produced more guilty verdicts and higher aggression ratings in the simulation.

headline: Can looking attractive help at a bail hearing?
title: Natural Observations of the Links between Attractiveness and Initial Legal Judgments
note: The authors compared appearance ratings and initial legal decisions. They reported a link with bail and fines for misdemeanor charges, with no corresponding relationship for felony charges.

headline: Do attractive faces look less guilty for some alleged crimes than for others?
title: The Relationship Between Facial Attractiveness and Perceived Guilt Across Types of Crime
note: Participants rated faces paired with different crime scenarios. The study modeled how the association between attractiveness and perceived guilt changed across the scenarios. The outcome was a rating made for the study.

headline: Can a face look more criminal just by looking less trustworthy?
title: Do Characteristics of Faces That Convey Trustworthiness and Dominance Underlie Perceptions of Criminality?
note: Participants rated faces and the author analyzed which rated attributes covaried with looking criminal. The result concerns judgments of appearance and supplies no test of whether the pictured people had committed crimes.

headline: Can warnings about judging by faces erase the effect on mock sentencing?
title: Can We Reduce Facial Biases? Persistent Effects of Facial Trustworthiness on Sentencing Decisions
note: Experiments compared sentencing choices for faces perceived as more or less trustworthy and tested attempts to reduce the effect. Facial impressions continued to be associated with hypothetical sentencing choices.

headline: Can a foreign accent increase the sentence recommended by a mock juror?
title: Accentism on Trial: Categorization/Stereotyping and Implicit Biases Predict Harsher Sentences for Foreign-Accented Defendants
venue: Journal of Language and Social Psychology
note: Participants heard statements in a mock trial. The authors reported harsher recommendations for the foreign-accented defendant in the condition without background noise.

headline: Can the same eyewitness account sound less accurate in a different British accent?
title: The Impact of British Accents on Perceptions of Eyewitness Statements
note: Participants heard one of three versions of eyewitness testimony. Received Pronunciation received higher ratings on several dimensions than Multicultural London English. The experiment measured perceived accuracy, without testing the truth of competing accounts.

headline: Can showing remorse make a mock jury more likely to find you guilty?
title: The Influence of Accounts and Remorse on Mock Jurors’ Judgments of Offenders
note: In a simulated case, mock jurors more often found a remorseful defendant guilty when the defendant offered no explanation. The reported comparison depended on what explanation, if any, accompanied the display.

headline: Can a witness’s displayed emotion change how credible court judges find the same testimony?
title: Credibility of the Emotional Witness: A Study of Ratings by Court Judges
note: Judges rated filmed testimony performed with different emotional displays. The outcome was credibility assigned to the reenacted account.

headline: Does police bodycam footage make the same action look less intentional than dashcam footage?
title: Body Camera Footage Leads to Lower Judgments of Intent Than Dash Camera Footage
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Observers rated the same incidents as less intentional from body-camera footage than from dashboard footage across eight experiments. The study measured observers’ judgments of intent, without independently measuring the actor’s intent.

headline: Can moving the camera change whether a recorded confession looks voluntary?
title: Videotaped Interrogations and Confessions: A Simple Change in Camera Perspective Alters Verdicts in Simulated Trials
note: Viewers saw interrogation footage with different people visible or emphasized. The authors reported changes in ratings of voluntariness and in mock verdicts, even when the simulation included a potentially corrective instruction.

headline: Do color crime-scene photos produce more guilty verdicts than grayscale versions?
title: Seeing Red: Disgust Reactions to Gruesome Photographs in Color (but Not in Black and White) Increase Convictions
note: The author varied the presentation of gruesome photographs in mock trials and reported a relationship between disgust and guilty verdicts for color photos. The measured outcomes came from simulated judgments.

headline: Can graphic photos double guilty verdicts in a simulated murder trial?
title: The Impact of Graphic Photographic Evidence on Mock Jurors’ Decisions in a Murder Trial: Probative or Prejudicial?
note: In a 120-person simulation, guilty verdicts were about twice as frequent with graphic images as without them. Both color and black-and-white photos showed this pattern, giving a comparison for the later color-specific claim (doi:10.1037/law0000122).

headline: Can rearranging the same evidence change a mock juror’s verdict?
title: Explaining the Evidence: Tests of the Story Model for Juror Decision Making
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors varied how easily evidence could be assembled into a story. Verdict judgments changed even though participants remembered comparable amounts of evidence across conditions.

headline: Can adding genetic and brain evidence shorten a judge’s suggested sentence?
title: The Double-Edged Sword: Does Biomechanism Increase or Decrease Judges’ Sentencing of Psychopaths?
note: U.S. judges assigned sentences in a hypothetical case. Adding a biological explanation reduced the mean recommendation. A later experiment with German judges found a different pattern and no change in sentence duration (doi:10.1136/jmedgenet-2015-103284).

headline: Can a brain image make a mock juror more likely to accept an insanity defense?
title: The Effects of Neuroimaging and Brain Injury on Insanity Defenses
note: Mock jurors evaluated hypothetical defendants. The reported pattern depended on information about brain injury and on how neuroimaging evidence was presented.

headline: Can a black eye make a face harder for eyewitnesses to identify?
title: “All I Remember Is the Black Eye”: A Distinctive Facial Feature Harms Eyewitness Identification
note: In a photo lineup experiment, a black eye on the original face made target identification less discriminating. The pattern was reported both when lineup faces copied the feature and when it was removed.

headline: Can describing a robber’s face make it harder to pick him out of a lineup?
title: Verbal Overshadowing of Visual Memories: Some Things Are Better Left Unsaid
note: The study asked some participants to describe a face after viewing a filmed event. Those participants had more trouble identifying the face in the later test. A registered multi-lab replication examined the dependence on timing.

headline: Can seeing an innocent person’s mugshot make a witness pick them later?
title: Mug Shot Exposure Prior to Lineup Identification: Interference, Transference, and Commitment Effects
note: In two staged-crime experiments, seeing mugshots before a lineup distorted some later identifications. The researchers compared general interference, familiarity with a mugshot and commitment to an earlier choice.

headline: Can telling an eyewitness they picked the right person rewrite how well they think they saw the culprit?
title: “Good, You Identified the Suspect”: Feedback to Eyewitnesses Distorts Their Reports of the Witnessing Experience
note: After witnesses made a false lineup choice, the researchers varied whether they received confirmatory feedback. The feedback shifted reports of confidence and of how clearly the witness remembered seeing the culprit.

headline: Can being told who confessed make eyewitnesses change whom they identify?
title: On the Presumption of Evidentiary Independence: Can Confessions Corrupt Eyewitness Identifications?
note: Witnesses to a staged theft made lineup choices and then received new information about a purported confession. Some redirected their identifications toward the person said to have confessed.

headline: Can an out-of-place object distract a witness as much as a weapon?
title: Unusualness and Threat as Possible Causes of “Weapon Focus”
note: Participants watched scenes with objects chosen to vary in expectedness and threat. The author used differences in memory for the person and the object to argue that unexpectedness can contribute to the weapon-focus effect.

headline: Can innocent people sign a confession to crashing a computer and then supply details that never happened?
title: The Social Psychology of False Confessions: Compliance, Internalization, and Confabulation
note: Participants were wrongly accused of pressing a key in a computer task. The authors interpreted signed statements, later reports of responsibility and invented details as distinct forms of response to the accusation.

headline: Can a sleepless night lead innocent participants to sign a false admission?
title: Sleep Deprivation and False Confessions
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Lab participants who stayed awake overnight more often signed a false statement saying they had pressed a prohibited key. The outcome was signing a lab statement about a computer task.

headline: Can bluffing about future evidence make innocent students confess to cheating?
title: Inside Interrogation: The Lie, the Bluff, and False Confessions
note: In staged investigations of experimental rule violations, some innocent participants confessed more often after being told that evidence would later be checked. The paper interprets the pattern as an effect of an interrogator’s bluff.

headline: Can police investigators spot a false confession better than college students?
title: “I’d Know a False Confession if I Saw One”: A Comparative Study of College Students and Police Investigators
note: College students and police investigators judged recorded true and fabricated accounts. Investigators were more confident and showed a stronger tendency to judge confessions as true. The judgments used a controlled set of recorded accounts.

headline: Does a false confession travel with other errors in wrongful-conviction files?
title: Confessions That Corrupt: Evidence From the DNA Exoneration Case Files
note: In DNA exoneration files, false-confession cases more often contained multiple evidence errors. The paper used which errors co-occurred and which came first to support an evidence-contamination interpretation.

headline: Can case background make fingerprint experts reverse a previous identification?
title: Contextual Information Renders Experts Vulnerable to Making Erroneous Identifications
note: Five examiners reassessed prints they had previously matched. Most changed their decisions when given misleading case context. This small expert experiment provided a striking demonstration without estimating an error rate for routine casework.

headline: Can a TV crime report make the same suspect look guiltier by showing prison clothes and restraints?
title: Guilty and Threatening: Visual Bias in Television News Crime Stories
note: In a small experiment, viewers rated suspects as more threatening and guilty after seeing visual custody cues in a TV report. The study collected judgments of perceived guilt rather than verdicts.

headline: Can testosterone change scores on an eye-reading test in a way that depends on finger lengths?
title: Testosterone Administration Impairs Cognitive Empathy in Women Depending on Second-to-Fourth Digit Ratio
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Women scored lower on the eye-photo test after testosterone administration, with the estimated difference related to their finger-length ratio.

headline: Do spouses with lower blood sugar stick more pins into a doll representing their partner?
title: Low Glucose Relates to Greater Aggression in Married Couples
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Participants measured their glucose and could insert pins into a doll representing their spouse. Lower glucose readings were associated with more pins.

headline: Do lap dancers earn more tips near ovulation?
title: Ovulatory cycle effects on tip earnings by lap dancers: economic evidence for human estrus?
note: The authors compared self-reported tips and menstrual cycle timing among 18 dancers.

headline: Does leaning slightly left make people guess the Eiffel Tower is shorter?
title: Leaning to the Left Makes the Eiffel Tower Seem Smaller: Posture-Modulated Estimation
note: Participants standing on a balance board gave numerical estimates with their weight subtly shifted. The authors reported smaller values when participants leaned left than when they leaned right.

headline: Does believing in a punishing god make you share more with a distant stranger of the same faith?
title: Moralistic gods, supernatural punishment and the expansion of human sociality
note: Participants in eight communities played games allocating coins to themselves or fellow believers. Ratings of how much gods know and punish predicted allocations to distant co-religionists. The authors connected the game results to the historical expansion of cooperation. A later study across 15 cultures found limited support for a direct effect of gods' moral concerns, a related but distinct measure. https://doi.org/10.1017/ehs.2023.15

headline: Do people change their minds about what God believes when they change their own minds?
title: Believers' estimates of God's beliefs are more egocentric than estimates of other people's beliefs
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: The authors compared participants' own policy views with estimates of God's views and of other people's views. Experiments that shifted participants' views also shifted their estimates of God's views. A separate fMRI comparison was interpreted as evidence of self-referential reasoning.

headline: Can local climate help explain where societies believe in morally judging gods?
title: The ecology of religious beliefs
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: The researchers combined ethnographic classifications of religious beliefs in 583 societies with measures of climate, ecological risk, and social structure. They used the geographical patterns to argue that environmental conditions help shape where beliefs in moralizing high gods occur.

headline: Who is most likely to report hearing a god or sensing a spirit in the room?
title: Sensing the presence of gods and spirits across cultures and faiths
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: The authors compared reports of sensory spiritual experiences with measures of imaginative absorption and beliefs about the boundary between mind and world. They used cross-cultural patterns in these measures to propose how people come to experience gods and spirits as present.

headline: Do firewalkers' heartbeats synchronize with people who know them?
title: Synchronized arousal between performers and related spectators in a fire-walking ritual
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: At a Spanish fire-walking ritual, researchers compared heart-rate time series from walkers and spectators. They interpreted patterns of similarity involving socially connected pairs as shared arousal, even though walkers and spectators performed different actions.

headline: Does being in a good mood make a ghost or UFO video more believable?
title: Ghosts, UFOs, and Magic: Positive Affect and the Experiential System
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors reported that an induced mood interacted with a measure of intuitive thinking in predicting how believable participants found purported ghost or UFO videos. They used that interaction, along with two other tasks, to argue that good moods favor intuitive processing.

headline: Can a staged curse make people think they gave someone a headache?
title: Everyday magical powers: the role of apparent mental causation in the overestimation of personal influence
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: In a staged curse experiment, another person reported a headache, and participants rated their responsibility. The authors related those ratings to whether participants had been prompted to think hostile thoughts and used the result to explain mistaken perceptions of personal influence.

headline: Would dreaming about a plane crash make you less willing to fly?
title: When dreaming is believing: the (motivated) interpretation of dreams
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Participants considered scenarios in which they dreamed about a crash or received other information before travel. The authors compared reported travel intentions and used them to argue that people give dreams special weight when making decisions.

headline: Can the way you picture God shape who looks like a leader?
title: God as a White man: A psychological barrier to conceptualizing Black people and women as leadership worthy
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The studies related beliefs about God's race and gender to leadership judgments. In an experiment using a made-up society, participants evaluated potential leaders after learning how its god was depicted. The authors proposed that beliefs about divine authority can carry over into beliefs about human authority.

headline: Can thinking about death make you predict your culture will last thousands of years longer?
title: Long live A(me)rica! An examination of the interplay between nationalistic-symbolic immortality striving and belief in life after death
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: After a death reminder, participants who did not believe in an afterlife gave longer estimates of how long their national culture would last. The authors treated their numerical forecasts as evidence of a search for symbolic immortality.

headline: Does thinking about God change what you return to someone from another faith?
title: In their God we trust: Religious cognition increases cooperation across religious divides
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: In preregistered trust games using real money, players decided how much to return to partners from their own or another religious group. The authors used game behavior under a God reminder to study whether religious beliefs can extend cooperation across group boundaries.

headline: Do societies invoke spirits more often for storms and disease than for war?
title: Supernatural explanations across 114 societies are more common for natural than social phenomena
note: The authors coded ethnographic texts from 114 societies for supernatural explanations of events such as illness and conflict. They used the relative frequency of those explanations to assess theories linking religious belief to the tendency to see agency in nature.

headline: Do people give more money after taking part in or watching a painful ritual?
title: Extreme rituals promote prosociality
note: After two religious ceremonies in Mauritius, researchers compared anonymous donations by participants and observers. The high-ordeal ceremony group donated more on average, and the authors used the difference to argue that intense rituals promote generosity.

headline: Can a video about effective police make people less distrustful of atheists?
title: Reminders of secular authority reduce believers' distrust of atheists
note: After a video about police effectiveness or subtler reminders of secular authority, participants responded to measures of distrust toward atheists. The authors took differences across conditions as evidence that reminders of secular monitoring can shift religion-based distrust.

headline: Does thinking about God change the brain's response to making a mistake?
title: Reflecting on God: religious primes can reduce neurophysiological response to errors
note: In two experiments, the researchers measured an EEG component after task errors. Religious reminders reduced its amplitude in believers. The authors interpreted the change in that electrical signal as evidence that religious belief can buffer distress.

headline: Do countries where more people believe in hell report less crime?
title: Divergent effects of beliefs in heaven and hell on national crime rates
note: The researchers regressed reported national crime rates on survey estimates of belief in heaven and hell. The two coefficients went in opposite directions in the fitted model. The authors linked the pattern to supernatural punishment as a possible deterrent to crime.

headline: Do atheists show a stress response when they dare God to do something awful?
title: Atheists Become Emotionally Aroused When Daring God to Do Terrible Things
venue: The International Journal for the Psychology of Religion
note: Participants read aloud statements daring God to cause harm and comparison statements. The study interpreted changes in skin conductance as arousal. This measure captures a physiological response to the prompt, which also contains upsetting content.

headline: Does repeating a ritual more times make people think the magic will work better?
title: Evaluating ritual efficacy: evidence from the supernatural
note: Participants evaluated descriptions of folk rituals with features such as repeated steps and religious icons. The authors used efficacy ratings to infer which cues people use when judging unfamiliar causal processes.

headline: Can a reminder of death make people score as more religious on an implicit test?
title: Foxhole atheism, revisited: The effects of mortality salience on explicit and implicit religious belief
note: Participants received a death reminder and completed questionnaires or response-time tasks concerning supernatural agents. The authors interpreted changes on the indirect measures as increased implicit belief, while explicit responses depended on prior religious identification.

headline: Does having to prepare a public speech make you clean an object more ritualistically?
title: Effects of Anxiety on Spontaneous Ritualized Behavior
note: The researchers recorded hand movements during an object-cleaning task after an anxiety manipulation. They quantified repetition and movement patterns and interpreted those features as spontaneous ritualization under uncertainty.

headline: Can the kind of grain a region grows explain how its people think?
title: Large-scale psychological differences within China explained by rice versus wheat agriculture
note: The researchers tested 1,162 Han Chinese participants in six locations using tasks such as grouping objects and drawing social networks. They linked task differences to historical rice versus wheat cultivation and proposed that rice farming fosters interdependence. Region and farming history were measured geographically.

headline: Can the way people move chairs at Starbucks reveal a legacy of rice farming?
title: Moving chairs in Starbucks: Observational studies find rice-wheat cultural differences in daily life in China
note: In cafés in different Chinese cities, the researchers counted people sitting alone and observed whether customers moved chairs partially obstructing an aisle or squeezed through. They interpreted regional differences in these behaviors as evidence of individualism and interdependence linked to local farming history.

headline: Can a hurricane change the sounds parents choose for baby names?
title: From Karen to Katie: Using Baby Names to Understand Cultural Evolution
note: The authors analyzed historical baby-name frequencies and compared subsequent naming patterns with phonemes made salient by hurricane names. They interpreted the patterns as an effect of exposure to similar-sounding names on parents' choices.

headline: Does growing up somewhere close to 22°C change your personality?
title: Regional ambient temperature is associated with human personality
note: The authors compared regional temperatures with personality questionnaire scores in China and the United States. People from regions closer to 22°C scored differently on several traits. The proposed explanation runs from a regional temperature measure to the development of individual personality.

headline: Can smelling someone else's sweat transmit happiness?
title: A Sniff of Happiness
note: The study collected body odor from donors in different emotional conditions and measured recipients' facial muscle activity and perceptual-task performance. The authors interpreted differences after exposure to odor from happy donors as transmission of happiness.

headline: Can ancient sculptures prove that facial expressions are universal?
title: Universal facial expressions uncovered in art of the ancient Americas: A computational approach
note: Participants in the United States rated facial expressions depicted in ancient American sculptures and the emotions they expected in the depicted situations. The authors used agreement between the two sets of judgments to infer cross-cultural similarities in emotional expression.

headline: Can older adults tell from a face who was likely to betray someone in a trust game?
title: Neither inaccurate nor biased in later life: Age-related differences in the accuracy and bias of facial trustworthiness judgment
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Participants judged photographs of men selected from the high and low ends of betrayal rates in a repeated trust game. The authors used those game outcomes as the benchmark for facial trustworthiness judgments and reported comparable accuracy across age groups.

headline: Can a country's history of infectious disease explain how outgoing its people are?
title: Pathogens, personality, and culture: Disease prevalence predicts worldwide variability in sociosexuality, extraversion, and openness to experience
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors correlated historical pathogen prevalence with aggregate scores for extraversion, openness, and attitudes toward casual sex. They proposed disease avoidance as an explanation for national differences in personality and behavior.

headline: Can hormone levels predict which days women wear red?
title: Lady in Red: Hormonal Predictors of Women's Clothing Choices
note: The researchers tracked salivary hormones and coded clothing color across women’s cycles. They reported that hormone measures consistent with higher fertility predicted red clothing choices and interpreted the association as a possible fertility signal. A later study found little support when analyzing several clothing colors jointly. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.yhbeh.2017.03.005

headline: Does a bottle of water look closer when you are thirsty?
title: Wishful Seeing: More Desired Objects Are Seen as Closer
note: The authors tested whether desirable objects seemed closer, using measures such as verbal distance estimates and beanbag throws. They interpreted shorter estimates and throws as evidence that wanting something changes perceived distance.

headline: Does calling someone a consumer make you trust them less?
title: Cuing consumerism: situational materialism undermines personal and social well-being
note: In a hypothetical water-shortage scenario, participants given consumer language reported less trust in others to conserve water. Many Labs 2 found a substantially smaller difference for this trust rating, with standardized effect size d = 0.12 versus d = 0.87 in the original experiment. https://doi.org/10.1177/2515245918810225

headline: Does wearing a university sweatshirt before admission make rejection feel more likely?
title: Why people are reluctant to tempt fate
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Participants assigned likelihoods to ironic bad outcomes after hypothetical acts said to tempt fate. The authors attributed the ratings to which outcomes came to mind and predicted stronger effects under cognitive load. A registered multisite replication did not recover the cognitive-load interaction. https://doi.org/10.1177/2515245918785165

headline: Does making an attractive stranger harder to look at make them more memorable?
title: Forbidden fruit: inattention to attractive alternatives provokes implicit relationship reactance
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors used an attention task that directed participants away from attractive faces. They linked changes in attention and memory for those faces to a proposed reaction to restrictions on noticing romantic alternatives.

headline: Do people with more siblings grow up to be more cooperative?
title: Development of prosocial, individualistic, and competitive orientations: theory and preliminary evidence
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The researchers classified people as prosocial, individualistic, or competitive from their choices in allocation tasks. They compared these classifications with family composition and used the association to propose a developmental role for siblings. Many Labs 2 did not recover the original difference in sibling counts. https://doi.org/10.1177/2515245918810225

headline: Can personality questionnaires divide the United States into three psychological regions?
title: Divided we stand: three psychological regions of the United States and their political, economic, social, and health correlates
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The study clustered regional Big Five profiles into three groups and related them to state-level indicators. The three psychological regions were derived from clusters of aggregated questionnaire scores.

headline: Can saying “I’m excited” make you sing karaoke better?
title: Get excited: reappraising pre-performance anxiety as excitement
note: Participants used short self-statements before tasks such as karaoke, public speaking, and math. The authors interpreted differences in task performance as an effect of reinterpreting anxiety as excitement.

headline: Can describing a game as “for really, really smart children” change who wants to play?
title: Gender stereotypes about intellectual ability emerge early and influence children's interests
note: Children assigned the description of high intelligence to people and rated their interest in games with different descriptions. The authors used the age and gender differences in those responses to infer when a stereotype about brilliance starts shaping interests.

headline: Can a jersey number change how good you think an athlete is?
title: Incidental environmental anchors
note: The study varied an athlete's jersey number and compared ratings of his performance. Other experiments changed a product model number or a number in a restaurant's name. The authors interpreted shifts in numerical judgments as incidental anchoring.

headline: Can calculating your hourly wage spoil a song?
title: Time, money, and happiness: How does putting a price on time affect our ability to smell the roses?
note: Participants asked to think about income as an hourly wage reported less happiness after listening to music. The authors used reported impatience as a proposed explanation. An independent replication project failed to reproduce the original pattern. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jesp.2015.08.005

headline: Can signing your name change how you shop?
title: The Signature Effect: Signing Influences Consumption-Related Behavior by Priming Self-Identity
note: Across four studies the authors compared consumption-related responses after signing one's name and interpreted differences in engagement and conformity as activation of a consumer identity.

headline: Do baby names fade faster if they become popular too quickly?
title: How adoption speed affects the abandonment of cultural tastes
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: The authors analyzed more than a century of baby-name frequencies in France and the United States and surveyed expecting parents about names. They proposed that rapid growth in popularity makes names look like short-lived fads and discourages adoption.

headline: Can listing more examples of being assertive make you think you are less assertive?
title: Ease of retrieval as information: Another look at the availability heuristic
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The experiment asked participants to recall six or twelve examples of assertive or unassertive behavior and then rate themselves. The authors interpreted the reversal in self-ratings as use of perceived retrieval difficulty as information.

headline: Could spelling DIE with your initials predict a shorter life?
title: What’s in a Name: Mortality and the Power of Symbols
note: Using California death records, the authors reported different lifespans among men with initials they classified as positive or negative words.

headline: Can flashing a stimulus to one person produce an EEG signal in someone sitting apart?
title: Electroencephalographic Evidence of Correlated Event-Related Signals Between the Brains of Spatially and Sensory Isolated Human Subjects
venue: Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine
note: The authors reported time-linked EEG changes in some isolated partners who were not themselves shown the visual stimulus.

headline: Can drinking sugar make a hill look less steep?
title: Direct Evidence for the Economy of Action: Glucose and the Perception of Geographical Slant
note: Participants who drank a glucose-sweetened drink gave lower visual estimates of a hill’s slope than participants who drank an artificially sweetened drink.

headline: Can a vaccination reminder or hand wipe shift attitudes toward immigrants?
title: Immunizing Against Prejudice: Effects of Disease Protection on Attitudes Toward Out-Groups
note: Across studies, cues to protection from disease reduced some associations between disease concerns and negative attitudes toward outsiders.

headline: So hungry you could use a few more binder clips?
title: Hunger Promotes Acquisition of Nonfood Objects
note: Researchers used office binder clips to test whether hunger changes how people acquire things they cannot eat. They reported that hungrier participants took more clips without saying they liked them any better.

headline: Does lying out loud make mouthwash more appealing while typing a lie makes hand sanitizer more appealing?
title: Dirty Hands and Dirty Mouths: Embodiment of the Moral-Purity Metaphor Is Specific to the Motor Modality Involved in Moral Transgression
note: After communicating a lie by voice or text, participants showed different preferences for a mouth cleaner or a hand cleaner.

headline: Do people disproportionately marry someone whose surname starts with the same letter?
title: How Do I Love Thee? Let Me Count the Js: Implicit Egotism and Interpersonal Attraction
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors reported above-expected surname-initial matching in marriage records and greater attraction to people with related name cues in experiments.

headline: Does a hurricane with your initial get more of your donation money?
title: In the “I” of the Storm: Shared Initials Increase Disaster Donations
note: In donation records, people whose first initial matched a hurricane’s name were disproportionately represented among donors to the corresponding relief effort.

headline: Does the smell of fish protect your memory from misinformation?
title: Resisting misinformation via discrepancy detection: effects of an unaware suspicion cue
note: The authors used fishy or neutral room odors during exposure to misleading information to investigate whether suspicion cues affect memory errors.

headline: Can counting money make physical pain hurt less?
title: The symbolic power of money: reminders of money alter social distress and physical pain
note: The authors reported that reminders of money reduced distress from social exclusion and ratings of physical pain.

headline: Are people more likely to marry someone with the same birthday numbers?
title: When Tex and Tess Carpenter Build Houses in Texas: Moderators of Implicit Egotism
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Can a fishy smell help you spot a misleading question?
title: Something smells fishy: Olfactory suspicion cues improve performance on the Moses illusion and Wason rule discovery task
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Can an EEG distinguish when a medium says they are communicating with the dead?
title: Electrocortical Activity Associated With Subjective Communication With the Deceased
note: In a small study of self-identified mediums, the authors reported EEG differences across subjective communication and comparison tasks. The condition was based on the mediums’ experience.

headline: Can the smell of cleaner make you clean up your crumbs?
title: Smells like clean spirit. Nonconscious effects of scent on cognition and behavior
note: Participants exposed to a cleaning-product scent reportedly removed more crumbs while eating than those without the scent.

headline: Can a bad smell make you more morally judgmental?
title: Disgust as embodied moral judgment
note: The experiments exposed people to incidental disgust and recorded moral ratings.

headline: Can guilt make your body feel heavier?
title: The Weight of a Guilty Conscience: Subjective Body Weight as an Embodiment of Guilt
note: Participants' reported sense of body weight was compared after recalling different actions.

headline: Are people who like bitter flavors more likely to score high on sadism questionnaires?
title: Individual Differences in Bitter Taste Preferences Are Associated With Antisocial Personality Traits
note: In two surveys, participants rated tastes and completed personality questionnaires. The authors reported associations between a preference for bitter tastes and several traits, including everyday sadism.

headline: Can believing you drank alcohol make you rate yourself as more attractive?
title: ‘Beauty Is in the Eye of the Beer Holder’: People Who Think They Are Drunk Also Think They Are Attractive
note: In a balanced-placebo experiment with 94 people, the group told it had consumed alcohol rated its own videotaped performance more favorably. Independent judges’ ratings did not show the corresponding boost.

headline: Can smile intensity in a baseball photograph predict how long the player lived?
title: Smile Intensity in Photographs Predicts Longevity
note: The authors categorized smiles in archival baseball photographs and related the categories to survival times, reporting a longer lifespan for players with full smiles in their data.

headline: Does feeling powerful make people draw an E that looks backward to someone facing them?
title: Power and Perspectives Not Taken
note: Participants primed with power were more likely to draw a letter on their forehead oriented for themselves. Other experiments measured perspective-taking errors.

headline: Do people prompted to feel powerful judge others’ cheating more harshly while cheating more themselves?
title: Power Increases Hypocrisy: Moralizing in Reasoning, Immorality in Behavior
note: The authors reported that some power manipulations increased the gap between judgments of others’ misconduct and participants’ own choices.

headline: Can reading Kafka improve performance at finding patterns in letter strings?
title: Connections From Kafka: Exposure to Meaning Threats Improves Implicit Learning of an Artificial Grammar
note: After reading a surreal story or a comparison text, participants classified letter strings. The authors interpreted performance differences as increased pattern learning following a threat to meaning.

headline: Can a drug change whether people say they would directly harm one person to save several?
title: Serotonin Selectively Influences Moral Judgment and Behavior Through Effects on Harm Aversion
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: The authors compared hypothetical moral choices and bargaining decisions after drug or placebo administration. They interpreted shifted choices as increased aversion to harming others.

headline: Can repeated interviews lead people to describe a crime researchers suggested they had committed?
title: Constructing Rich False Memories of Committing Crime
note: The authors suggested false events during repeated interviews and coded participants’ reports. The headline result depended on which reports counted as false memories. A published reanalysis challenged which responses qualified as memories (doi:10.1177/0956797617703667).

headline: Can a briefcase on the table make a bargaining partner less generous?
title: Material priming: The influence of mundane physical objects on situational construal and competitive behavioral choice
venue: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
note: Across experiments, exposure to business-related objects such as briefcases and boardroom tables was reported to increase competitive thoughts, make ambiguous interactions seem less cooperative, and increase how much participants kept for themselves in an ultimatum game.

headline: Can a glimpse of red hurt your test score?
title: Color and psychological functioning: the effect of red on performance attainment
note: The authors reported poorer achievement-task performance following brief exposure to red compared with control colors.

headline: Can just reading the word RED make you worse at reasoning?
title: The semantic red effect: Processing the word red undermines intellectual performance
note: Four experiments reportedly found poorer intellectual task performance after processing the word red.

headline: Can men smell when ovulation is approaching?
title: Body odor attractiveness as a cue of impending ovulation in women: evidence from a study using hormone-confirmed ovulation
note: Men rated scent samples collected at different points in women's cycles.

headline: Can a disgust cue change how people answer a question about same-sex marriage?
title: Disgust and the Politics of Sex: Exposure to a Disgusting Odorant Increases Politically Conservative Views on Sex and Decreases Support for Gay Marriage
note: The authors reported that exposure to a foul odor shifted answers to several sex-related political questions in a conservative direction.

headline: After a disgusting film clip, does washing your hands make you judge others less harshly?
title: With a Clean Conscience: Cleanliness Reduces the Severity of Moral Judgments
note: After watching a clip meant to provoke disgust, some participants washed their hands. The authors reported that those who washed up gave more lenient judgments when presented with a series of moral dilemmas.

headline: Spatial reasoning test coming up? Cue Mozart.
title: Music and Spatial Task Performance
note: College students took spatial reasoning tests after listening to a Mozart sonata for two pianos, hearing relaxation instructions or sitting in silence. The paper reported a short-lived advantage after Mozart.

headline: Can a red or pink shirt give away where you are in your cycle?
title: Women Are More Likely to Wear Red or Pink at Peak Fertility
note: Researchers estimated the likelihood of conception from menstrual cycle dates and compared it with the shirt color participants reported wearing. The paper reported more red or pink shirts in the higher-fertility group.

headline: Does a heavier clipboard make a job applicant seem more important?
title: Incidental Haptic Sensations Influence Social Judgments and Decisions
note: Participants evaluated job applicants while holding lighter or heavier clipboards. The authors reported that the weight influenced the evaluations. Other experiments used rough puzzles and hard or soft chairs to test social judgments and bargaining decisions.

headline: Does dimming the lights make people cheat?
title: Good lamps are the best police: darkness increases dishonesty and self-interested behavior
note: Participants completing a task under dim lighting reportedly claimed more unearned money than those in brighter surroundings.

headline: Can thinking about time instead of money make you more honest?
title: Time, money, and morality
note: The authors reported that reminders of money increased cheating, whereas reminders of time reduced it in experimental tasks.

headline: Does being left out make the room feel colder?
title: Cold and Lonely: Does Social Exclusion Literally Feel Cold?
note: Participants recalled social exclusion or inclusion. The authors reported lower estimated room temperatures after exclusion and greater preference for warm food and drinks in a separate experiment.

headline: Can a fishy smell make you distrust a stranger?
title: Bidirectionality, mediation, and moderation of metaphorical effects: the embodiment of social suspicion and fishy smells
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors linked incidental fish odors with reduced cooperation in economic games, interpreting the result through the metaphor of suspicion.

headline: Can a messy room make you more creative?
title: Physical Order Produces Healthy Choices, Generosity, and Conventionality, Whereas Disorder Produces Creativity
note: The authors reported that people in a disordered room generated more creative ideas. A follow-up using orderly and disorderly workspaces found no creativity advantage for the latter. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2018.02662

headline: Can a reminder of God make you give away more money?
title: God is watching you: priming God concepts increases prosocial behavior in an anonymous economic game
note: Participants completed a word task and then allocated money in an anonymous game. The authors reported more generous allocations after religious cues.

headline: Does cleaning your hands make you MORE judgmental?
title: A clean self can render harsh moral judgment
note: The authors reported harsher moral evaluations after participants cleaned their hands or imagined themselves clean.

headline: Can your bathing habits reveal loneliness?
title: The Substitutability of Physical and Social Warmth in Daily Life
note: The researchers linked self-reported loneliness to more frequent, longer and warmer baths or showers in one student sample.

headline: Does liking sweets make you a sweeter person?
title: Sweet taste preferences and experiences predict prosocial inferences, personalities, and behaviors
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors related a preference for sweet foods to prosocial personality measures, intentions and behaviors.

headline: Can wiping your hands change the goals you pursue?
title: Embodiment as Procedures: Physical Cleansing Changes Goal Priming Effects
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Does warmth make you seek company after a threat?
title: Embodied effects are moderated by situational cues: Warmth, threat, and the desire for affiliation
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Would women guard their partners from a woman in red?
title: Red and Romantic Rivalry
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Does thinking about karma or God make believers less selfish?
title: Supernatural norm enforcement: Thinking about karma and God reduces selfishness among believers
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Can religious words make people spend money punishing unfairness?
title: Wrath of God: religious primes and punishment
venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Do women dress more attractively near ovulation?
title: Ovulatory shifts in human female ornamentation: near ovulation, women dress to impress
note: The study compared photographs of women taken during different cycle phases.

headline: Can men spot fertility from the way women dance or walk?
title: Women’s body movements are a potential cue to ovulation
note: Men rated movement silhouettes from recordings at two cycle phases.

headline: Does a woman's face look better during her fertile phase?
title: Female facial attractiveness increases during the fertile phase of the menstrual cycle
venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences
note: The authors compared ratings of facial attractiveness at different cycle phases.

headline: Can wearing a swimsuit make women perform worse on a math test?
title: That swimsuit becomes you: Sex differences in self-objectification, restrained eating, and math performance
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Women who tried on a swimsuit were compared with women who tried on a sweater. The authors reported more body shame and restrained eating, and lower math performance, among women in the swimsuit condition; the reported effects did not appear for men.

headline: Does chocolate smell stronger when it is linked to your national identity?
title: Swiss identity smells like chocolate: Social identity shapes olfactory judgments
note: Participants’ national identity was made salient before they rated odors. The authors reported that Swiss participants rated chocolate as more pleasant or intense after Swiss identity cues, while the effect did not extend to an unrelated popcorn odor.

headline: Can distracted “unconscious thought” pick the better car or apartment?
title: Think different: The merits of unconscious thought in preference development and decision making
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Across five experiments, participants considered multi-attribute options such as cars, then either deliberated or completed a distraction task. The paper reported that distracted participants made higher-quality choices on complex decisions.

headline: Do complex choices improve if people stop thinking about them for a while?
title: On making the right choice: The deliberation-without-attention effect
note: Participants chose among alternatives with multiple attributes, including cars and houses. The authors reported that complex choices were better after a distraction period than after deliberate conscious thought.

headline: Can a banknote’s “moral history” change how people judge economic choices?
title: Dirty Money: The Role of Moral History in Economic Judgments
note: Across eight experiments, participants considered currency associated with different moral histories. The authors reported that people treated physical money as if traces of its prior use could affect later economic judgments.

headline: Does an unpleasant smell make a monetary loss feel worse?
title: Unpleasant odors increase aversion to monetary losses
note: Participants made monetary gamble choices while exposed to pleasant or unpleasant odors. The authors reported greater loss aversion in the unpleasant-odor condition.

headline: Can a smell people cannot identify make them trust a stranger with more money?
title: The Subtle Signaling Strength of Smells: A Masked Odor Enhances Interpersonal Trust
note: In two experiments, participants exposed to hexanal masked by clove odor gave more money to a trustee and rated faces as more trustworthy than participants exposed to the mask odor alone. The study reported the shift even though participants could not tell the masked odor apart.

headline: Can a smell below conscious detection change how likable a face seems?
title: Subliminal smells can guide social preferences
note: Participants rated neutral faces after pleasant, neutral, or unpleasant odors were delivered below the detection threshold. The paper reported that odor valence shifted face-liking ratings most among participants who could not consciously detect the odors.

headline: Can someone’s unpleasant body odor make strangers more helpful toward them?
title: Smells like cooperation? Unpleasant body odor and people’s perceptions and helping behaviors
