note: Across three experiments, an unpleasant body odor was reported to elicit pity and increase helping, but only when the person was not held responsible for the odor.

headline: Can drinking something bitter make unrelated moral violations seem worse?
title: A bad taste in the mouth: Gustatory disgust influences moral judgment
note: Participants sampled bitter, sweet, or neutral drinks before rating moral scenarios. The original study reported harsher judgments after the bitter drink, especially among a subgroup of participants.

headline: Can thinking about virtue make a bland drink taste better?
title: The bitter truth about morality: Virtue, not vice, makes a bland beverage taste nice
note: Across experiments, participants considered moral or immoral actions and then rated a bland beverage. The paper reported that reflecting on virtuous behavior made the drink taste better, while reflecting on vice did not produce the same pattern.

headline: Does unfair treatment make people wrinkle their noses like they tasted something disgusting?
title: In bad taste: Evidence for the oral origins of moral disgust
note: Researchers compared facial muscle activity after unpleasant tastes, pictures of contaminants, and unfair treatment in an economic game. The authors reported overlapping facial responses to physical disgust and unfairness.

headline: Can a photocopied pair of eyes nearly triple payment for shared tea and coffee?
title: Cues of being watched enhance cooperation in a real-world setting
note: In a shared workplace kitchen with an honesty box, researchers alternated a poster showing eyes with a poster showing flowers. They reported that people paid nearly three times as much for drinks when the eyes were displayed.

headline: Can a nasal spray change how much money someone entrusts to a stranger?
title: Oxytocin increases trust in humans
note: Participants received intranasal oxytocin or placebo and played an investment game with anonymous partners. The authors reported that oxytocin increased the amount investors entrusted to strangers, while not increasing risk-taking in a nonsocial control task.

headline: Can odorless tears reduce men’s attraction to women’s faces?
title: Human tears contain a chemosignal
note: Men smelled odorless emotional tears collected from women or a control saline solution while rating images. The paper reported reduced ratings of women’s sexual appeal after smelling tears, alongside lower testosterone and reduced activity in brain regions linked to sexual arousal.

headline: Can oxytocin make people give more money to an anonymous stranger?
title: Oxytocin increases generosity in humans
note: Participants received oxytocin or placebo and decided how much money to share with an anonymous stranger in an ultimatum game. The authors reported an 80% increase in generosity after oxytocin.

headline: Did athletes wearing red win more often at the 2004 Olympics?
title: Red enhances human performance in contests
note: The authors analyzed men’s combat-sport matches at the 2004 Olympic Games. Across several sports, athletes assigned red uniforms were reported to win more often than those assigned blue.

headline: Does briefly holding a cold pack make people trust a stranger with less money?
title: Physical temperature effects on trust behavior: The role of insula
note: Participants briefly held a warm or cold pack before playing an economic trust game. The study reported that cold, compared with warm, reduced the amount participants invested in a stranger in the behavioral experiment.

headline: Are strangers more likely to give money when a panhandler asks for exactly 17 cents?
title: Hey Buddy, Can You Spare Seventeen Cents? Mindful Persuasion and the Pique Technique
note: In a field experiment, a panhandler made either a typical request or an oddly specific request for 17 cents. The authors reported greater compliance with the unusual request, which they argued interrupted people’s routine refusal response.

headline: Can seeing a picture of a library make people speak more quietly?
title: The silence of the library: Environment, situational norm, and social behavior
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Across experiments, participants were exposed to pictures of settings such as a library or a train station. The authors reported that the library image activated the norm of silence and reduced participants’ voice volume on a later task.

headline: Can a cold object make people less helpful after good service but more helpful after bad service?
title: The “warm” side of coldness: Cold promotes interpersonal warmth in negative contexts
note: Across experiments, participants touched cold or warm objects before evaluating or responding to another person. The authors reported a context-dependent reversal: cold cues reduced helping after good service but increased helping after poor service.

headline: Can an Israeli flag you do not consciously see shift your political attitudes?
title: Subliminal Exposure to National Flags Affects Political Thought and Behavior
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: The authors reported that a briefly flashed Israeli flag shifted political attitudes toward the center and also affected reported voting behavior.

headline: Do skateboarders crash more often when an attractive woman is watching?
title: The Presence of an Attractive Woman Elevates Testosterone and Physical Risk Taking in Young Men
note: The field experiment reported more risky tricks, including both successful landings and crashes, with a female observer than with a male observer; measured testosterone also differed.

headline: Do favorable parole rulings spike just after a break?
title: Extraneous Factors in Judicial Decisions
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: In an observational dataset of Israeli parole rulings, favorable decisions were more frequent early in a session and after breaks. The study recorded ruling order and breaks, not judges’ hunger.

headline: Can bronze medalists look happier than silver medalists?
title: When Less Is More: Counterfactual Thinking and Satisfaction Among Olympic Medalists
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Observers rated bronze medalists’ televised reactions as happier than silver medalists’ reactions at the 1992 Olympics.

headline: Does thinking faster make people take more risks?
title: Fast Thought Speed Induces Risk Taking
note: The authors reported that experimentally speeding up the pace of participants’ thoughts increased risk taking across two experiments.

headline: Can thinking about your death make you more supportive of George W. Bush?
title: Deliver Us From Evil: The Effects of Mortality Salience and Reminders of 9/11 on Support for President George W. Bush
note: In one experiment, participants prompted to think about their own death expressed more support for Bush and his counterterrorism policies than the comparison group.

headline: Can writing about your death make a charismatic candidate more appealing?
title: Fatal Attraction: The Effects of Mortality Salience on Evaluations of Charismatic, Task-Oriented, and Relationship-Oriented Leaders
note: Participants who wrote about death were more likely to favor a hypothetical candidate presented as charismatic.

headline: Can crossing your arms make you stick with an unsolvable puzzle?
title: The Effect of Arm Crossing on Persistence and Performance
note: Participants instructed to cross their arms persisted longer on an unsolvable anagram than controls; a second experiment reported better performance on solvable anagrams.

headline: Can the smell of window cleaner make people send more money to a stranger?
title: The Smell of Virtue: Clean Scents Promote Reciprocity and Charity
note: Participants in a room scented with a citrus cleaner returned more money in a trust game; another experiment reported greater willingness to volunteer or donate.

headline: Can a hypnotic cue make an arbitrary word change a moral verdict?
title: Hypnotic Disgust Makes Moral Judgments More Severe
note: Participants were hypnotically instructed to feel disgust at a particular word. The authors reported harsher ratings for vignettes containing that word.

headline: Can washing your hands after failure make you more optimistic but worse at the next task?
title: Washing One’s Hands After Failure Enhances Optimism but Hampers Future Performance
note: After a difficult task, participants who washed their hands reported more optimism about another attempt, but performed worse than those who did not wash.

headline: Can red dye make a white wine smell like red wine to trained tasters?
title: The Color of Odors
note: Wine tasters switched to odor descriptors associated with red wine when the white wine they smelled was colored red with an odorless dye.

headline: Can the same wine taste better with an expensive price tag?
title: Marketing Actions Can Modulate Neural Representations of Experienced Pleasantness
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Participants gave higher pleasantness ratings to the same wine when it was presented as more expensive; the paper also reported a difference in imaging signals.

headline: Can an unpleasant smell shift implicit judgments about gay men?
title: Disgusting Smells Cause Decreased Liking of Gay Men
note: In a lab experiment, exposure to a bad smell was associated with less favorable implicit evaluations of gay men than a control condition.

headline: Can a heavy backpack make a person feel guiltier or choose a lighter snack?
title: The Burden of Guilt: Heavy Backpacks, Light Snacks, and Enhanced Morality
note: Across experiments, the authors linked wearing a heavier backpack to greater reported guilt and to downstream choices such as choosing lighter snacks.

headline: Can reminiscing make a cold room feel warmer?
title: Heartwarming Memories: Nostalgia Maintains Physiological Comfort
note: Across studies, colder conditions were associated with greater nostalgia, and nostalgic recollection led to higher estimates of room temperature or longer cold tolerance.

headline: Does enjoying spicy food and other unpleasant sensations relate to antisocial traits?
title: Common, Nonsexual Masochistic Preferences Are Positively Associated With Antisocial Personality Traits
note: The authors reported positive associations between enjoyment of ordinarily unpleasant experiences and questionnaire measures of antisocial traits.

headline: Can a sugary drink reverse a drop in self-control on a subsequent task?
title: Self-Control Relies on Glucose as a Limited Energy Source: Willpower Is More Than a Metaphor
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Across studies, the authors reported lower glucose after some self-control tasks and better subsequent task performance after a drink containing glucose.

headline: Can drinking something bitter make people more hostile toward an unrelated person?
title: Bitter Taste Causes Hostility
note: Across experiments, the authors reported that bitter tastes increased measures of hostility relative to comparison conditions.

headline: Can listeners guess someone’s history of infidelity from a short recording of their voice?
title: Your Cheatin’ Voice Will Tell on You: Detection of Past Infidelity from Voice
note: Listeners rated recordings of people who reported different histories of infidelity. The authors reported that ratings differentiated the groups.

headline: Can standing next to a friend make a hill look less steep?
title: Social Support and the Perception of Geographical Slant
note: Participants estimated a hill as less steep when accompanied by a friend or after imagining a supportive person, compared with their respective controls.

headline: Can throwing a heavy ball make a target look farther away?
title: Perceiving Distance: A Role of Effort and Intent
note: Participants who expected to throw a heavier ball gave larger distance estimates than those who expected to throw a lighter one.

headline: Does putting on a heavy backpack make the same hill look steeper?
title: Visual-Motor Recalibration in Geographical Slant Perception
venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
note: The authors reported larger explicit slope estimates under increased physical load, with a different pattern in a hand adjustment task.

headline: Can sitting in a roomier seat make people cheat or keep money they were overpaid?
title: The Ergonomics of Dishonesty: The Effect of Incidental Posture on Stealing, Cheating, and Traffic Violations
note: Experiments linked more expansive postures with keeping an overpayment or cheating. A separate street observation linked larger driver seats with double parking.

headline: Can handwashing reverse the effect of a winning or losing streak on the next gamble?
title: Washing Away Your (Good or Bad) Luck: Physical Cleansing Affects Risk-Taking Behavior
note: In laboratory tasks, handwashing shifted risk taking in opposite directions after prior good and bad luck.

headline: Can red lipstick change how much men tip their waitress?
title: Lipstick and Tipping Behavior: When Red Lipstick Enhance Waitresses Tips
note: In a restaurant field study, male diners tipped more often or more generously in the red lipstick condition. The authors did not report the same pattern for female diners.

headline: Can an ugly font help students remember what they read?
title: Fortune Favors the Bold (and the Italicized): Effects of Disfluency on Educational Outcomes
note: The authors reported higher retention after participants read material in harder-to-read fonts, including in a classroom study.

headline: Can a shared birthday make someone more willing to do a favor for a stranger?
title: What a Coincidence! The Effects of Incidental Similarity on Compliance
note: Participants were more likely to comply with requests from people with whom they had been led to believe they shared an incidental similarity, such as a birthday.

headline: Do names show statistical links to what people do for a living?
title: Does the First Letter of One’s Name Affect Life Decisions? A Natural Language Processing Examination of Nominative Determinism
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Word embedding analyses linked first names to cities and occupations starting with the same letter. The data came from published text.

headline: Can adding a middle initial make the author of the same essay look smarter?
title: The Impact of Middle Names: Middle Name Initials Enhance Evaluations of Intellectual Performance
note: Readers gave more favorable intellectual evaluations when an author’s displayed name included middle initials.

headline: Can strangers match a person’s first name to a photo above chance?
title: We Look Like Our Names: The Manifestation of Name Stereotypes in Facial Appearance
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Participants selected the correct first name from alternatives more often than chance in several face-matching experiments.

headline: Do adults’ faces fit their names more than children’s faces do?
title: Can Names Shape Facial Appearance?
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Human judges matched names to adult faces above chance. The authors reported a different pattern for children and also compared adult and child faces computationally.

headline: Do babies pick a puppet that mistreated another puppet with different snack tastes?
title: Not Like Me = Bad: Infants Prefer Those Who Harm Dissimilar Others
note: Infants saw puppets share or differ from their own food preferences. The authors reported that infants sometimes selected a puppet that had hindered the dissimilar character.

headline: Can smelling another person’s sweat shift your facial expression toward fear or disgust?
title: Chemosignals Communicate Human Emotions
note: Women exposed to sweat collected from men watching fear or disgust videos showed different patterns of facial muscle activity and visual exploration.

headline: Do men’s testosterone levels differ after smelling shirts worn near ovulation?
title: Scent of a Woman: Men’s Testosterone Responses to Olfactory Ovulation Cues
note: The authors reported higher testosterone responses after men smelled shirts worn by women near ovulation than in comparison conditions.

headline: Can labeling the same coat a doctor’s coat or a painter’s coat change attention scores?
title: Enclothed Cognition
note: The authors reported different attention scores depending on whether participants wore the coat and what the experimenter called it.

headline: Do people who hit better remember the softball as bigger?
title: See the Ball, Hit the Ball: Apparent Ball Size Is Correlated With Batting Average
note: After games, better-performing softball players selected larger circles when asked to match the size of the ball.

headline: Can irrelevant neuroscience jargon make a bad psychological explanation seem better?
title: The Seductive Allure of Neuroscience Explanations
note: In the nonexpert groups, irrelevant neuroscience details made poor explanations seem more satisfying, even though the details added no explanatory information.

headline: Can a poster with staring eyes reduce bicycle theft on the rack beside it?
title: ‘Cycle Thieves, We Are Watching You’: Impact of a Simple Signage Intervention Against Bicycle Theft
note: Reported thefts fell at university racks with warning posters displaying eyes. Theft reports increased at other sites over the same period.

headline: Can a red screen improve detail work while a blue screen improves creativity?
title: Blue or Red? Exploring the Effect of Color on Cognitive Task Performances
note: Across experiments, participants performed differently on detail-oriented and creative tasks depending on the background color used.

headline: Can a glimpse of a fast-food logo make people read faster even with no deadline?
title: You Are How You Eat: Fast Food and Impatience
note: Across studies, fast-food cues were linked to quicker reading, stronger preference for time-saving products, or less willingness to wait for a financial reward.

headline: Can briefly holding a warm drink make someone feel closer to people they know?
title: The Thermometer of Social Relations: Mapping Social Proximity on Temperature
note: The authors reported greater perceived social proximity after exposure to warmth, and also tested whether perceived social proximity affected estimates of room temperature.

headline: Can room temperature change whether people imagine themselves moving through time or time moving toward them?
title: Taking the Temperature of Time: The Influence of Temperature on People’s Metaphorical Perspectives on Time Through Emotion
note: The authors reported that temperature affected responses to tasks distinguishing two different ways of thinking about movement through time.

headline: Can ratings of a nonprofit CEO’s face predict anything about the organization’s finances?
title: Predicting Firm Success From the Facial Appearance of Chief Executive Officers of Non-Profit Organizations
note: The researchers compared impressions formed from CEO photos with organizational financial records and reported statistical associations between the two.

headline: Does arranging a salad like a Kandinsky painting make it taste better?
title: A Taste of Kandinsky: Assessing the Influence of the Artistic Visual Presentation of Food on the Dining Experience
note: Diners gave higher taste ratings to a salad arranged to resemble a Kandinsky painting than to other presentations of the same ingredients.

headline: Can tasting something sweet make a potential date look more appealing?
title: Sweet Love: The Effects of Sweet Taste Experience on Romantic Perceptions
venue: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
note: The authors reported more favorable ratings of a hypothetical romantic relationship in sweet-taste conditions across several experiments.

headline: Do men with higher testosterone add more hot sauce to their food?
title: Some Like It Hot: Testosterone Predicts Laboratory Eating Behavior of Spicy Food
note: Men were allowed to season mashed potatoes with hot sauce. Salivary testosterone was positively associated with how much hot sauce they added.

headline: Can seeing fast food make someone enjoy a piece of music less?
title: Too Impatient to Smell the Roses: Exposure to Fast Food Impedes Happiness
note: In experiments, prior fast-food cues reduced reported pleasure from savoring experiences such as listening to music or viewing nature photos.

headline: Can 18-month-olds track somebody else mistaking one penguin-shaped object for another?
title: Which Penguin Is This? Attributing False Beliefs About Object Identity at 18 Months
note: Infants’ looking times varied across scenes involving penguin-shaped objects that looked alike but differed in a property an actor had or had not seen.

headline: Do babies expect a smaller animated block to yield to a larger one?
title: Big and Mighty: Preverbal Infants Mentally Represent Social Dominance
note: Infants looked longer when a larger animated character yielded right of way to a smaller one than when the smaller character yielded.

headline: Do five-month-olds look longer when a hidden doll seems to vanish during addition?
title: Addition and Subtraction by Human Infants
note: Dolls were added to or removed from behind a screen. The infants looked longer at some final displays that did not match the number implied by the preceding events.

headline: Can strangers sort Democrat and Republican candidates by their faces?
title: Democrats and Republicans Can Be Differentiated From Their Faces
note: Participants guessed candidates’ party affiliations from faces at above-chance rates in the reported experiments.

headline: Can an equation that never reaches awareness prime its answer?
title: Reading and Doing Arithmetic Nonconsciously
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Participants’ responses to visible numbers were faster in some conditions when the numbers matched the solution to a preceding suppressed arithmetic expression.

headline: Can people learn to choose a cue they cannot consciously see?
title: Subliminal Instrumental Conditioning Demonstrated in the Human Brain
note: Participants’ choices gradually favored masked symbols associated with monetary rewards rather than losses, according to the authors.

headline: Does watching an art film change how well viewers answer mental-state questions?
title: Art Films Foster Theory of Mind
note: The researchers compared later test scores across film conditions and reported higher scores following art films.

headline: Can an oxytocin nasal spray improve scores on a test made of photos of eyes?
title: Oxytocin Improves “Mind-Reading” in Humans
note: The authors reported that men given oxytocin performed better than under placebo on a task requiring them to select mental-state words for pictures of eyes.

headline: Does taking acetaminophen lower how much pain you attribute to a stranger?
title: From Painkiller to Empathy Killer: Acetaminophen (Paracetamol) Reduces Empathy for Pain
note: After receiving acetaminophen or placebo, participants rated others’ pain in several tasks. The authors reported lower empathy ratings in the acetaminophen group.

headline: Does taking acetaminophen change how much social rejection hurts?
title: Acetaminophen Reduces Social Pain: Behavioral and Neural Evidence
note: The authors reported lower daily ratings of hurt feelings in one experiment and different brain activity during a virtual social exclusion task in another.

headline: Does telling children that an invisible princess is watching make them less likely to cheat?
title: “Princess Alice Is Watching You”: Children’s Belief in an Invisible Person Inhibits Cheating
note: Children played a rule-based game after the experimenter left. Those who believed that an invisible person was present were reported to be less likely to break the rules.

headline: Can ratings of minds place a fetus, a robot and God along two dimensions?
title: Dimensions of Mind Perception
note: Participants rated different beings for mental capacities. The authors used factor analysis to group the ratings along dimensions they called experience and agency.

headline: Can how stereotypical a defendant’s face looks predict a death sentence?
title: Looking Deathworthy: Perceived Stereotypicality of Black Defendants Predicts Capital-Sentencing Outcomes
note: Among the Black defendants in the study whose victims were White, higher ratings of stereotypical appearance were associated with a greater likelihood of a death sentence.

headline: Can viewers guess the sexual orientation of men in selected photos after 50 milliseconds?
title: Brief Exposures: Male Sexual Orientation Is Accurately Perceived at 50 ms
note: The researchers reported above-chance classification of self-identified orientation in a set of selected face photographs, including after very brief exposures.

headline: Can hearing a word make you think you stopped a cursor that somebody else stopped?
title: Apparent Mental Causation: Sources of the Experience of Will
note: Participants reported more perceived control over a cursor stop when they heard a word naming the target just before the stop, which could be imposed by another person.

headline: Can a spoken instruction make someone feel they controlled another person’s hands?
title: Vicarious Agency: Experiencing Control Over the Movements of Others
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Participants sometimes reported a greater feeling of control when a verbal preview matched gestures made by somebody else’s hands in front of them.

headline: Can a coin shown too briefly to identify change how hard you squeeze?
title: How the Brain Translates Money Into Force: A Neuroimaging Study of Subliminal Motivation
note: Participants squeezed a grip for monetary rewards. The authors reported greater force after higher-value coin images in some masked conditions.

headline: Will preverbal infants use their gaze to trigger punishment of an animated aggressor?
title: Third-Party Punishment by Preverbal Infants
note: Infants could trigger a stone to fall on an animated agent by looking at it. The authors reported that infants targeted a character that had acted aggressively more often in the relevant condition.

headline: Can feeling powerful make people more likely to switch off an annoying fan?
title: From Power to Action
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: In one experiment, participants assigned to a high-power condition were more likely to act on an annoying fan than participants in the comparison condition.

headline: Can Googling an explanation make people think they know more about unrelated subjects?
title: Searching for Explanations: How the Internet Inflates Estimates of Internal Knowledge
note: People who searched online for answers subsequently gave higher ratings of their own ability to explain new topics.

headline: Can Facebook Likes beat a friend’s personality judgment on a questionnaire benchmark?
title: Computer-Based Personality Judgments Are More Accurate Than Those Made by Humans
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: In the study sample, models using Facebook Likes predicted participants’ self-rated personality scores more accurately than certain groups of human judges.

headline: Can someone’s Facebook Likes predict personal traits they never put on their profile?
title: Private Traits and Attributes Are Predictable From Digital Records of Human Behavior
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Models trained on Facebook Likes predicted several reported traits and attributes above baseline within the study dataset.

headline: Do competence ratings of a CEO’s face correlate with how profitable their company is?
title: The Face of Success: Inferences From Chief Executive Officers’ Appearance Predict Company Profits
note: Ratings from CEO photographs were statistically associated with profits among firms in the study.

headline: Can being left out of a virtual ball game cool a person’s finger?
title: Cold-Blooded Loneliness: Social Exclusion Leads to Lower Skin Temperatures
note: The researchers recorded finger temperature during an online inclusion or exclusion manipulation and reported lower temperatures in the excluded group.

headline: Can being told you may end up alone make you tolerate more physical pain?
title: Alone but Feeling No Pain: Effects of Social Exclusion on Physical Pain Tolerance and Pain Threshold, Affective Forecasting, and Interpersonal Empathy
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Participants given a forecast of future social isolation showed higher pressure-pain thresholds and tolerance in some experiments.

headline: Can dimming the lights improve scores on creative problem-solving tasks?
title: Freedom From Constraints: Darkness and Dim Illumination Promote Creativity
note: The authors reported improved creative performance under some dim-light conditions and linked the result to feeling less constrained.

headline: Does losing a sense of control make people see images in noise or connections in random events?
title: Lacking Control Increases Illusory Pattern Perception
note: Across experiments, low-control conditions were associated with more perceived patterns in noisy images and more interpretations invoking superstition or conspiracies.

headline: Do people who see patterns in random coin tosses report more supernatural beliefs?
title: Connecting the Dots: Illusory Pattern Perception Predicts Belief in Conspiracies and the Supernatural
note: Across studies, pattern ratings for random sequences or chaotic art were associated with measures of supernatural and conspiracy belief.

headline: Can buying eco-friendly goods make people cheat more in a later task?
title: Do Green Products Make Us Better People?
note: The authors reported more generous behavior after merely seeing green goods, but more cheating in a separate task after participants purchased them.

headline: Can holding a heavier object make a topic seem more important?
title: From Physical Weight to Psychological Significance: The Contribution of Semantic Activations
note: Across experiments, the authors linked physical weight to judgments of importance and considered when cues to the meaning of weight changed those judgments.

headline: Can editing a Facebook News Feed change the words people use in their own posts?
title: Experimental Evidence of Massive-Scale Emotional Contagion Through Social Networks
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Reducing exposure to positive or negative posts shifted the proportion of corresponding emotional words in users’ own posts by small amounts. The journal published an editorial expression of concern about informed consent.

headline: Can one manufactured upvote start a cascade of positive ratings?
title: Social Influence Bias: A Randomized Experiment
note: The researchers randomly added positive or negative votes to comments. Positive votes produced a lasting upward shift in later ratings, while negative votes were often counteracted.

headline: Can dancing in sync with someone change how much pressure you can tolerate?
title: Synchrony and Exertion During Dance Independently Raise Pain Threshold and Encourage Social Bonding
note: The authors reported higher measured pain thresholds and greater feelings of closeness after synchronized or more physically demanding dance conditions.

headline: Does loneliness make people attribute more agency to gadgets or pets?
title: Creating Social Connection Through Inferential Reproduction: Loneliness and Perceived Agency in Gadgets, Gods, and Greyhounds
note: Across studies, measures or manipulations of loneliness were associated with differences in the perceived agency of pets, gadgets or supernatural agents.

headline: Can recalling social exclusion make supernatural explanations more appealing?
title: The Dark Side of Meaning-Making: How Social Exclusion Leads to Superstitious Thinking
note: Across experiments, the authors linked social-exclusion manipulations to greater endorsement of selected superstitious or supernatural explanations.

headline: Does being told you did well make you stick with an unrelated task longer?
title: Pride and Perseverance: The Motivational Role of Pride
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors reported greater persistence on a subsequent task after manipulations intended to induce pride.

headline: Can holding chopsticks in a way that produces a smile change heart rate after stress?
title: Grin and Bear It: The Influence of Manipulated Facial Expression on the Stress Response
note: Participants held chopsticks to create different facial configurations while doing stressful tasks. The authors reported lower heart rates during recovery in the smile conditions.

headline: Can reading a job pitch make the candidate seem less intelligent than hearing the same words?
title: The Sound of Intellect: Speech Reveals a Thoughtful Mind, Increasing a Job Candidate’s Appeal
note: Evaluators rated candidates more favorably when they heard their pitches than when they read the transcripts.

headline: Can adding vocal fry to a short recording make listeners less willing to hire the speaker?
title: Vocal Fry May Undermine the Success of Young Women in the Labor Market
note: Listeners heard alternate recordings by the same speakers. Vocal fry was associated with lower stated willingness to hire, with a larger penalty for women in the study.

headline: Can merely imagining yourself in a crowd make you volunteer less afterward?
title: Crowded Minds: The Implicit Bystander Effect
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Participants who imagined being with a group later offered less help in some tasks than participants in comparison conditions.

headline: Can seeing achievement-related words make people persist without realizing why?
title: The Automated Will: Nonconscious Activation and Pursuit of Behavioral Goals
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors reported changes in task performance, persistence or cooperation after participants were exposed to words related to those goals.

headline: Can a sad film make people sell something for less but pay more to buy it?
title: Heart Strings and Purse Strings: Carryover Effects of Emotions on Economic Decisions
note: After watching clips designed to evoke particular emotions, participants gave different selling prices or buying prices for an unrelated item.

headline: Can drifting off for seconds make a hidden shortcut easier to discover?
title: Sleep Onset Is a Creative Sweet Spot
note: Participants who spent some time in the first stage of sleep before returning to a number task discovered its hidden rule more often than participants who stayed awake.

headline: Can a sound played while you sleep strengthen the memory of where an object was located?
title: Strengthening Individual Memories by Reactivating Them During Sleep
note: The experimenters replayed sounds associated with selected objects during sleep. Later location errors were smaller for cued objects than for uncued objects.

headline: Can someone see falling Tetris pieces as they fall asleep without remembering playing Tetris?
title: Replaying the Game: Hypnagogic Images in Normals and Amnesics
note: Participants with amnesia reported game-related imagery at sleep onset even though they could not explicitly recall playing the game.

headline: Can a sleeper learn to change their breathing when they hear a tone?
title: Humans Can Learn New Information During Sleep
note: The researchers paired tones with pleasant or unpleasant odors during sleep. Later tones alone produced different sniff responses without participants reporting awareness of the pairing.

headline: Can a made-up word heard during deep sleep influence a later guess about its meaning?
title: Implicit Vocabulary Learning During Sleep Is Bound to Slow-Wave Peaks
note: Participants heard pairs of words during sleep and later guessed whether objects linked to the novel words were larger or smaller than a shoebox. Accuracy depended on when the words had been played relative to sleep slow waves.

headline: Can viewers guess a stranger’s income group from a neutral face photograph?
title: The Visibility of Social Class From Facial Cues
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors compared face classifications with income-group labels and reported above-chance classification. They also found that perceived class affected judgments of suitability for a job.

headline: Can sorting coins instead of buttons make children work longer but help less?
title: Children Reminded of Money Shift Into Market Mode
note: The authors compared persistence and helping after children handled money or other objects. They interpreted the resulting group differences as a shift toward a market mindset.

headline: Can handling physically dirty money change whether people share or help?
title: Diverging Effects of Clean Versus Dirty Money on Attitudes, Values, and Interpersonal Behavior
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Across experiments, participants who handled clean or dirty money differed on measures including fairness and reciprocity. The authors linked the contrast to meanings attached to money and physical dirt.

headline: Can exposure to money-related words shift people toward unethical choices?
title: Seeing Green: Mere Exposure to Money Triggers a Business Decision Frame and Unethical Outcomes
venue: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
note: Across experiments, money primes were followed by higher rates of some choices coded as unethical. The authors attributed the contrast in part to a business decision frame.

headline: Do people make fewer dishonest responses in the morning than in the afternoon?
title: The Morning Morality Effect: The Influence of Time of Day on Unethical Behavior
note: The authors compared outcomes in earlier and later lab or online sessions and reported less cheating on some tasks in the morning.

headline: Can an algorithm classify political orientation from a profile photo?
title: Facial Recognition Technology Can Expose Political Orientation From Naturalistic Facial Images
note: The study used labeled profile photos and reported above-chance discrimination of liberal and conservative labels. Photos were collected in natural settings, where self-presentation and context vary.

headline: Does looking out from a doll-sized body make nearby objects seem larger?
title: Being Barbie: The Size of One’s Own Body Determines the Perceived Size of the World
note: After a body-ownership illusion using bodies of different sizes, participants gave different size and distance estimates for the same surroundings.

headline: Can feeling invisible change your physical response to a crowd?
title: Illusory Ownership of an Invisible Body Reduces Autonomic and Subjective Social Anxiety Responses
note: Participants experienced a body-ownership illusion involving empty space or a mannequin. The researchers compared self-reported stress and heart-rate responses while facing an audience.

headline: Do women select more revealing clothes near estimated peak fertility, especially after seeing attractive women?
title: Ovulation, Female Competition, and Product Choice: Hormonal Influences on Consumer Behavior
note: The authors compared hypothetical product choices across estimated fertility and exposure conditions, interpreting the contrasts as a sign of competition for mates.

headline: Do preferences for out-earning other women vary across the menstrual cycle?
title: Money, Status, and the Ovulatory Cycle
note: Across economic choice tasks, the authors compared absolute and relative monetary gains at different estimated levels of fertility. They linked some differences to competition for relative status.

headline: Does remembering a major secret make a hill look steeper or a target seem harder to reach?
title: The Physical Burdens of Secrecy
note: Compared with smaller-secret or control conditions, some large-secret conditions produced higher slope estimates and different beanbag throws. The authors interpreted the differences as a physical burden of secrecy.

headline: Can briefly flashing positive words about aging improve older adults’ physical-performance scores?
title: Subliminal Strengthening: Improving Older Individuals’ Physical Function Over Time With an Implicit-Age-Stereotype Intervention
note: The authors compared repeated physical-function scores across intervention groups. They reported a stronger improvement following implicit exposure to positive age stereotypes.

headline: Do people think an identical harm hurts less when it happens to someone in poverty?
title: Thick Skin Bias in Judgments About People in Poverty
note: Across vignette experiments, the researchers varied the depicted person’s socioeconomic status and compared ratings of how much the same negative experiences would hurt.

headline: Can imagining a large car repair bill change performance on a reasoning test?
title: Poverty Impedes Cognitive Function
note: The authors compared test scores under different hypothetical financial demands and also compared the same farmers before and after harvest. They interpreted the score differences as evidence that financial concerns consume cognitive resources.

headline: Can looking up at tall trees make people pick up more pens for a stranger?
title: Awe, the Small Self, and Prosocial Behavior
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: A field experiment compared helping after participants looked at tall trees or a building. Other experiments related induced awe and ratings of a smaller sense of self to prosocial choices.

headline: Can a video that elicits awe make people feel they have more time?
title: Awe Expands People’s Perception of Time, Alters Decision Making, and Enhances Well-Being
note: The studies compared ratings of available time and choices such as willingness to volunteer after awe or comparison inductions.

headline: Can expecting a face lead people to report seeing one in pure visual noise?
title: Seeing Jesus in Toast: Neural and Behavioral Correlates of Face Pareidolia
note: Participants made face or letter judgments about noise images. The authors compared reported detections and imaging signals and linked face reports to activity in a face-selective region.

headline: Can wearing a low-status item with a high-status outfit make someone look higher status?
title: Trickle-Round Signals: When Low Status Is Mixed With High
note: The authors compared audience status ratings across combinations of high- and low-status cues and argued that some deliberately mixed combinations signal status.

headline: Do people expect somebody who caused harm to feel less pain themselves?
title: Moral Typecasting: Divergent Perceptions of Moral Agents and Moral Patients
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Across experiments, moral-role framing shifted ratings of how capable a person was of acting or of experiencing harm. The authors interpreted the contrasts as moral typecasting.

headline: Can oxytocin change how people respond to names linked to different national groups?
title: Oxytocin Promotes Human Ethnocentrism
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Men given oxytocin or placebo completed implicit evaluations and hypothetical moral choices involving names associated with different national groups. The authors linked the group contrasts to in-group favoritism.

headline: Do Mandarin and English speakers respond differently after seeing vertical or horizontal arrangements?
title: Does Language Shape Thought? Mandarin and English Speakers’ Conceptions of Time
note: Spatial primes were followed by judgments about time. The authors compared response times across prime directions and language groups and interpreted the pattern as evidence that language habits influence temporal thought.

headline: Can an unusually warm day make global warming seem more believable?
title: How Warm Days Increase Belief in Global Warming
note: Across surveys and experiments, the authors related departures from expected local temperatures to climate-belief ratings and examined whether attention to recent warm days helped account for the association.

headline: Can giving somebody a high-power role change how the very same passage sounds when they read it?
title: The Sound of Power: Conveying and Detecting Hierarchical Rank Through Voice
note: The authors compared acoustic measurements after assigning speakers to different power roles. Separate listeners judged the speakers’ power from recordings.

headline: Can turning up the bass in the same music make people feel more powerful?
title: The Music of Power: Perceptual and Behavioral Consequences of Powerful Music
note: Across studies, the authors compared ratings of power and power-related responses after different music, including versions altered in bass level.

headline: Can feeling powerful make people overestimate how tall they are?
title: Living Large: The Powerful Overestimate Their Own Height
note: The authors compared height estimates after power manipulations and reported larger estimates in the higher-power conditions, including estimates of participants’ own height.

headline: Can placing a word higher on a screen change how quickly people classify the group it names as powerful?
title: Your Highness: Vertical Positions as Perceptual Symbols of Power
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Across experiments, vertical position affected response speed and power judgments. The authors interpreted the interactions as evidence that vertical space helps represent social power.

headline: Can a smile flashed below awareness change how much someone pours and drinks?
title: Unconscious Affective Reactions to Masked Happy Versus Angry Faces Influence Consumption Behavior and Judgments of Value
note: The authors compared beverage consumption and willingness to pay after masked happy and angry faces. Some differences were concentrated among thirsty participants without corresponding changes in reported feelings.

headline: Can squeezing a hard ball make an ambiguous face more likely to be classified as male?
title: Tough and Tender: Embodied Categorization of Gender
note: Participants categorized gender-ambiguous faces while experiencing hard or soft touch. The authors interpreted differences in category responses as evidence that touch can activate gender stereotypes.

headline: Can the smile in an old class photo predict divorce decades later?
title: Smile Intensity in Photographs Predicts Divorce Later in Life
note: The researchers coded smiles in old photographs and modeled divorce status. They reported an association between lower smile intensity and divorce.

headline: Can a woman’s college yearbook smile predict her well-being decades later?
title: Expressions of Positive Emotion in Women’s College Yearbook Pictures and Their Relationship to Personality and Life Outcomes Across Adulthood
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The researchers rated expressions in yearbook photos and compared them with later personality, marriage and well-being measures, reporting associations with several outcomes.

headline: Can a party’s members look happier in photos while the other party reports greater happiness in surveys?
title: Conservatives Report, but Liberals Display, Greater Happiness
note: The researchers compared self-reports with indicators such as smile coding and word choice from other datasets. The political direction of the difference reversed across kinds of measures.

headline: Do cognitive test scores correlate with sperm count or motility?
title: Intelligence and Semen Quality Are Positively Correlated
note: The authors combined cognitive scores and related them to semen measures from a sample of veterans, interpreting positive associations as consistent with shared influences on bodily and cognitive functioning.

headline: Can the width-to-height ratio of hockey players’ faces predict penalty minutes?
title: In Your Face: Facial Metrics Predict Aggressive Behaviour in the Laboratory and in Varsity and Professional Hockey Players
venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B
note: The authors related face measurements to penalty minutes and separately to responses on a laboratory task, interpreting the associations as evidence that facial shape predicts aggression.

headline: Can the proportions of a man’s face predict whether he lies during a negotiation game?
title: Bad to the Bone: Facial Structure Predicts Unethical Behaviour
venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B
note: The researchers modeled deception in a negotiation and cheating in a game using men’s facial width-to-height ratio, reporting positive associations.

headline: Do people who click immediately as friends smell more alike?
title: There Is Chemistry in Social Chemistry
note: An electronic nose measured similarity in body odor among established pairs, and a separate experiment related odor similarity to strangers’ reported connection after a nonverbal interaction.

headline: Do people prefer the smell of shirts worn by someone with dissimilar immune-system genes?
title: MHC-Dependent Mate Preferences in Humans
venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B
note: Participants rated odors from worn T-shirts. The authors compared ratings across genetic similarity and contraceptive-use groups and interpreted the differences in terms of mate preference.

headline: Can positive words in a nun’s autobiography predict how long she lives?
title: Positive Emotions in Early Life and Longevity: Findings From the Nun Study
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Researchers coded emotional content in short autobiographies written early in adulthood and related the scores to survival decades later.

headline: Will people press a shock button when left alone with their thoughts?
title: Just Think: The Challenges of the Disengaged Mind
note: Across studies, the authors compared enjoyment of thinking with other activities. In one small session, some participants who had rated a shock as unpleasant administered at least one to themselves.

headline: Can touching a teddy bear make excluded adults give more money to someone else?
title: Touching a Teddy Bear Mitigates Negative Effects of Social Exclusion to Increase Prosocial Behavior
note: The researchers compared prosocial outcomes after exclusion with and without touching a teddy bear and interpreted the interaction as mitigation of the effects of exclusion.

headline: Do people approaching a new decade of age behave differently at 29, 39 or 49?
title: People Search for Meaning When They Approach a New Decade in Chronological Age
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: The authors compared ages ending in nine with neighboring ages across surveys and archival measures such as first-time marathon running. They interpreted the patterns as a search for meaning.

headline: Can reading an argument against free will make people cheat on a later task?
title: The Value of Believing in Free Will: Encouraging a Belief in Determinism Increases Cheating
note: The authors compared cheating proxies after reading passages differing in their treatment of free will or after related belief manipulations. They interpreted the contrasts as effects of weakening belief in free will.

headline: Can describing the same golf task as measuring intelligence or athletic ability reverse a group performance gap?
title: Stereotype Threat Effects on Black and White Athletic Performance
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The researchers compared golf scores by participant race and how the task was described. They interpreted the interaction as consistent with threat from different stereotypes.

headline: Will children wait longer for a second marshmallow after an adult keeps an unrelated promise?
title: Rational Snacking: Young Children’s Decision-Making on the Marshmallow Task Is Moderated by Beliefs About Environmental Reliability
note: Before the marshmallow task, the experimenter kept or broke promises regarding other materials. The authors compared waiting times and interpreted the difference as evidence that the task also measures expectations about reliability.

headline: Can silhouettes colored in by participants distinguish pride from shame or fear?
title: Bodily Maps of Emotions
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Participants marked where they felt more or less bodily activity on silhouettes. The authors statistically compared the self-reported maps across emotion categories and language groups.

headline: Can a radiologist look straight at a gorilla in a scan and miss it?
title: The Invisible Gorilla Strikes Again: Sustained Inattentional Blindness in Expert Observers
note: While 24 radiologists searched lung CT scans for nodules, 20 missed an inserted gorilla. Eye tracking showed that several who missed it had looked at its location.

headline: Can a cold room make people more inclined to choose a romance movie?
title: Warm It Up With Love: The Effect of Physical Coldness on Liking of Romance Movies
note: Experiments compared genre preferences under cold and warmer conditions. The authors also analyzed rental and temperature records, interpreting the results as a link between physical and psychological warmth.

headline: Can scores on mental-state attribution measures help explain who believes in a personal God?
title: Mentalizing Deficits Constrain Belief in a Personal God
note: The authors analyzed questionnaire data and group differences, then fitted mediation models linking measures of mentalizing to reported belief in a personal God.

headline: Can putting people under stress make them knock on wood more often?
title: The Effects of Stress and Desire for Control on Superstitious Behavior
note: The researchers counted knocking on wood in conditions with different stress levels and examined how the difference depended on participants’ desire for control.

headline: Does the effect of a sugary drink on task performance depend on what you believe about willpower?
title: Beliefs About Willpower Determine the Impact of Glucose on Self-Control
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: The authors compared self-control task scores by drink condition and by whether participants held or were led to adopt a limited-resource view of willpower.

headline: Can drinking sugary lemonade make someone better at ignoring an irrelevant option?
title: Toward a Physiology of Dual-Process Reasoning and Judgment: Lemonade, Willpower, and Expensive Rule-Based Analysis
note: After a self-control task, participants drank sweetened or artificially sweetened lemonade. Choice rates involving a decoy option were used to infer changes in rule-based reasoning.

headline: Can a reminder of God make people more willing to take a physical risk?
title: Anticipating Divine Protection? Reminders of God Can Increase Nonmoral Risk Taking
note: The authors compared reported or observed risk choices following God-related or neutral cues. They interpreted some differences as expectations of protection and distinguished risks with and without moral implications.

headline: Can reminders of God make people resist cookies but do less work toward a goal?
title: Divergent Effects of Activating Thoughts of God on Self-Regulation
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Different experiments compared temptation resistance and active goal pursuit after God-related cues. The authors reported effects in opposite directions across these outcomes.

headline: Can knocking away from yourself make bad luck feel less likely?
title: Reversing One’s Fortune by Pushing Away Bad Luck
note: After participants made a tempting-fate statement, the authors compared likelihood judgments under actions directed away from or toward the body.

topic: Control and belief in external systems
headline: Can recalling a loss of control make people report stronger belief in a controlling God?
title: God and the Government: Testing a Compensatory Control Mechanism for the Support of External Systems
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors compared support for external systems under different personal-control conditions and interpreted some changes in belief or endorsement as compensatory.

headline: Can calling the same odor “body odor” instead of “cheddar cheese” change how it smells?
title: Cognitive Modulation of Olfactory Processing
note: The same odor received different pleasantness ratings across labels. The authors also compared fMRI signals and related some differences to those ratings.

headline: Can rinsing your mouth with carbohydrates affect a self-control task without swallowing?
title: Motivational Versus Metabolic Effects of Carbohydrates on Self-Control
note: The researchers compared subsequent task performance after carbohydrate and control rinses. They interpreted the contrast as evidence for a motivational response to oral carbohydrate cues.

headline: Do people report more pain relief from the same placebo if told it costs more?
title: Commercial Features of Placebo and Therapeutic Efficacy
note: Participants received an identical placebo labeled with different prices. The investigators compared changes in ratings of experimentally induced pain.

headline: Are people talking on phones less likely to notice a clown riding a unicycle?
title: Did You See the Unicycling Clown? Inattentional Blindness While Walking and Talking on a Cell Phone
note: The field study compared how often pedestrians in different walking and phone-use conditions reported noticing the same conspicuous event.

headline: Can a hypnotic suggestion to see gray alter brain responses to a colored image?
title: Hypnotic Visual Illusion Alters Color Processing in the Brain
note: Researchers compared imaging signals under color and grayscale suggestions in highly hypnotizable participants, including when the physical stimulus conflicted with the suggestion.

headline: Can altered video make someone confess to breaking a rule they did not actually break?
title: Innocent but Proven Guilty: Eliciting Internalized False Confessions Using Doctored-Video Evidence
note: The authors compared confessions and belief in the alleged rule violation across types of purported video evidence.

headline: Can a doctored childhood photo make someone describe a balloon ride that never happened?
title: A Picture Is Worth a Thousand Lies: Using False Photographs to Create False Childhood Memories
note: After viewing edited childhood photos and being interviewed, some participants gave accounts of the fictitious balloon ride. Researchers coded these accounts for recalled details.

headline: Can reading a trolley problem in a foreign language change willingness to push someone off a bridge?
title: Your Morals Depend on Language
note: The authors compared hypothetical answers across native- and foreign-language conditions. The reported shift was concentrated in the version requiring direct physical harm.

headline: Do intoxicated participants find more solutions to puzzles that link three unrelated words?
title: Uncorking the Muse: Alcohol Intoxication Facilitates Creative Problem Solving
note: The authors compared scores and response times on a word-association task across intoxicated and sober groups and interpreted the result in terms of creative problem solving.

headline: Can simply expecting to interact with a woman lower men’s scores on an attention task?
title: The Mere Anticipation of an Interaction With a Woman Can Impair Men’s Cognitive Performance
note: The researchers compared cognitive task scores when participants believed another person was observing them or would interact with them. They interpreted some differences among men as an effect of anticipated opposite-sex interaction.

headline: Do men score lower on a cognitive task after a short conversation with a woman?
title: Interacting With Women Can Impair Men’s Cognitive Functioning
note: The authors compared task performance after different social interactions and examined whether men’s scores varied with their ratings of the interaction partner.

headline: Can making a person’s hand look larger change the temperature at which stimulation feels painful?
title: Visual Distortion of Body Size Modulates Pain Perception
note: Participants viewed magnified, reduced or unaltered images of their hands during a thermal task. The authors compared the temperatures at which participants first reported pain.

headline: Does looking at your own hand change how painful the same laser pulse feels?
title: Visually Induced Analgesia: Seeing the Body Reduces Pain
note: The researchers compared pain ratings and brain responses to calibrated laser stimulation while participants looked at their own hand or an object.

headline: Can someone show a facial reaction to an emotional image they report not seeing?
title: Unseen Facial and Bodily Expressions Trigger Fast Emotional Reactions
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: In people with visual-field loss, the researchers compared facial muscle and pupil responses to expressions shown in seen and unseen areas of the visual field.

headline: Same photo, red background. More attractive?
title: Romantic Red: Red Enhances Men's Attraction to Women
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Researchers changed the colors surrounding photos or the colors of women's clothing and asked men to rate attractiveness. The authors reported higher ratings in several of the red conditions.

headline: Does typing your notes make you learn less?
title: The pen is mightier than the keyboard: advantages of longhand over laptop note taking
note: The authors reported that laptop note takers performed worse on conceptual questions than longhand note takers in their lecture experiments.

headline: Can writing about a time you were in charge change whether you would fire someone?
title: From Power to Inaction: Ambivalence Gives Pause to the Powerful
note: In one experiment, participants wrote about a time they had high or low power, then decided whether they would fire a hypothetical employee. The study reported an interaction between felt power and ambivalence. A student replication did not reproduce the interaction. https://forrt.org/flora-replication-atlas/doi/10.1177/0956797616669947/

headline: Can a background question change someone’s math score?
title: Stereotype Susceptibility: Identity Salience and Shifts in Quantitative Performance
note: The authors reported different math scores among Asian American women depending on whether preceding questions cued ethnicity or gender. A larger replication recovered the predicted pattern after excluding participants unfamiliar with the relevant stereotypes. The full sample did not show the effect. https://doi.org/10.1027/1864-9335/a000184

headline: Are men more attractive to women when shown in red?
title: Red, rank, and romance in women viewing men
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Will a woman choose a red shirt to meet an attractive man?
title: Women's use of red clothing as a sexual signal in intersexual interaction
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Does the red-attraction effect extend across cultures?
title: Red enhances women's attractiveness to men: First evidence suggesting universality
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Does a red shirt change how men approach women?
title: Red and romantic behavior in men viewing women
note: Editorial headline; consult the linked original publication or its bibliographic record.

headline: Can French accordion music tilt a supermarket’s wine sales toward French bottles?
title: The influence of in-store music on wine selections
note: A supermarket alternated French and German music near wines from both countries. Sales shifted toward the wine whose country matched the music, while shoppers generally did not report that the music had influenced their choice.

headline: Can a drink’s color override what people say they know about its flavor?
title: The influence of color-generated expectations on the identification of flavored drinks
note: Adding a color associated with a particular flavor increased flavor-identification responses matching that expectation, even when participants were told color was uninformative. The effect weakened when the drink’s actual flavor strongly conflicted with the color cue.

headline: Can an unpleasant smell alter how people learn from social feedback?
title: Aversive smell associations shape social judgment
note: The study paired social information with an aversive odor and examined how participants later evaluated people. The authors reported that odor-associated learning changed subsequent social judgments.

headline: Can observers guess fertility from how a woman walks?
title: Gait and menstrual cycle: Ovulating women use sexier gaits and walk slowly ahead of men
note: Researchers secretly recorded women walking ahead of a male confederate and compared gait across cycle phases. The authors reported that gait ratings changed near ovulation, interpreting the pattern as a possible attractiveness cue.

headline: Do women report feeling more attractive around ovulation?
title: Self-perceived and observed variations in women’s attractiveness throughout the menstrual cycle—a diary study
note: In a daily diary study following women through a menstrual cycle, researchers tracked self-rated attractiveness and clothing. They reported cycle-linked variation in how attractive participants felt and in how others rated their appearance.

headline: Do clothing choices shift with the menstrual cycle?
title: Changes in women’s choice of dress across the ovulatory cycle: Naturalistic and laboratory task-based evidence
note: Across a naturalistic study and a laboratory choice task, the paper reported that women’s clothing choices became more revealing or sexy near the fertile phase, with differences depending on relationship and individual characteristics.

headline: Does relationship status change which male body odor women prefer near ovulation?
title: Women’s preference for dominant male odour: Effects of menstrual cycle and relationship status
note: Women rated male body odors, and the study compared odor preferences across menstrual-cycle phases and relationship status. The authors reported stronger fertile-phase preference for odors from men scoring higher on a dominance questionnaire, particularly among partnered women.

headline: When asked who is more likely to commit an extreme crime, do people pick atheists?
title: Everything Is Permitted? People Intuitively Judge Immorality as Representative of Atheists
note: Across five experiments, participants matched highly immoral acts—including serial murder and consensual incest—to social groups. The authors reported that even atheist participants were more likely to associate the acts with atheists than with other religious or cultural groups.

headline: Do pictures of eyes increase real-world donations more than pictures of noses or mouths?
title: Eyes, More Than Other Facial Features, Enhance Real-World Donation Behavior
note: Researchers alternated donation signs featuring eyes, noses, mouths, or chairs. They reported higher donations when eyes were displayed than when the other facial features or chairs were shown.

headline: Are shoppers more likely to help a stranger when the mall smells like baking cookies?
title: The Sweet Smell of... Helping: Effects of Pleasant Ambient Fragrance on Prosocial Behavior in Shopping Malls
note: In two shopping-mall field studies, passersby encountered a dropped-pen or change-making request near pleasant odors such as baking cookies or roasting coffee. The paper reported higher helping rates when pleasant fragrances were present.

headline: Does chocolate taste better when someone else tastes it at the same time?
title: Shared Experiences Are Amplified
note: In experiments, participants tasted chocolate or listened to music while another person either shared the experience at the same time or did a different task. The authors reported that pleasant and unpleasant experiences felt more intense when shared, even without talking.

headline: Can a brief touch on the arm increase how much money people sacrifice for a stranger?
title: Monetary sacrifice among strangers is mediated by endogenous oxytocin release after physical contact
note: In a monetary contribution experiment, physical contact followed by an intentional act of trust was reported to raise oxytocin and increase monetary sacrifice to a stranger by 243% relative to untouched controls.

headline: Do photographs of tearful people make strangers more willing to help?
title: The social impact of emotional tears
note: Across two studies, participants viewed images of people crying or not crying and reported willingness to help. The authors reported that tears increased helping intentions, with perceived helplessness and felt connection accounting for part of the difference.

headline: Can seeing an unfamiliar shape make you like it even when you cannot recognize it?
title: The Mere Exposure Effect Is Differentially Sensitive to Different Judgment Tasks
note: Participants saw random shapes so briefly that recognition was at chance in one experiment; repeated shapes were still judged more positively and brighter.

headline: Can an entire person change during a conversation without being noticed?
title: Failure to Detect Changes to People During a Real-World Interaction
note: During a staged conversation, a brief interruption allowed one person to be replaced by another. Many participants did not notice the change.

headline: Does knowing that a computer saved a fact make people forget the fact itself?
title: Google Effects on Memory: Cognitive Consequences of Having Information at Our Fingertips
note: Participants remembered less information when they expected it to remain available on a computer, while better remembering where it had been stored.

headline: Can changing only the uniform color change a referee’s score?
title: When the Referee Sees Red…
note: Taekwondo referees scored videos whose uniform colors were digitally swapped. The authors reported more points for the same contestant when shown in red.

headline: Can being unsure whether someone likes you make them more attractive?
title: “He Loves Me, He Loves Me Not…”: Uncertainty Can Increase Romantic Attraction
note: Women shown men's Facebook profiles reported the most attraction when told it was uncertain how much the men liked them.

headline: Does beer taste worse if you hear about the vinegar before drinking it?
title: Try It, You’ll Like It: The Influence of Expectation, Consumption, and Revelation on Preferences for Beer
note: Telling drinkers about the balsamic vinegar before tasting reduced their preference for the doctored beer; telling them afterward did not have the same effect.

headline: Do preverbal babies choose a puppet that helped another puppet climb a hill?
title: Social Evaluation by Preverbal Infants
note: Infants watched characters help or hinder another character going uphill. The authors reported that infants reaching for a character favored the helper.

headline: Can turning up bar music make people drink beer faster?
title: Sound Level of Environmental Music and Drinking Behavior: A Field Experiment With Beer Drinkers
note: In two bars, the authors reported faster beer drinking and higher consumption during louder music than during normal-volume music.

headline: Does a printed joke with the bill make diners tip more?
title: The Effects of a Joke on Tipping When It Is Delivered at the Same Time as the Bill
note: In a field experiment, the authors reported larger gratuities when a joke accompanied the bill than when it did not.

headline: Can thinking about death make people expect to spend more or take more from a shared resource?
title: Of Wealth and Death: Materialism, Mortality Salience, and Consumption Behavior
note: People reminded of their mortality projected more spending and, in a separate resource game, took more for themselves.

headline: Can putting your feet on someone’s desk make you look more powerful?
title: Breaking the Rules to Rise to Power: How Norm Violators Gain Power in the Eyes of Others
note: Observers rated norm violators, including a person who put their feet on another person’s desk, as more powerful than people who followed the relevant norm.

headline: Can red sneakers make someone look higher status in a formal setting?
title: The Red Sneakers Effect: Inferring Status and Competence from Signals of Nonconformity
note: Across studies, observers sometimes inferred greater status and competence from deliberate departures from dress conventions.

headline: Can the color of a waitress’s shirt change how much she earns in tips?
title: Clothing Color and Tipping: Gentlemen Patrons Give More Tips to Waitresses With Red Clothes
note: The study reported that male diners gave larger tips to waitresses wearing red, with no corresponding increase among female diners.

headline: Can crouching at the table earn a server a bigger tip?
title: Effect of Server Posture on Restaurant Tipping
note: Two restaurant field experiments reported larger tips when servers squatted beside the table instead of standing.

headline: Can singing and moving in time make strangers contribute more to a common pot?
title: Synchrony and Cooperation
note: Groups assigned to activities such as synchronized walking or singing later showed greater cooperation in experimental tasks.

headline: Do infants prefer a puppet that harms a previously antisocial puppet?
title: How Infants and Toddlers React to Antisocial Others
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: In puppet displays, older infants’ choices depended on whether the target of a positive or negative action had previously behaved prosocially or antisocially.

headline: Can 15-month-olds track where someone mistakenly expects to find a hidden toy?
title: Do 15-Month-Old Infants Understand False Beliefs?
note: Infants looked longer when an actor reached in a way inconsistent with the location the actor had previously seen. The authors interpreted the pattern as evidence of false-belief understanding.

headline: Can turning up the crunch make the same potato chip taste fresher?
title: The Role of Auditory Cues in Modulating the Perceived Crispness and Staleness of Potato Chips
note: Participants rated chips as crisper and fresher when the sound of their bite was amplified or its high frequencies were boosted.

headline: Can a soundtrack make the same toffee taste more bitter?
title: A Bittersweet Symphony: Systematically Modulating the Taste of Food by Changing the Sonic Properties of the Soundtrack Playing in the Background
note: Participants gave different ratings of the same toffee while listening to soundtracks designed to evoke sweetness or bitterness.

headline: Do people think more abstractly when dressed formally?
title: The Cognitive Consequences of Formal Clothing
note: Across observational and experimental studies, more formal dress was associated with more abstract responses on laboratory tasks.

headline: Can adding a brain scan make the same scientific argument seem stronger?
title: Seeing Is Believing: The Effect of Brain Images on Judgments of Scientific Reasoning
note: Readers gave more favorable ratings to scientific reasoning when summaries were accompanied by brain images than when they had other illustrations or no image.

headline: Can your own phone on the desk lower your score even if you never touch it?
title: Brain Drain: The Mere Presence of One’s Own Smartphone Reduces Available Cognitive Capacity
venue: Journal of the Association for Consumer Research
note: Participants scored differently on cognitive tasks depending on whether their own phone was on the desk, elsewhere on their person, or in another room.

headline: Can hearing your own phone ring across the room make word puzzles harder?
title: The Extended iSelf: The Impact of iPhone Separation on Cognition, Emotion, and Physiology
note: Participants performed worse on a word search when their own iPhone rang out of reach. The authors also reported higher heart rate and blood pressure.

headline: Can a difference in starting wealth make someone cheat to help or hurt a stranger?
title: Dishonesty in the Name of Equity
note: An initial lottery assigned participants different wealth levels. In subsequent tasks, the researchers reported more dishonest acts that benefited poorer partners or harmed wealthier partners.

headline: Will people defend their choice after a researcher secretly swaps it for the one they rejected?
title: Failure to Detect Mismatches Between Intention and Outcome in a Simple Decision Task
note: Participants picked the more attractive of two faces. Many did not detect when they were handed the face they had rejected and offered reasons for supposedly choosing it.

headline: Will people defend a moral opinion opposite to the one they just marked on a survey?
title: Lifting the Veil of Morality: Choice Blindness and Attitude Reversals on a Self-Transforming Survey
note: Researchers covertly reversed some survey items. Participants often accepted the altered answers as their own and sometimes defended them aloud.

headline: Can people switch which jam or tea they prefer after a researcher secretly swaps the samples?
title: Magic at the Marketplace: Choice Blindness for the Taste of Jam and the Smell of Tea
note: Shoppers sampled jams or smelled teas and stated a preference. Many failed to catch a covert substitution and gave reasons that fit the substituted sample.

headline: Can printed eyes make people less likely to drop a leaflet on the ground?
title: Do Images of ‘Watching Eyes’ Induce Behaviour That Is More Pro-Social or More Normative? A Field Experiment on Littering
note: A campus field experiment reported that printed eyes changed littering rates, with the effect depending on whether other people were nearby.

headline: Can the shape of a glass change how fast people drink the same beer?
title: Glass Shape Influences Consumption Rate for Alcoholic Beverages
note: In the experiment, participants drank a full serving of lager more quickly from a curved glass than from a straight one. The researchers did not find the same pattern for a soft drink.

headline: Can a burst of noise as a racket hits the ball make the shot direction harder to judge?
title: A Preliminary Investigation Regarding the Effect of Tennis Grunting: Does White Noise During a Tennis Shot Have a Negative Impact on Shot Perception?
note: Viewers judged tennis shot direction from videos. An added burst of sound around ball contact led to slower responses and more errors.

headline: Can louder tennis grunts make opponents expect the ball to land farther away?
