title: The Sound of Speed: How Grunting Affects Opponents’ Anticipation in Tennis
note: When identical stroke videos were paired with louder grunts, participants predicted deeper landings.

headline: Can a tennis grunt’s pitch tell listeners who is losing the match?
title: Tennis Grunts Communicate Acoustic Cues to Sex and Contest Outcome
note: Players’ grunt pitch differed between matches they won and lost. The authors also reported that listeners could use acoustic cues to judge likely match outcome.

headline: Does smelling sweat collected during fear change how observers react to faces?
title: Titrating the Smell of Fear: Initial Evidence for Dose-Invariant Behavioral, Physiological, and Neural Responses
note: The authors reported measurable responses to sweat collected under fear, with little evidence of a graded response to increasing doses.

headline: Will babies copy an adult who turns on a light with their forehead?
title: Rational Imitation in Preverbal Infants
note: Infants copied an adult’s unusual head action more often when the adult’s hands had been free than when the hands had been visibly occupied.

headline: Will children copy a pointless step even after being warned to ignore silly actions?
title: The Hidden Structure of Overimitation
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Children copied unnecessary steps demonstrated by adults, including under conditions designed to discourage copying irrelevant actions.

headline: Can a different soundtrack change how people rate the same beer?
title: Music Influences Hedonic and Taste Ratings in Beer
note: The researchers reported differences in ratings of the same beer when served with different label and music contexts.

headline: Can a seven-month-old’s gaze follow what somebody else mistakenly expects to see?
title: The Social Sense: Susceptibility to Others’ Beliefs in Human Infants and Adults
note: Infants’ looking times and adults’ object-detection times varied with what an on-screen agent had seen. The authors interpreted this pattern as automatic sensitivity to others’ beliefs.

headline: Will two-year-olds look where someone mistakenly expects to find a toy?
title: Action Anticipation Through Attribution of False Belief by 2-Year-Olds
note: The researchers measured where children looked before an actor could search. The reported gaze bias favored the location consistent with the actor’s outdated information.

headline: Do 13-month-olds expect somebody to search in the wrong place for an object?
title: Attribution of Beliefs by 13-Month-Old Infants
note: Infants watched animated events. Looking times differed depending on whether an agent searched in a location consistent with what it had previously seen.

headline: Can an 18-month-old tell which box a mistaken adult actually needs help opening?
title: Eighteen-Month-Old Infants Show False Belief Understanding in an Active Helping Paradigm
note: Toddlers helped adults with different boxes depending on whether the adult had witnessed a toy being moved.

headline: Will a toddler stop a mistaken adult before the adult reaches into the wrong box?
title: 18-Month-Olds Predict Specific Action Mistakes Through Attribution of False Belief, Not Ignorance, and Intervene Accordingly
note: Toddlers intervened differently when an adult had outdated information about an object’s location than when the adult lacked that information altogether.

headline: Do babies expect an adult to mistake a silent object for a rattling one?
title: Attributing False Beliefs About Non-Obvious Properties at 18 Months
note: The experiments used identical-looking objects with different hidden properties. The authors interpreted differences in looking time as sensitivity to the properties the adult believed the objects had.

headline: Can 18-month-olds infer that a remark corrected an adult’s mistaken belief?
title: Can an Agent’s False Belief Be Corrected by an Appropriate Communication? Psychological Reasoning in 18-Month-Old Infants
note: Infants’ looking patterns differed after a relevant verbal message about an object’s location versus a control message.

headline: Do infants prepare for another person’s reach when it reflects a mistaken belief?
title: Belief-Based Action Prediction in Preverbal Infants
note: The study recorded sensorimotor EEG signals while infants watched an agent. The authors linked changes in those signals to whether the agent was expected to act given what the agent had seen.

headline: Do babies infer who will comfort a distressed puppet from who shared food with it?
title: Early Concepts of Intimacy: Young Humans Use Saliva Sharing to Infer Close Relationships
note: After a puppet became distressed, young participants directed their gaze differently depending on whether a person had previously shared saliva with the puppet or played with it in another way.

headline: Can babies infer who will win a confrontation based on how many allies each side has?
title: Infants Use Relative Numerical Group Size to Infer Social Dominance
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Infants’ looking times differed when an individual backed by a larger group yielded to a member of a smaller group.

headline: Do babies expect two members of the same group to copy each other’s actions?
title: Preverbal Infants Expect Members of Social Groups to Act Alike
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Looking times differed when animated members of the same group acted differently. The authors interpreted the results as evidence of early expectations about group conformity.

headline: Can eight-month-olds tell which sample of colored balls is unlikely?
title: Intuitive Statistics by 8-Month-Old Infants
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Infants looked for different durations at samples drawn from boxes containing different proportions of colored balls. The authors interpreted this as sensitivity to sampling probabilities.

headline: Do babies look longer when the least likely animated object exits a container?
title: Intuitions of Probabilities Shape Expectations About the Future at 12 Months and Beyond
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Looking time varied with the number of objects of each kind in a simulated container and which object subsequently exited.

headline: Do babies combine time, location and number to anticipate which object will leave a container?
title: Pure Reasoning in 12-Month-Old Infants as Probabilistic Inference
note: The authors compared infants’ looking times across animated outcomes with predictions from a model incorporating object counts and spatial and temporal details.

headline: Can seconds of silent footage predict students’ evaluations of their teacher?
title: Half a Minute: Predicting Teacher Evaluations From Thin Slices of Nonverbal Behavior and Physical Attractiveness
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Average ratings by strangers viewing brief silent clips correlated with end-of-course teaching evaluations.

headline: Can people pick the intended mental state from a photograph that shows only the eyes?
title: The “Reading the Mind in the Eyes” Test Revised Version: A Study With Normal Adults, and Adults With Asperger Syndrome or High-Functioning Autism
venue: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry
note: Participants selected among four words describing mental states for each photograph. The study reported group differences in how often answers matched the scoring key.

headline: Can a suggestion to see words as meaningless symbols reduce interference from reading them?
title: Hypnotic Suggestion Reduces Conflict in the Human Brain
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: A posthypnotic suggestion reduced color-word interference among highly hypnotizable participants. The authors also reported differences in brain activity.

headline: Does what somebody else can see slow you down when you count visible dots?
title: Seeing It Their Way: Evidence for Rapid and Involuntary Computation of What Other People See
venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance
note: Participants were slower to report their own view of dots when an on-screen person could see a different number. The authors interpreted the interference as spontaneous perspective taking.

headline: Can someone pass a verbal false-belief test without showing the expected gaze pattern?
title: Mindblind Eyes: An Absence of Spontaneous Theory of Mind in Asperger Syndrome
note: The authors compared adults’ anticipatory gaze during a filmed search task and found a group difference despite success on explicit verbal false-belief tests.

headline: Does guessing what someone is feeling depend on how much the person shows?
title: It Takes Two: The Interpersonal Nature of Empathic Accuracy
note: Viewers inferred how people in recordings felt over time. Accuracy varied with both cues from the person expressing emotion and characteristics of the viewer.

headline: Will a baby help a stranger more after bouncing in time with them?
title: Interpersonal Synchrony Increases Prosocial Behavior in Infants
note: After being bounced in time or out of time with an adult, infants in the synchrony group were more likely to pick up objects the adult dropped.

headline: Do toddlers prefer a winner who gets their way without force?
title: Toddlers Prefer Those Who Win but Not When They Win by Force
note: Toddlers chose between puppets after watching conflicts. They tended to select a winner when the other puppet yielded and showed a different preference when the winner used force.

headline: Can a familiar accent shape whom a baby reaches toward or whom a child picks as a friend?
title: The Native Language of Social Cognition
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Infants and children showed preferences for native-language or native-accent speakers on several looking, reaching and choice tasks.

headline: Do babies look longer when two people get unequal shares?
title: Fairness Expectations and Altruistic Sharing in 15-Month-Old Human Infants
note: The authors compared infants’ looking times during equal and unequal food distributions and related their looking patterns to later toy sharing.

headline: Will a hungry toddler give away fruit to an adult who drops it?
title: Altruistic Food Sharing Behavior by Human Infants After a Hunger Manipulation
note: Some toddlers handed the experimenter desirable fruit when the experimenter reached for it, including in a group tested near their usual mealtime.

headline: Do babies expect an animated disc to stop jumping when there is no longer an obstacle?
title: Taking the Intentional Stance at 12 Months of Age
note: Infants watched a disc take a detour over a barrier. When the barrier was removed, their looking times differed depending on whether the disc repeated the detour.

headline: Can one tenth of a second be enough to form a lasting impression of a stranger’s face?
title: First Impressions: Making Up Your Mind After a 100-ms Exposure to a Face
note: Trait ratings after 100 milliseconds of exposure correlated with ratings made without a time limit. The study compared impressions across viewing times.

headline: Can strangers infer someone’s personality from their bedroom or office?
title: A Room With a Cue: Personality Judgments Based on Offices and Bedrooms
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Observers rated room occupants on personality traits. Some ratings agreed with personality measures collected from the occupants or people who knew them.

headline: Can observers estimate personality traits from a single full-body photograph?
title: Personality Judgments Based on Physical Appearance
note: The authors compared impressions from posed and less constrained photographs with personality reports and found that some trait judgments correlated with the reports.

headline: Can remembering a favor make someone wait longer for a larger payment?
title: Gratitude: A Tool for Reducing Economic Impatience
note: Participants asked to recall a gratitude-inducing event made more patient choices between smaller immediate and larger delayed cash payments.

headline: Does remembering a favor make people cheat less on a private coin toss?
title: The Grateful Don’t Cheat: Gratitude as a Fount of Virtue
note: The researchers compared how often participants reported the favorable outcome of a private coin toss after different emotion inductions. The gratitude group reported fewer favorable outcomes.

headline: Can an unused phone on a table make a conversation feel less close?
title: Can You Connect With Me Now? How the Presence of Mobile Communication Technology Influences Face-to-Face Conversation Quality
venue: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
note: Pairs spoke with a phone or a notebook nearby. Some measures of conversational quality and closeness were lower with the phone present, particularly for meaningful conversations.

headline: Can seeing a false headline only once make it seem more accurate the next time?
title: Prior Exposure Increases Perceived Accuracy of Fake News
note: Previously seen fabricated headlines received higher accuracy ratings than unfamiliar ones. The authors examined how plausibility and warnings affected the pattern.

headline: Can a night of sleep help people discover a shortcut they missed while awake?
title: Sleep Inspires Insight
note: After training on a task with a hidden shortcut, participants who slept were more likely to discover the shortcut than groups that stayed awake.

headline: Can a chance to show that you are unbiased make you more willing to express a potentially biased choice?
title: Moral Credentials and the Expression of Prejudice
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Participants given an opportunity to establish apparently unbiased credentials were more willing to make a subsequent choice that could be interpreted as prejudiced.

headline: Do babies expect a leader to step in when someone takes another person’s share?
title: Infants Expect Leaders to Right Wrongs
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Infants watched a character take a resource from another. Their looking times depended on whether a third character with a leadership role intervened.

headline: Can the car someone drives predict whether they cut off a pedestrian?
title: Higher Social Class Predicts Increased Unethical Behavior
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: In a field study, observers coded vehicle status and whether drivers yielded to a pedestrian. The association between the two was used alongside lab comparisons to argue that higher social class predicts more unethical behavior.

headline: Can hearing brief speech change judgments of a job candidate’s social class and starting salary?
title: Evidence for the Reproduction of Social Class in Brief Speech
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Listeners’ class estimates were compared with speakers’ reported class. In a hiring experiment, people with hiring experience formed different competence and salary judgments after hearing brief speech samples.

headline: Can getting left out make a risky bet seem more appealing?
title: Show Me the Honey! Effects of Social Exclusion on Financial Risk-Taking
note: Spending and gambling experiments compared socially excluded and included participants. The authors reported more risk taking in the exclusion condition and interpreted it in terms of the perceived value of money.

headline: Does being left out make people copy a new interaction partner’s movements?
title: I Am Too Just Like You: Nonconscious Mimicry as an Automatic Behavioral Response to Social Exclusion
note: After an inclusion or exclusion manipulation, the researchers counted participants’ mimicry of a partner. Excluded participants copied more in some conditions.

headline: Can a briefly shown face change how quickly people recognize an object as a weapon?
title: Prejudice and Perception: The Role of Automatic and Controlled Processes in Misperceiving a Weapon
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The researchers compared response times and classification errors for tools and weapons after Black or White face primes, including under a response deadline.

headline: Can a target’s race affect split-second decisions in a video game about armed and unarmed people?
title: The Police Officer’s Dilemma: Using Ethnicity to Disambiguate Potentially Threatening Individuals
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The researchers compared response times and errors across target race and whether the target held a gun in a simulated decision task.

headline: Can exposure to a Black face change how easily a person recognizes a blurred image related to crime?
title: Seeing Black: Race, Crime, and Visual Processing
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Across visual tasks, the researchers compared object recognition and attention after racial or crime-related cues. They interpreted the contrasts as evidence that associations can affect visual processing.

headline: Can a masked tea-brand name sway beverage choice among people who are already thirsty?
title: Beyond Vicary’s Fantasies: The Impact of Subliminal Priming and Brand Choice
note: The authors compared beverage choices or intentions after briefly flashing a brand or a control stimulus. The reported increase in preference depended on thirst.

headline: Can the Russian vocabulary for shades of blue speed up a blue-matching task?
title: Russian Blues Reveal Effects of Language on Color Discrimination
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Russian speakers responded faster to pairs crossing a lexical boundary between blues than to within-category pairs in the study. The advantage was disrupted under verbal interference.

headline: Can speakers of one language name the same odors more consistently than speakers of another?
title: Odors Are Expressible in Language, as Long as You Speak the Right Language
note: The researchers quantified naming agreement for odor and color samples. Jahai speakers used more consistent odor labels than English speakers in the study.

headline: Can oxytocin make people more likely to report a favorable result when their group gets paid?
title: Oxytocin Promotes Group-Serving Dishonesty
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: The researchers compared self-reported coin-prediction success under oxytocin and placebo. Higher reported success in the group-payoff condition was interpreted as greater dishonesty.

headline: Can oxytocin make people more willing to spend money defending their own group in a game?
title: The Neuropeptide Oxytocin Regulates Parochial Altruism in Intergroup Conflict Among Humans
note: The researchers compared allocations in intergroup games under oxytocin and placebo, linking differences to in-group cooperation and defensive choices.

headline: Does a person’s social class predict how long their eyes linger on strangers?
title: Social Class and the Motivational Relevance of Other Human Beings: Evidence From Visual Attention
note: Eye-tracking studies compared attention to other people across participants with different measured or reported social class. The authors interpreted the association as a difference in the motivational relevance of others.

headline: Can a defendant’s apparent body weight change guilt ratings in a mock case?
title: The Influence of a Defendant’s Body Weight on Perceptions of Guilt
note: Participants rated a hypothetical defendant after seeing a photograph. The authors reported that body-weight cues affected guilt ratings in some combinations of observer and defendant gender.

headline: Can one sleepless night increase reports of a detail that appeared only in a misleading account?
title: Sleep Deprivation and False Memories
note: The authors compared false recognition after misinformation across sleep conditions. The effect depended in part on when sleep loss occurred relative to encoding.

headline: Can a partner’s wrong recollection make someone report having seen an object that was never there?
title: Social Contagion of Memory
note: After seeing scenes, participants recalled objects with a partner who sometimes supplied incorrect items. Those suggestions increased later reports of the absent items.

headline: Can seeing an artificially aged image of yourself shift how much you allocate to retirement?
title: Increasing Saving Behavior Through Age-Progressed Renderings of the Future Self
note: Participants exposed to aged or current representations of themselves made different allocations in experimental saving tasks. The authors interpreted the contrasts as an effect of making the future self feel more concrete.

headline: Does copying someone’s posture make the same conversation feel smoother?
title: The Chameleon Effect: The Perception-Behavior Link and Social Interaction
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors counted unintentional movements and compared liking and smoothness ratings between interactions in which a partner did or did not mimic participants.

headline: Can having your movements copied make you more generous toward an unrelated person?
title: Mimicry and Prosocial Behavior
note: The authors compared helping and giving behavior after participants had been mimicked or not, including outcomes directed toward someone other than the mimicker.

headline: Can seeing a picture of one’s partner change pain ratings during a heat task?
title: A Picture’s Worth: Partner Photographs Reduce Experimentally Induced Pain
note: The researchers compared reported pain during thermal stimulation while participants viewed different photographs or received other social cues. Partner photographs were associated with lower reported pain.

headline: Do children say a dead character can still want or know things?
title: The Natural Emergence of Reasoning About the Afterlife as a Developmental Regularity
note: Children answered questions about a dead story character. The authors compared responses about biological and psychological states across age groups and drew conclusions about how afterlife reasoning develops.

headline: Does using a foreign language change how people respond to equivalent gain and loss descriptions?
title: The Foreign-Language Effect: Thinking in a Foreign Tongue Reduces Decision Biases
note: The researchers compared choices made in native and foreign languages in framing and betting tasks. They interpreted some choice differences as reduced decision bias.

headline: Will people build fewer Lego models if each one is dismantled as soon as they finish it?
title: Man’s Search for Meaning: The Case of Legos
note: As piece rates declined, the authors compared how long participants kept building when completed models were retained or immediately dismantled.

headline: Can a person look at the spot where a magician drops an object and still miss the drop?
title: Misdirection in Magic: Implications for the Relationship Between Eye Gaze and Attention
note: The researchers scored detection of a magic method and recorded gaze, comparing overt fixation patterns with whether viewers saw the critical event.

headline: Can someone’s eyebrows give away their narcissism score?
title: Eyebrows cue grandiose narcissism
note: Judges rated faces of people who had completed a grandiose-narcissism questionnaire. Studies isolating and swapping brows implicated eyebrow appearance in the correspondence between ratings and questionnaire scores.

headline: Does being closer to ovulation make women better at guessing men’s sexual orientation from photos?
title: Mating Interest Improves Women’s Accuracy in Judging Male Sexual Orientation
note: The authors related judgments of selected faces to estimated proximity to ovulation. The reported relationship was for judging men's faces. They interpreted the pattern in terms of mating interest.

headline: Can your reaction time tell when someone lied, even if your answer can’t?
title: Some Evidence for Unconscious Lie Detection
note: Participants judged people in recorded mock interviews. The researchers compared explicit judgments with reaction-time measures of associations between interviewees and deception-related words, interpreting the latter as evidence of unconscious detection.

headline: Can women guess a stranger’s history of infidelity from his face?
title: Women can judge sexual unfaithfulness from unfamiliar men’s faces
note: Observers judged opposite-sex photographs. Women's ratings showed a modest relationship with male targets' self-reported history of unfaithfulness. The corresponding relationship was not found for men judging women.

headline: Can a photograph of your shoes give away your attachment anxiety?
title: Shoes as a source of first impressions
note: Judges saw photographs of the shoes targets said they wore most often. The authors compared ratings with the owners' self-reports, including their attachment-anxiety scores.

headline: Can seconds of interview footage give away a person’s psychopathy score?
title: Detecting psychopathy from thin slices of behavior
note: Lay observers rated clips of interviews with 96 maximum-security inmates. Ratings from short clips were correlated with scores from a standardized assessment in that sample.

headline: Can strangers guess your personality from your taste in music?
title: Message in a Ballad: The Role of Music Preferences in Interpersonal Perception
note: Observers formed impressions from targets' music preferences. The researchers assessed correspondence between the personality impressions and the targets' personality measures.

headline: Can ten seconds of a moving outline give away someone’s sexual orientation?
title: Accuracy of Judgments of Sexual Orientation From Thin Slices of Behavior
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors compared judgments from short clips against targets’ reported sexual orientation. They reported above-chance accuracy even for ten-second animated outlines retaining mainly gestures, within their selected stimuli.

headline: Do children expect God to know what their mother gets wrong?
title: God’s Beliefs Versus Mother’s: The Development of Nonhuman Agent Concepts
note: Researchers compared children's answers across human and nonhuman agents in false-belief and perspective-taking tasks. They interpreted response patterns as evidence that children can apply different notions of knowledge to God and ordinary people.

headline: Can a one-year-old tell that a made-up word passed along a hidden intention?
title: Twelve-Month-Old Infants Recognize That Speech Can Communicate Unobservable Intentions
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: After a speaker produced a novel word or coughed, the researchers compared infants' looking times across outcomes. A speech-by-outcome interaction supported their interpretation that infants expected words to communicate an unseen goal.

headline: Does seeing an attractive stranger change how accurately couples guess each other’s thoughts?
title: When the Head Protects the Heart: Empathic Accuracy in Dating Relationships
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Couples discussed photos of potential dates and later inferred each other's reported thoughts and feelings from video. Accuracy varied with photo attractiveness, relationship closeness, and insecurity.

headline: After one conversation, can you tell whether two other strangers liked each other?
title: Because You Know They Like Me So: Examining the Accuracy of Dyadic and Triadic Meta-Liking Judgments in Initial Social Encounters
note: In a round-robin study of 403 strangers, a social-relations model compared guesses about who liked whom with the targets' liking ratings. The researchers reported partial accuracy alongside perceived reciprocity and assumed agreement.

headline: Can strangers guess a man’s IQ from a still photo of his face?
title: Perceived Intelligence Is Associated with Measured Intelligence in Men but Not Women
note: Observers rated photographs of 40 men and 40 women. The researchers compared perceived intelligence with measured IQ and reported a correspondence for male targets.

headline: Can the face someone makes at the moment of a decision give away whether they’ll defect?
title: You can judge a book by its cover: the sequel. A kernel of truth in predictive cheating detection
note: Observers rated cooperation from photos taken before or during decisions in a prisoner's dilemma game. The authors interpreted their comparisons with actual decisions as evidence for a limited cheater-detection ability.

headline: Can bedroom calendars and postage stamps give away your politics?
title: The Secret Lives of Liberals and Conservatives: Personality Profiles, Interaction Styles, and the Things They Leave Behind
note: Observers coded furnishings and possessions in rooms. The authors related items such as calendars and postage stamps to occupants’ reported political orientation and interpreted patterns of neatness and organization in terms of political personality.

headline: Do conservatives really prefer nouns?
title: On the Grammar of Politics—or Why Conservatives Prefer Nouns
note: The studies compared noun preferences and language use against political orientation. The authors interpreted differences in parts of speech as evidence that grammatical choices can reflect a preference for certainty.

headline: Can nursery-school personality ratings foreshadow your politics twenty years later?
title: Nursery school personality and political orientation two decades later
note: The researchers matched preschool personality assessments to political orientation at age 23. The trait descriptions came from comparisons within a longitudinal cohort.

headline: Can a parent’s answers when their baby is one month old predict that child’s politics at 18?
title: Developmental Antecedents of Political Ideology: A Longitudinal Investigation From Birth to Age 18 Years
note: Parents reported parenting attitudes, and the project assessed children's early temperament. The authors related those measures to ideology at age 18, including a link between early parental authoritarian attitudes and later conservatism.

headline: Can the words you use on social media give away what you value politically?
title: Political Psycholinguistics: A Comprehensive Analysis of the Language Habits of Liberal and Conservative Social Media Users
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Automated text analyses related political leanings to word categories in social media posts. The authors used patterns such as counts of certainty- and tradition-related language to draw conclusions about ideological motivations.

headline: Can a few words in a celebrity’s tweet give away their political orientation?
title: Brief Textual Indicators of Political Orientation
venue: Journal of Language and Social Psychology
note: The studies scored student responses, excerpts from unanimous court opinions, and celebrity tweets for threat and resistance-to-change language. The latter category was related to political orientation across the selected samples.

headline: Can a pastor’s word choices reveal a liberal or conservative moral framework?
title: Liberals and Conservatives Rely on Different Sets of Moral Foundations
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The paper compared moral judgments across ideological groups using questionnaires and an analysis of sermons. The sermon study counted words assigned to moral categories and compared the patterns across religious traditions labeled liberal or conservative.

headline: Can cognitive flexibility tasks tell how strongly someone sides with a party?
title: The Partisan Mind: Is Extreme Political Partisanship Related to Cognitive Inflexibility?
note: The researchers related performance on three cognitive flexibility tasks to self-reported political partisanship in a sample of more than 700 Americans. They reported lower flexibility at stronger levels of partisanship on both sides.

headline: Do liberals and conservatives follow someone’s gaze at different speeds?
title: The Politics of Attention: Gaze-Cuing Effects Are Moderated by Political Temperament
note: The experiment measured how much a face’s gaze direction sped up detection of a target. The authors reported different reaction-time cueing effects across political temperament groups and interpreted them as differences in responsiveness to social cues.

headline: Do liberals try more kinds of beer, music and hobbies?
title: Liberals as Cultural Omnivores
venue: Journal of the Association for Consumer Research
note: In a survey of more than 20,000 people, the authors related ideology to the number of cultural experiences and products people reported, including beer brands. They interpreted the broader range reported by liberals in light of openness to experience.

headline: Can a person’s iris pattern give away their personality?
title: Associations between iris characteristics and personality in adulthood
note: The researchers scored visible features in photographs of the iris and compared them with personality questionnaire measures. The interpretation concerns associations with specific iris features and questionnaire dimensions.

headline: Can you smell how neurotic a stranger is?
title: Does Personality Smell? Accuracy of Personality Assessments Based on Body Odour
note: Judges rated the personalities of strangers from body-odor samples. The strongest correlations with criterion personality ratings were reported for extraversion, neuroticism and dominance.

headline: Can the way someone walks on a treadmill give away their aggression score?
title: Evidence of Big Five and Aggressive Personalities in Gait Biomechanics
note: The authors compared measured gait movements with questionnaire measures of aggression and the Big Five. An association between upper- and lower-body movement patterns and reported aggression in the sample was interpreted as a possible gait signal.

headline: Does the ratio of two fingers track men’s physical aggression scores?
title: Finger length ratio (2D:4D) correlates with physical aggression in men but not in women
note: The researchers measured finger lengths and compared digit ratios with aggression questionnaire scores. The reported relationship was with physical aggression scores among male participants.

headline: Can a handshake give away how extraverted you are?
title: Handshaking, gender, personality, and first impressions
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Trained coders scored handshake characteristics over repeated introductions. The researchers related firmness and other handshake measures to self-reported personality and the impressions formed by coders.

headline: Does a lower voice go with higher dominance and sociosexuality scores?
title: Do voices carry valid information about a speaker’s personality?
note: Across multiple samples, lower measured pitch was associated with higher self-reported dominance, extraversion and sociosexuality. The outcome measures were self-reports.

headline: How much personality do you hear in a stranger saying hello?
title: How Do You Say ‘Hello’? Personality Impressions from Brief Novel Voices
note: Listeners rated short recordings of a single greeting. Agreement among listeners was analyzed as a space of voice-based impressions, including trustworthiness and dominance. The criterion was agreement among raters.

headline: Can strangers pick out narcissism from a full-body photo?
title: Portrait of a narcissist: Manifestations of narcissism in physical appearance
note: Observers rated targets based on full-body photographs. The researchers compared their snap judgments with a narcissism questionnaire and examined visible cues such as dress and grooming.

headline: Can people spot dark personality traits in composite faces with neutral expressions?
title: Facing a psychopath: Detecting the dark triad from emotionally-neutral faces, using prototypes from the Personality Faceaurus
note: The researchers blended photos of targets selected for high or low trait scores into prototype faces. Observers judged the composites, allowing a comparison of group prototypes under an artificial task.

headline: Do people with darker personality scores gain more attractiveness from clothes and styling?
title: People With Dark Personalities Tend to Create a Physically Attractive Veneer
note: The authors compared attractiveness ratings of participants photographed with and without their usual adornment. They related the rating difference to a combined questionnaire index of dark personality traits.

headline: Are taller men less jealous, and is average height different for women?
title: Height predicts jealousy differently for men and women
note: The researchers fit different relationships between height and reported jealousy for men and women. The study treated the patterns as consistent with a theory linking stature to competition for partners.

headline: Can an email address give away your personality?
title: How extraverted is honey.bunny77@hotmail.de? Inferring personality from e-mail addresses
note: Observers rated personality using only email addresses. Researchers compared the consensus of these impressions with owners’ trait measures and examined which address cues raters used.

headline: Does how you take a selfie give away your Big Five scores?
title: What does your selfie say about you?
note: The researchers coded features of selfies and compared them with the photographers’ Big Five scores and observers’ impressions. Associations between photo cues and scores were treated as personality signals.

headline: Do people with higher narcissism scores post more selfies?
title: #Me: Narcissism and its facets as predictors of selfie-posting frequency
note: The authors related self-reported selfie-posting frequency to questionnaire subscales of narcissism. Associations varied across facets of narcissism.

headline: Can a Facebook profile give away how narcissistic its owner is?
title: Narcissism and Social Networking Web Sites
note: The study compared questionnaire scores with profile features such as social activity and profile photos, and with impressions from independent viewers.

headline: Do Facebook pages show the owner’s personality or the person they wish they were?
title: Facebook Profiles Reflect Actual Personality, Not Self-Idealization
note: The researchers compared impressions formed from profiles with measures of actual and ideal personality. Correlations with actual personality measures drove the interpretation of the profiles as authentic.

headline: Does your taste in music point to how empathic you score?
title: Musical Preferences are Linked to Cognitive Styles
note: The studies compared preferences for musical excerpts and attributes with questionnaire measures of empathizing and systemizing. The authors interpreted different preference patterns as signatures of cognitive style.

headline: Do music tastes sort listeners into personality profiles?
title: The Do Re Mi’s of Everyday Life: The Structure and Personality Correlates of Music Preferences
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors extracted four music-preference dimensions and related them to questionnaires about personality and self-views. They interpreted the resulting groupings as a psychological structure of taste.

headline: Do self-identified dog people and cat people have different Big Five profiles?
title: Personalities of Self-Identified “Dog People” and “Cat People”
note: An online survey grouped respondents by whether they called themselves dog people, cat people, both or neither. The study compared Big Five averages between those groups.

headline: Does liking spicy food give away how much you seek thrills?
title: Personality factors predict spicy food liking and intake
note: The authors compared personality measures with liking for capsaicin-containing samples and reported spicy-food intake. Sensation seeking was among the measures related to spicy-food liking.

headline: Do night owls score higher on dark personality traits?
title: Creatures of the night: Chronotypes and the Dark Triad traits
note: Questionnaire measures of morningness and eveningness were compared with measures of narcissism, Machiavellianism and psychopathy. The authors interpreted the associations in terms of an evening niche.

headline: Do the bacteria in a stool sample track how sociable someone is?
title: Gut microbiome composition and diversity are related to human personality traits
note: The study compared gut microbiome profiles with questionnaire measures. It linked reported sociability to community diversity and to the abundance of particular bacterial groups in the sample.

headline: Can a blood inflammation marker track how conscientious you are?
title: High Neuroticism and Low Conscientiousness Are Associated with Interleukin-6
note: The researchers related circulating interleukin-6 to personality questionnaire scores. The reported associations concerned higher neuroticism and lower conscientiousness among participants.

headline: Are middle children really more agreeable and modest?
title: Personality differences between birth order categories and across sibship sizes
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Across large online samples, self-reported agreeableness and honesty–humility differed by birth-order category and number of siblings. The authors also examined the effect of holding sibship size fixed.

headline: Can having been breastfed show up in an adult personality questionnaire?
title: Breastfeeding and Adult Personality
note: The researchers compared early caregiver reports of breastfeeding with later adult personality and well-being measures in a longitudinal cohort. They adjusted for selected early-life and demographic variables.

headline: Can a personality questionnaire tell how fast you’ll walk years later?
title: Personality and Walking Speed Across Adulthood: Prospective Evidence From Five Samples
note: Across five cohorts, the researchers related personality measurements to gait speed in adulthood. The timing and measurements varied by cohort, and some analyses examined change in speed.

headline: Does sharing money in lab games reveal a stable cooperative personality?
title: Humans display a ‘cooperative phenotype’ that is domain general and temporally stable
note: The study compared decisions across economic games and later sessions. It interpreted correlations among cooperation, generosity and trust-related choices as evidence of a stable cooperative phenotype.

headline: Can an honesty questionnaire tell who will cheat when they think someone is watching?
title: On the impact of Honesty-Humility and a cue of being watched on cheating behavior
note: The authors compared a HEXACO honesty–humility score and a cue of being watched with opportunities to misreport a payoff-relevant outcome. The behavior was measured in an experimental cheating task.

headline: Do observers see a more extraverted personality after you’ve been drinking?
title: An Experimental Investigation of Drunk Personality Using Self and Observer Reports
note: Participants rated perceived personality changes and observers judged behaviors in group interactions. Extraversion was the clearest observer-rated difference following alcohol administration, while self-reports suggested broader changes.

headline: Can questionnaire scores sort drinkers into Hemingways, Mary Poppinses and Mr. Hydes?
title: Searching for Mr. Hyde: A five-factor approach to characterizing “types of drunks”
note: The authors clustered sober and intoxicated personality reports from college drinkers. They interpreted the clusters as types of drunks and gave them names drawn from popular culture.

headline: Does the season you were born in track how much novelty you seek?
title: The Temperament Scale of Novelty Seeking in adolescents shows an association with season of birth opposite to that in adults
note: The authors compared adolescent novelty-seeking scores across birth seasons. The association differed in direction from a previously reported adult result.

headline: Can two finger lengths tell you anything about the Big Five?
title: Second to fourth digit ratio and the ‘big five’ personality factors
note: The authors correlated measured digit ratios with Big Five questionnaire scores and reported sex-specific links. The ratio was treated as an indirect indicator in a developmental interpretation.

headline: Can the width of a man’s face give away whether he’ll keep the money?
title: Valid facial cues to cooperation and trust: Male facial width and trustworthiness
note: The authors related face proportions to both observers’ trust decisions and the photographed men’s choices in a laboratory game. The behavioral criterion was cooperation in the game.

headline: Can a smile’s timing predict what a partner will do with your money?
title: Facial dynamics as indicators of trustworthiness and cooperative behavior
note: The researchers varied timing features of animated smiles, then measured ratings and decisions in a trust game. The measures capture responses to manipulated displays in that game.

headline: Can a few inner facial features give away a personality questionnaire score?
title: Internal facial features are signals of personality and health
note: Observers judged faces formed from people grouped by their questionnaire scores. The accuracy comparisons concerned selected or composite stimuli and the authors’ grouping criteria.

headline: Can a stranger get your personality right from a photograph alone?
title: Can you judge a book by its cover? Evidence of self–stranger agreement on personality at zero acquaintance
note: The authors compared observers’ personality ratings from photographs with targets’ ratings of themselves. Agreement was defined as statistical correspondence between ratings.

headline: Can a few seconds of staged behavior give away personality and intelligence?
title: Thin slices of behavior as cues of personality and intelligence
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Observers judged short recordings of people doing different tasks. The authors linked aggregated impressions to personality reports and measured intelligence.

headline: Do men hear dominance in another man’s voice pitch?
title: Men’s voices as dominance signals: Vocal fundamental and formant frequencies influence dominance attributions among men
note: The authors examined how acoustic properties of men’s voices affected other men’s dominance ratings. The outcome was perceived dominance.

headline: Does changing a voice’s pitch change who sounds like they would cheat on a partner?
title: Voice pitch influences perceptions of sexual infidelity
note: Participants rated pitch-manipulated voices on perceived infidelity risk. The outcome was a judgment of likely infidelity from an altered recording.

headline: Can trustworthiness and dominance ratings fit on two axes of a face model?
title: The functional basis of face evaluation
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: The researchers reduced correlated ratings of faces to dimensions anchored by trustworthiness and dominance. They used statistical face models to manipulate those perceived dimensions.

headline: Do selfies give away Dark Triad scores in men?
title: The Dark Triad and trait self-objectification as predictors of men’s use and self-presentation behaviors on social networking sites
note: The authors related self-reports about online self-presentation, including selfie behavior, to questionnaire measures of dark traits and self-objectification.

headline: Does posting selfies give away narcissism differently for men and women?
title: Selfie posting behaviors are associated with narcissism among men
note: The authors compared types of selfie posting with narcissism scores across two samples. The reported associations varied by sex and type of selfie.

headline: Can posting a selfie tell you whether someone scored high on grandiose or vulnerable narcissism?
title: Personality and selfies: Narcissism and the Dark Triad
note: The authors related reported selfie behavior and motivations to personality inventories, including measures of grandiose and vulnerable narcissism.

headline: Does a Facebook questionnaire detect narcissism through friend collecting and attention seeking?
title: Narcissism on Facebook: Self-promotional and anti-social behavior
note: Self-reported Facebook behaviors were compared with narcissism subscales. The study connected different subscales with patterns such as self-promotion and responses to negative comments.

headline: Do decades of pop lyrics read like a society-wide personality test?
title: Tuning in to psychological change: Linguistic markers of psychological traits and emotions over time in popular U.S. song lyrics
venue: Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts
note: The authors tracked counts of pronouns and emotional words in popular songs over time. They interpreted lyrical changes as markers of broader cultural shifts in self-focus and emotion.

headline: Can counting the word I tell you who is narcissistic?
title: Narcissism and the use of personal pronouns revisited
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The team compared first-person singular pronoun use with several narcissism measures across data from five labs. It found essentially no overall relationship, providing a direct test of a common personality inference.

headline: Can counting I and me reveal a general tendency toward negative emotion?
title: Depression, negative emotionality, and self-referential language: A multi-lab, multi-measure, and multi-language-task research synthesis
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors combined original data from multiple labs and language tasks. They compared pronoun counts with measures of depression and negative emotionality and interpreted their overlap as a clue to what self-reference indexes.

headline: Do narcissism scores predict who looks like a better short-term date?
title: Are narcissists sexy? Zeroing in on the effect of narcissism on short-term mate appeal
note: The studies related questionnaire measures of narcissism to perceived short-term mate appeal. The authors examined perceived attractiveness and social boldness as explanations for the association.

headline: Why did strangers initially like people with higher narcissism scores?
title: Why are narcissists so charming at first sight? Decoding the narcissism-popularity link at zero acquaintance
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Participants rated fellow group members at an initial meeting. The authors related first-impression popularity to narcissism scores and considered observed appearance and behavior as intervening cues.

headline: Do strangers see self-esteem when the questionnaire says narcissism?
title: Misperceiving grandiose narcissism as self-esteem: Why narcissists are well liked at zero acquaintance
note: The authors compared observers’ first impressions with targets’ narcissism and self-esteem measures. They interpreted the association with liking as partly driven by impressions of high self-esteem.

headline: Can someone score high on narcissism, look like an effective leader and still make the team share less information?
title: Reality at odds with perceptions: Narcissistic leaders and group performance
note: The researchers related leaders’ narcissism scores to evaluations and to information exchange in a group decision task. Perceived effectiveness and the observed group process gave different results.

headline: Do people with higher narcissism scores end up leading groups of strangers?
title: Leader emergence: The case of the narcissistic leader
note: The authors examined associations between narcissism and who emerged as a leader in unassigned groups. They distinguished emergence from how well a group performed.

headline: Do job interviews reward a narcissist’s way of talking about themselves?
title: Self-presentation style in job interviews: The role of personality and culture
note: The authors compared interview self-presentation styles and evaluations with personality and cultural measures. The evaluation involved interview performances and how observers rated them.

headline: Can a made-up dating profile with Dark Triad traits look more attractive?
title: The Dark Triad personality: Attractiveness to women
note: Women rated constructed male character descriptions that varied Dark Triad characteristics. Differences in responses concerned the selected profiles.

headline: Do Dark Triad scores go with a short-term mating strategy?
title: The dark triad: Facilitating a short-term mating strategy in men
note: The authors related Dark Triad questionnaires to self-reported mating orientation and behavior. They interpreted the correlations in terms of a short-term strategy.

headline: Can twelve questions sort out narcissism, psychopathy and Machiavellianism?
title: The Dirty Dozen: A concise measure of the Dark Triad
note: The authors reduced three personality constructs to 12 items and evaluated their correspondence with longer inventories and other measures.

headline: Can three overlapping questionnaires define a Dark Triad?
title: The Dark Triad of personality: Narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathy
note: The original study compared three personality inventories and linked them to self-enhancement and other traits. It treated patterns of overlap and divergence as evidence for three related constructs.

headline: Does military training make young men less agreeable years later?
title: Military Training and Personality Trait Development: Does the Military Make the Man, or Does the Man Make the Military?
note: The authors compared personality trajectories for young men entering military versus civilian service. They distinguished measured differences before service from trajectories after it.

headline: Does feeling younger than your birth certificate predict personality changes?
title: Subjective age and personality development: A 10-year study
note: The authors related how old participants felt to later change in questionnaire traits using longitudinal data.

headline: Do agreeable people earn less money?
title: Do nice guys—and gals—really finish last? The joint effects of sex and agreeableness on income
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The researchers modeled income together with agreeableness and sex across samples. They also used an experiment on hypothetical employee evaluations to explore a possible explanation.

headline: Do wealthy people score higher on entitlement and narcissism?
title: Wealth and the inflated self: Class, entitlement, and narcissism
note: The authors related social-class measures to entitlement and narcissism measures and examined responses to a manipulation emphasizing egalitarian values.

headline: Can a personality questionnaire predict how many children someone has?
title: Personality and reproductive success in a high-fertility human population
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: The authors related measures of extraversion and neuroticism to reproductive measures in rural Senegal. They interpreted sex-specific associations in terms of potential reproductive trade-offs.

headline: Can an activity or conscientiousness score predict who lives longer?
title: Personality predictors of longevity: Activity, emotional stability, and conscientiousness
note: The authors related personality measures to subsequent mortality using longitudinal survival models. The predictor was questionnaire score and the outcome was observed survival.

headline: Do happy people become more agreeable or conscientious over time?
title: Is happiness good for your personality? Concurrent and prospective relations of the Big Five with subjective well-being
note: The authors compared repeated personality and well-being measures and estimated prospective relationships in both directions.

headline: Can the version of a snack you leave for someone else measure social mindfulness?
title: Social mindfulness: Skill and will to navigate the social world
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The researchers scored whether participants left options for another chooser when selecting among objects. They related the task measure to personality and prosocial measures.

headline: Can a trait questionnaire tell which kind of generosity you show in bargaining games?
title: Pillars of cooperation: Honesty–Humility, social value orientations, and economic behavior
note: The authors compared questionnaire measures and social-value orientations with allocations in economic games and interpreted differences in bargaining behavior using trait scores.

headline: When nobody can check the answer, does a questionnaire say who will cheat?
title: When the cat’s away, some mice will play: A basic trait account of dishonest behavior
note: The authors related honesty–humility to reports of privately observed payoff outcomes under different incentives. The task measures behavior under a particular elicitation format.

headline: Can an insult and a narcissism survey predict how loud a noise blast someone chooses?
title: Threatened egotism, narcissism, self-esteem, and direct and displaced aggression: Does self-love or self-hate lead to violence?
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors compared questionnaire scores and reactions to insults or praise in an experiment using a laboratory aggression task. They interpreted selected noise levels as aggression.

headline: Do people with lower self-esteem scores show more aggression?
title: Low self-esteem is related to aggression, antisocial behavior, and delinquency
note: The studies related self-esteem measures to different aggression and antisocial-behavior indicators across samples, including reports from others.

headline: Can differences in self-esteem explain why kids become more materialistic at certain ages?
title: Growing up in a Material World: Age Differences in Materialism in Children and Adolescents
note: The authors compared materialism scores across ages and studied how self-esteem related to the age pattern. One study also experimentally manipulated self-esteem.

headline: Can waiting for a treat in preschool predict adolescent self-control?
title: Predicting adolescent cognitive and self-regulatory competencies from preschool delay of gratification: Identifying diagnostic conditions
note: The study related preschool waiting times under different experimental conditions to later competence measures. The reported predictive relationships depended on the waiting conditions.

headline: Does a beard make a man look more aggressive when he’s angry?
title: Beards augment perceptions of men’s age, social status, and aggressiveness, but not attractiveness
note: The researchers compared ratings of photos with and without beards. Aggressiveness and status were attributed by observers rather than measured as individual traits.

headline: Does a childhood personality rating follow you all the way to the grave?
title: Does childhood personality predict longevity?
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors related childhood personality ratings in a historical cohort to recorded longevity. Associations with conscientiousness and other traits were estimated using survival data.

headline: Does a fuller face signal that someone is dominant?
title: In the face of dominance: Self-perceived and other-perceived dominance are positively associated with facial-width-to-height ratio in men
note: The authors compared facial proportions to ratings of dominance and to measures supplied by targets. The paper distinguishes perceptions from self-report.

headline: Can a fragment of a stranger’s voice or face give you accurate personality impressions?
title: Accuracy in social perception: Contributions of facial and vocal information
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors compared personality impressions across stimulus channels and related them to target personality measures, distinguishing agreement among judges from accuracy criteria.

headline: What happens when strangers try to spot who can be trusted just from a face?
title: Accuracy and consensus in judgments of trustworthiness from faces: Behavioral and neural correlates
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The researchers compared agreement in facial trustworthiness ratings with multiple criteria. The study tested the statistical distinction between impressions that observers share and impressions that match the criteria.

headline: Does a smile rated as genuine make people trust you with more money?
title: Honest signaling in trust interactions: Smiles rated as genuine induce trust and signal higher earning opportunities
note: The authors related perceived smile genuineness to monetary stakes, receiver decisions, and previous choices in a trust game. They interpreted the associations through a costly-signaling account.

headline: Does sharing initials make people produce better group work?
title: The Name-Letter-Effect in Groups: Sharing Initials with Group Members Increases the Quality of Group Work
note: The studies related naturally occurring overlap in initials to group performance and used collective efficacy to explain the reported pattern.

headline: Does feeling powerful make you think you can control a dice roll?
title: Illusory control: A generative force behind power's far-reaching effects
note: After a power manipulation, participants chose whether to roll a die themselves or let someone else do it. The authors treated the choice as an indicator of illusory control.

headline: Does seeing the letter A before a test boost your score?
title: A versus F: The effects of implicit letter priming on cognitive performance
note: The authors compared test performance after exposure to an A or F cue. A later attempt did not replicate the effect (https://doi.org/10.2466/04.03.PR0.112.2.533-544).

headline: Can thinking about chicken soup make you feel less lonely?
title: Chicken Soup Really Is Good for the Soul: “Comfort Food” Fulfills the Need to Belong
note: One experiment used chicken noodle soup and measured accessibility of relationship words. Another used writing about comfort food and measured loneliness. Follow-up attempts did not confirm the overall loneliness result across three countries (https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.00314).

headline: Can seeing money make people enjoy chocolate less?
title: Money Giveth, Money Taketh Away: The Dual Effect of Wealth on Happiness
note: After a money cue or control, the researchers timed chocolate eating and coded visible enjoyment. They treated these outcomes as measures of savoring.

headline: Can three dots arranged like a face make people share more?
title: Minimal social cues in the dictator game
note: Participants saw three dots in different configurations. The authors interpreted differences in allocation-game transfers as an effect of a minimal social cue.

headline: Can riding a roller coaster make another person look more attractive?
title: Love at First Fright: Partner Salience Moderates Roller-Coaster-Induced Excitation Transfer
note: Researchers compared photo ratings from people waiting to ride or just getting off. The reported result varied with whether a romantic partner was present.

headline: Does thinking about romance make people score higher on a creativity task?
title: Peacocks, Picasso, and parental investment: The effects of romantic motives on creativity
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Experiments used romantic-motive prompts and compared rated creative output. The authors interpreted conditional results as evidence of courtship display.

headline: Are people less likely to help right after using a cash machine?
title: Behavioral consequences of money: When the automated teller machine reduces helping behavior
note: The two field studies compared passersby who had just handled money at an ATM with passersby who had not. Helping meant agreeing to a survey or alerting someone that she had dropped an item.

headline: Does recalling a time you had power make an interviewer want to hire you?
title: Power gets the job: Priming power improves interview outcomes
note: Participants recalled high or low power before writing an application or attending a mock interview. The main outcomes were evaluations by raters or interviewers.

headline: Do some men look unfaithful in a photo?
title: Sexual unfaithfulness can be judged with some accuracy from men's but not women's faces
note: The authors compared strangers’ ratings of face photographs with targets’ self-reported sexual behavior. Accuracy was assessed statistically across faces.

headline: Can your favorite TV show temporarily substitute for belonging?
title: Social surrogacy: How favored television programs provide the experience of belonging
note: Several studies used favorite programs or recalled experiences and measured feelings of belonging or responses to social threats.

headline: Can thinking about your favorite show restore self-control?
title: Energized by Television: Familiar Fictional Worlds Restore Self-Control
note: The authors used diary data and a laboratory experiment to link familiar fictional worlds with later measures of self-control.

headline: Does social rejection make people choose different brands?
title: Social Exclusion and Consumer Switching Behavior: A Control Restoration Mechanism
note: Across experiments, the authors compared choices to switch products or brands after exclusion and interpreted the shift as an attempt to restore control.

headline: Does being left out make brands with human features more appealing?
title: The effect of social exclusion on consumer preference for anthropomorphized brands
note: The researchers manipulated exclusion and compared preferences for brands with and without humanlike features.

headline: Does being excluded make people buy things that might get them accepted?
title: Social Exclusion Causes People to Spend and Consume Strategically in the Service of Affiliation
note: The authors compared choices after social exclusion, including spending and consuming to match people with whom participants expected to interact.

headline: Can being told you will end up alone lower your reasoning score?
title: Effects of social exclusion on cognitive processes: Anticipated aloneness reduces intelligent thought
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: Participants received forecasts about their future social lives before cognitive tests. The authors interpreted differences in reasoning performance as a consequence of anticipated exclusion.

headline: Does a message predicting loneliness make people give someone louder noise blasts?
title: If you can't join them, beat them: Effects of social exclusion on aggressive behavior
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The studies used laboratory aggression outcomes, including noise blasts, after social exclusion manipulations.

headline: Does social exclusion make you describe your own personality differently?
title: Ostracism negatively impacts working self-perceptions of personality
note: The authors compared immediate self-ratings under ostracism and control conditions. The inference concerns working perceptions of one's traits.

headline: Does making an object unpredictable make it seem more like it has a mind?
title: Making sense by making sentient: Effectance motivation increases anthropomorphism
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The studies manipulated predictability or motivation to understand an entity and compared humanlike attributions.

headline: Can feeling powerful make the day seem less rushed?
title: The power to control time: Power influences how much time (you think) you have
note: The studies related manipulations or measures of power to reports of available time. The interpretation concerned perceived time pressure.

headline: Does feeling powerful make people overestimate how much they know?
title: Power and overconfident decision-making
venue: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
note: The researchers compared confidence and accuracy under different power conditions. They connected miscalibrated estimates to overconfident choices.

headline: Does feeling powerful make people rely more on an arbitrary number?
title: Power Increases Anchoring Effects on Judgment
note: The experiment compared how power conditions changed the influence of anchor values on judgments.

headline: Are people higher in a workplace hierarchy more likely to report affairs?
title: Power increases infidelity among men and women
note: The authors modeled self-reports of professional power, confidence, infidelity and intentions. They interpreted confidence as a mediator.

headline: Does feeling powerful make people prefer others who are useful to them?
title: Power and the objectification of social targets
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The studies examined whether people in a position of power attended to or chose social targets based on their usefulness for a goal.

headline: Does recalling power change a motor response while watching another person act?
title: Power changes how the brain responds to others
note: The researchers primed power and measured motor-evoked responses during action observation. They interpreted differences as altered motor resonance.

headline: Can the same feeling of power make people cheat more or less depending on what they just thought about?
title: Power can increase but also decrease cheating depending on what thoughts are validated
note: The authors varied power and thoughts related to honesty or dishonesty and tested for interactions on laboratory cheating measures.

headline: Does power make people want more distance while feeling closer?
title: Psychological power increases the desire for social distance but reduces the sense of social distance
note: The authors separated desired social distance from perceived distance and reported opposite patterns across those measures.

headline: Does writing about your own virtues make you pledge less to charity?
title: Sinning Saints and Saintly Sinners: The Paradox of Moral Self-Regulation
note: The researchers varied whether participants wrote about virtue or vice. Their interpretation drew on donation pledges and choices in hypothetical scenarios.

headline: Can expecting to do a good deed later change what you feel entitled to do now?
title: Prospective moral licensing: Does anticipating doing good later allow you to be bad now?
note: Studies compared subsequent judgments or choices after participants expected different opportunities to do good.

headline: Can endorsing Obama make people later favor a White job candidate?
title: Endorsing Obama licenses favoring Whites
note: The experiments used an endorsement manipulation and hypothetical allocation or personnel choices. The authors interpreted the responses as moral licensing.

headline: Can choosing a good deed give you permission to pick a luxury item?
title: Licensing Effect in Consumer Choice
note: After a virtuous choice or commitment, the experiments compared choices between relatively indulgent and practical options.

headline: Does a Red Bull logo on a virtual car change how people race?
title: Red Bull “Gives You Wings” for better or worse: A double-edged impact of brand exposure on consumer performance
note: Participants drove cars displaying different brands in a racing game. The authors compared driving performance and behavior.

headline: Can a fleeting failure cue lower a cognitive test score?
title: Failure cue priming and impaired cognitive performance—analyses of avoidance motivation as a mediator and fear of failure as a moderator
note: The researchers compared performance following a failure prime and modeled fear of failure and avoidance motivation.

headline: Can reading about another person’s goal make you pursue it yourself?
title: Goal contagion: Perceiving is for pursuing
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors used scenarios about another person’s behavior and inferred adoption of a goal from subsequent task behavior.

headline: Can words about old age make young adults walk more slowly?
title: Nonconscious priming of elderly or youthful stereotypes influences walking velocity in healthy undergraduates
note: The researchers timed walking after different age-related primes and attributed differences to stereotype activation.

headline: Can a photo that suggests achievement make workers more productive?
title: An exploratory field experiment of the effect of subconscious and conscious goals on employee performance
venue: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
note: The authors manipulated a visual achievement cue and explicit goals in a workplace task and compared performance.

headline: Can a picture of eyes make people donate more money at a bar?
title: Effects of Eye Images and Norm Cues on Charitable Donation: A Field Experiment in an Izakaya
note: The field experiment varied eye images and descriptive norms and measured donations at a Japanese pub.

headline: Does a picture of watching eyes make people give more in a covert donation task?
title: Effects of watching eyes and norm cues on charitable giving in a surreptitious behavioral experiment
note: The study used a real-money task and compared donations under watching-eyes and norm-cue conditions.

headline: Do faces that look affluent also look more trustworthy?
title: Are Rich People Perceived as More Trustworthy? Perceived Socioeconomic Status Modulates Judgments of Trustworthiness and Trust Behavior Based on Facial Appearance
note: The experiments examined associations between perceived status, face-based trustworthiness ratings and decisions in a trust game.

headline: Do Britain's business leaders have measurably wider faces?
title: Increased facial width-to-height ratio and perceived dominance in the faces of the UK's leading business leaders
note: The authors compared photographs of business leaders and controls on facial ratios and observer judgments of dominance.

headline: Can a stranger’s face reveal the same signs of unfaithfulness across cultures?
title: Impressions of sexual unfaithfulness and their accuracy show a degree of universality
note: The authors related face ratings across cultural samples to reported sexual behavior and interpreted some cross-group results as evidence of shared cues.

headline: Can trustworthiness impressions from faces change how much money you send a stranger?
title: Friend or foe: The effect of implicit trustworthiness judgments in social decision-making
note: The experiments compared decisions with partners whose faces differed in perceived trustworthiness.

headline: Do people with fewer resources give away more in lab games?
title: Having less, giving more: The influence of social class on prosocial behavior
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The studies related class measures and manipulations to generosity and helping in several research tasks.

headline: Do people lower in social class score higher at reading other people’s emotions?
title: Social Class, Contextualism, and Empathic Accuracy
note: The experiments compared social class with emotion and empathic-accuracy measures and linked the pattern to attention to context.

headline: Does oxytocin change how close a partnered man stands to a woman he just met?
title: Oxytocin Modulates Social Distance between Males and Females
note: The authors compared preferred distance under oxytocin and placebo and reported different results for single and partnered men.

headline: Can oxytocin make people more envious and more likely to gloat?
title: Intranasal Administration of Oxytocin Increases Envy and Schadenfreude (Gloating)
note: In a competitive task, participants reported reactions to relative wins or losses following oxytocin or placebo.

headline: Can reported sensitivity to smells predict who reports having an affair?
title: The Scent of Monogamy: Self-Reported Olfactory Function Predicts Sexual Well-Being and Infidelity in an Italian Population
note: The paper modeled questionnaire responses about olfaction, relationships and infidelity. The signal comes from self-reports.

headline: Can having too many Facebook friends make you seem less socially attractive?
title: Too Much of a Good Thing? The Relationship Between Number of Friends and Interpersonal Impressions on Facebook
note: Participants rated mock profiles displaying different friend counts. The authors fit a curvilinear relationship to judgments of social attractiveness.

headline: Can matching letters in your name make a company sound like a better place to work?
title: Implicit letter preferences in job choice: An experimental test of the role of cognitive load
note: The authors manipulated cognitive load during a job-choice task with names designed to vary in letter overlap.

headline: Does your initial affect which everyday products you like?
title: Testing the generality of the name letter effect: Name initials and everyday attitudes
note: Experiments tested whether preference for the letters of one’s name extended to ratings of named everyday items.

headline: Does seeing your initial in a product name make you say you are more likely to buy it?
title: Name-Letter Branding under Scrutiny: Real Products, New Algorithms, and the Probability of Buying
note: Participants rated how likely they were to buy products. The authors adjusted the ratings for response tendencies and letter popularity.

headline: Does seeing another woman in red make her seem more like a romantic rival at certain cycle phases?
title: The Woman in Red: Examining the Effect of Ovulatory Cycle on Women's Perceptions of and Behaviors Toward Other Women
note: The authors examined associations between estimated cycle phase, target clothing color and ratings or responses toward other women.

headline: Can changing a background color make an objectionable behavior seem more acceptable?
title: When colors backfire: The impact of color cues on moral judgment
note: The authors used red or green and, in a separate experiment, colors conditioned to have different valences. They compared moral acceptability ratings for consumer behaviors.

headline: Does thinking about crisp banknotes make employees more helpful and creative?
title: When Money Makes Employees Warm and Bright: Thoughts of New Money Promote Warmth and Competence
note: The authors compared cues involving new versus used banknotes with measures including creative idea generation, concern for coworkers and helping.

headline: Does putting an hourly price on your time reduce volunteering?
title: The stingy hour: How accounting for time affects volunteering
note: The authors used surveys and experiments to link hourly accounting with reported or intended volunteering.

headline: Does thinking about time instead of money make people socialize more?
