title: The Pursuit of Happiness: Time, Money, and Social Connection
note: The studies primed time or money and compared subsequent intentions and behavior. The field study measured socializing and happiness in a café setting.

headline: Could stylized eyes make a participant give away more money?
title: Nobody’s watching? Subtle cues affect generosity in an anonymous economic game
note: The authors varied cues of observation in an anonymous allocation task and interpreted changes in generosity as reputational concern. Later meta-analyses found no overall increase in generosity (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.evolhumbehav.2016.07.001).

headline: Do watching eyes change whether you give anything, even if they do not change how much you give?
title: The watching eyes effect in the Dictator Game: It's not how much you give, it's being seen to give something
note: The paper distinguished the probability of making any donation from the size of transfers under observation cues.

headline: Do printed eyes on a piece of litter make people less likely to drop it?
title: Watching eyes on potential litter can reduce littering: evidence from two field experiments
note: The authors compared littering when flyers bore eye images or control imagery and examined whether the surroundings changed the effect.

headline: Can a picture of eyes make people lie less when the lie would help someone else?
title: The Watching-Eye Effect on Prosocial Lying
note: The experiment used die reports that could benefit another person. The conclusion came from comparing each condition’s reported distribution with a fair die distribution.

headline: Can wanting a date make men pick flashier purchases?
title: Blatant benevolence and conspicuous consumption: When romantic motives elicit strategic costly signals
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The studies used imagined mating scenarios and measured stated choices about consumption and public helping.

headline: Does seeing a man buy a Porsche make him look more interested in short-term dating?
title: Peacocks, Porsches, and Thorstein Veblen: Conspicuous consumption as a sexual signaling system
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The experiments linked mating motives with conspicuous spending choices and compared observers’ impressions of male consumers.

headline: Can the phrase “don’t be a cheater” change honesty more than “don’t cheat”?
title: When cheating would make you a cheater: Implicating the self prevents unethical behavior
note: The researchers varied whether instructions named an identity or an action and analyzed reported outcomes in tasks that allowed dishonest reporting.

headline: Do children help more after being called a helper?
title: “Helping” Versus “Being a Helper”: Invoking the Self to Increase Helping in Young Children
note: The experiment varied noun versus verb wording and counted children’s subsequent helping behavior.

headline: Are people more likely to misreport a die roll when they have to answer quickly?
title: Honesty requires time (and lack of justifications)
note: The study varied time pressure and opportunities for justification. Misreporting was inferred from the distribution of claimed rolls.

headline: Can a phone sitting nearby change the perceived quality of a conversation?
title: The iPhone Effect: The Quality of In-Person Social Interactions in the Presence of Mobile Devices
note: Observers recorded whether mobile devices were present, and participants rated conversation quality and empathy.

headline: Can a smile make the exact same promise sound more or less credible?
title: Face Value and Cheap Talk: How Smiles Can Increase or Decrease the Credibility of Our Words
note: The experiments examined the interaction of smiles and verbal messages on judgments or decisions involving trust.

headline: Do people who report feeling awe more often score higher on measures of scientific thinking?
title: Awe as a Scientific Emotion
note: Across six studies, the authors related dispositional awe to selected measures of scientific thinking, including understanding how science works and rejecting certain explanations based on purpose.

headline: Can watching something awe-inspiring make you more likely to see an invisible agent behind an event?
title: Awe, Uncertainty, and Agency Detection
note: The experiments induced awe and measured willingness to attribute events to agents, together with related beliefs and uncertainty.

headline: Can someone else’s ethical choice make you like that person less?
title: Do-Gooder Derogation: Disparaging Morally Motivated Minorities to Defuse Anticipated Reproach
note: The studies examined reactions to morally motivated others and tested anticipated moral reproach as an explanation.

headline: Do people drop a taste when it becomes associated with the wrong group?
title: Who drives divergence? Identity signaling, outgroup dissimilarity, and the abandonment of cultural tastes
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
note: The authors examined whether people abandon preferences associated with groups they see as dissimilar, with particular emphasis on identity-relevant choices.
